title: 1 Synesis: Language Reference Guide
text:
PROJECT project_name
    TEMPLATE "filename.synt"
    INCLUDE BIBLIOGRAPHY "filename.bib"
    INCLUDE ANNOTATIONS "annotations"
    INCLUDE ONTOLOGY "filename.syno"

    METADATA
        version: 1.0
        author: Research team
    END METADATA

    DESCRIPTION
    Free text describing the project.
    END DESCRIPTION

    QUESTIONS
        Q1: Which barriers are reported?
    END QUESTIONS

    EXPORT JSON
        OUTPUT "out/project.json"
    END EXPORT
END PROJECT



TEMPLATE name version: "1.0"

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quote
    OPTIONAL chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD quote TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Literal excerpt
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    RELATIONS
        ENABLES: condition that makes possible
    END RELATIONS
    GUIDELINES
        Filling instructions.
    END GUIDELINES
END FIELD



SOURCE @bibref
END SOURCE

ITEM @bibref
    quote: Excerpt from the source
    chain: A -> ENABLES -> B
END ITEM



ONTOLOGY concept_name
    description: Definition of the concept
END ONTOLOGY

title: Language Grammar
text:
Who is this document for?



Developers who need to understand, extend or debug the Synesis syntax. The grammar below is the canonical specification — the compiler runs it literally. If the compiler accepts or rejects something at the syntax level, the answer is here. This page follows the file synesis/grammar/synesis.lark of synesis 0.16.0.
For the whole compilation flow (not only the grammar), see Inside the Compiler.

title: Language Grammar
text:
1 How to Read This Document
The grammar uses the Lark EBNF format:







Syntax
Meaning




rule: A B C
rule is A, then B, then C, in that order


A \| B
A or B (alternative)


A*
Zero or more repetitions of A


A+
One or more repetitions of A


A?
A is optional (zero or one)


"text"
Exact literal


/regex/
Regex pattern


/regex/i
Case-insensitive regex


TOKEN.N
Token with priority N (higher wins in case of ambiguity)


_INDENT / _DEDENT
Indentation tokens generated automatically



Lowercase rules (project_block) are grammar rules — they produce nodes in the syntax tree. UPPERCASE rules (IDENTIFIER) are tokens — atomic units recognized by the lexer.






Permissive grammar, strict semantics



Several restrictions of the language are not in the grammar but in the semantic validator. This is deliberate: a grammar error is an “unexpected token”; a semantic error explains what to do. A grammar error teaches nothing; a semantic error does.

title: Language Grammar
text:
2 Starting Point
Every compilation starts here. The start rule accepts a sequence of blocks separated by blank lines:
start: (block | NEWLINE)* block (block | NEWLINE)*

block: project_block
     | source_block
     | item_block
     | ontology_block
     | template_header
     | field_spec_block
     | field_def_block
A Synesis file is a list of blocks. Which blocks make sense depends on the file type:

.synp holds a project_block
.syn holds source_block and item_block
.syno holds ontology_block
.synt holds template_header, field_spec_block and field_def_block

The grammar accepts any combination; the semantic validator checks the context. An empty .syn or .syno, or one with comments only, is handled before the parser and declares no block.

title: Language Grammar
text:
3 Keywords
All keywords are case-insensitive — PROJECT, project and Project are equivalent:
KW_PROJECT.5: /project/i
KW_SOURCE.5: /source/i
KW_ITEM.5: /item/i
KW_ONTOLOGY.5: /ontology/i
KW_TEMPLATE.5: /template/i
KW_FIELD.5: /field/i
KW_END.5: /end/i
KW_INCLUDE.5: /include/i
KW_SHARED.5: /shared(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_BIBLIOGRAPHY.5: /bibliography/i
KW_ANNOTATIONS.5: /annotations/i
KW_FIELDS.5: /fields/i
KW_REQUIRED.5: /required/i
KW_OPTIONAL.5: /optional/i
KW_FORBIDDEN.5: /forbidden/i
KW_BUNDLE.5: /bundle/i
KW_TYPE.5: /type/i
KW_SCOPE.5: /scope/i
KW_FORMAT.5: /format/i
KW_DESCRIPTION.5: /description(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_ARITY.5: /arity/i
KW_VALUES.5: /values/i
KW_RELATIONS.5: /relations/i
KW_METADATA.5: /metadata/i
KW_QUOTATION.5: /quotation(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_MEMO.5: /memo(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_CODE.5: /code(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_CHAIN.5: /chain(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_TEXT.5: /text(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_DATE.5: /date(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_SCALE.5: /scale(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_ENUMERATED.5: /enumerated(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_ORDERED.5: /ordered(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_TOPIC.5: /topic(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_GUIDELINES.5: /guidelines/i

// .synp blocks
KW_EXPORT.5: /export(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_MAP.5: /map(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_QUESTIONS.5: /questions(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_PHASE.5: /phase(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i

// FIELD properties and value origin
KW_ROLE.5: /role(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_IDENTIFIES.5: /identifies(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_REFERS.5: /refers(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_TO.5: /to(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_ON.5: /on(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_DATASET.5: /dataset(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_CONTEXT.5: /context(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
KW_FROM.5: /from(?![\p{L}\p{N}_-])/i
Priority .5 makes keywords win over IDENTIFIER and FIELD_NAME (priority .1). Without it, SOURCE would be read as a generic identifier.

3.1 Boundary Lookahead
The suffix (?![\p{L}\p{N}_-]) is a negative lookahead that stops a token from matching as a prefix of a longer name. Without it, the start of a field called code_quality would be consumed by the CODE keyword and the rest would become syntax garbage. This applies to type names and to short words: TO and ON would match inside total, to_do, on_hold or onset. With the lookahead, texto, chain_length, date_created and topic_area are field names.

title: Language Grammar
text:
4 PROJECT Block
project_block: KW_PROJECT IDENTIFIER NEWLINE project_body KW_END KW_PROJECT

project_body: _INDENT project_items _DEDENT
            | project_items

project_items: (include_stmt | metadata | description | questions
                | phase_block | export_block | NEWLINE)+
The body may be entirely indented or entirely at column 0.

4.1 TEMPLATE and INCLUDE
include_stmt: KW_TEMPLATE STRING NEWLINE
            | KW_INCLUDE include_type STRING NEWLINE
include_type: KW_SHARED? (KW_BIBLIOGRAPHY | KW_ANNOTATIONS | KW_ONTOLOGY | KW_DATASET)
PROJECT demo
    TEMPLATE "template.synt"
    INCLUDE BIBLIOGRAPHY "references.bib"
    INCLUDE ANNOTATIONS "annotations/"
    INCLUDE ONTOLOGY "ontology.syno"
    INCLUDE DATASET "records/*.toml"
    INCLUDE SHARED ONTOLOGY "../shared/vocabulary.syno"
END PROJECT
KW_SHARED? precedes any type, although it only applies to ONTOLOGY: INCLUDE SHARED BIBLIOGRAPHY parses and then receives error E084, with the explanation.


4.2 METADATA, DESCRIPTION and QUESTIONS
metadata: KW_METADATA NEWLINE _INDENT (metadata_line | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT KW_END KW_METADATA NEWLINE
metadata_line: TEXT_LINE NEWLINE

description: KW_DESCRIPTION NEWLINE description_lines KW_END KW_DESCRIPTION NEWLINE?
description_lines: (TEXT_LINE NEWLINE | NEWLINE)+

questions: KW_QUESTIONS NEWLINE _INDENT question_lines _DEDENT KW_END KW_QUESTIONS NEWLINE?
question_lines: (TEXT_LINE NEWLINE | NEWLINE)+
These are free-text blocks. Note the indentation difference: DESCRIPTION declares no _INDENT (its lines sit at the same level as the keyword), while METADATA and QUESTIONS require indented lines. The <id>: <text> form of questions is checked by the compiler (E091–E093).


4.3 PHASE and EXPORT
phase_block: KW_PHASE phase_scope IDENTIFIER NEWLINE _INDENT (export_prop | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT KW_END KW_PHASE NEWLINE?
phase_scope: KW_ANNOTATIONS | KW_ONTOLOGY

export_block: KW_EXPORT IDENTIFIER IDENTIFIER? NEWLINE _INDENT (map_stmt | export_prop | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT KW_END KW_EXPORT NEWLINE?
export_prop: (IDENTIFIER | KW_DESCRIPTION) TEXT_LINE NEWLINE

map_stmt: KW_MAP KW_RELATIONS? map_names (KW_FROM IDENTIFIER)? KW_TO map_target NEWLINE
map_names: field_key ("," field_key)*
map_target: IDENTIFIER+
The properties (OUTPUT, NAMESPACE, FIELDS, INPUT…) are ordinary words, and the EXPORT format is an identifier. The grammar does not change when a new property appears; the compiler checks them.

title: Language Grammar
text:
5 Annotation Blocks
source_block: KW_SOURCE BIBREF NEWLINE
              (_INDENT (field_entry | NEWLINE)* _DEDENT)?
              KW_END KW_SOURCE

item_block: KW_ITEM BIBREF NEWLINE
            (_INDENT (field_entry | NEWLINE)* _DEDENT)?
            KW_END KW_ITEM

ontology_block: KW_ONTOLOGY concept_name NEWLINE
                (_INDENT (field_entry | NEWLINE)* _DEDENT)?
                KW_END KW_ONTOLOGY

concept_name: CONCEPT_NAME

SOURCE and ITEM take a BIBREF (such as @smith2024).
ONTOLOGY takes a concept_name, which is more permissive (see Tokens).
The body is optional: empty blocks are syntactically valid, but the validator may reject them (E023).
Indentation (_INDENT/_DEDENT) delimits the body.

title: Language Grammar
text:
6 Fields and Values
field_entry: field_key ":" value NEWLINE continuation_block?
           | field_key ":" NEWLINE _INDENT text_block _DEDENT NEWLINE?
Two forms: a value on the same line (with optional continuation) or a value that starts on the next line, indented.

6.1 Field Keys
field_key: FIELD_NAME
         | KW_TOPIC | KW_DESCRIPTION | KW_CODE | KW_CHAIN
         | KW_TEXT | KW_MEMO | KW_QUOTATION | KW_DATE
         | KW_SCALE | KW_ENUMERATED | KW_ORDERED
Besides user-defined names (FIELD_NAME), type keywords can name fields — hence code:, chain: and description:.


6.2 Value Types
value: STRING
     | NUMBER TEXT_LINE
     | NUMBER
     | chain_expr
     | code_list
     | TEXT_LINE
Token priorities (.2, .3, .4) resolve ambiguities. The final interpretation of a value depends on the type declared in the template: a TEXT containing -> is still text.


6.3 Code Lists and Chain Expressions
code_list: CODE_ELEMENT ("," CODE_ELEMENT)*
chain_expr: CHAIN_ELEMENT ("->" CHAIN_ELEMENT)+
ITEM @smith2024
    code: Social_Cohesion, Collective_Action
    chain: Trust -> Cooperation -> Collective_Action
END ITEM


6.4 Multi-line Text
continuation_block: _INDENT text_block _DEDENT
text_block: TEXT_LINE (NEWLINE TEXT_LINE)* NEWLINE?
ITEM @smith2024
    note: Participant describes spontaneous collective action as a
        primary resilience mechanism, bypassing formal institutions.
        Suggests strong bonding social capital.
END ITEM
_INDENT and _DEDENT are generated by the SynesisIndenter, as in Python’s significant indentation. From synesis 0.16.0 on, continuation lines reach the value in full, also in code lists and chains.

title: Language Grammar
text:
7 TEMPLATE Block

7.1 Header
template_header: KW_TEMPLATE IDENTIFIER template_meta*
template_meta: IDENTIFIER ":" value
There is no NEWLINE in the rule: metadata goes on the same line as the name.


7.2 Fields by Scope
field_spec_block: scope_type KW_FIELDS NEWLINE _INDENT field_list _DEDENT
                  KW_END scope_type KW_FIELDS
scope_type: KW_SOURCE | KW_ITEM | KW_ONTOLOGY

field_list: (requirement_clause | NEWLINE)*
requirement_clause: KW_REQUIRED bundle_modifier? field_names
                  | KW_OPTIONAL bundle_modifier? field_names
                  | KW_FORBIDDEN field_names
                  | KW_REQUIRED field_key KW_ON KW_BIBLIOGRAPHY
                  | KW_OPTIONAL field_key KW_ON KW_BIBLIOGRAPHY
                  | KW_REQUIRED field_key KW_ON KW_DATASET STRING
                  | KW_OPTIONAL field_key KW_ON KW_DATASET STRING

bundle_modifier: KW_BUNDLE
field_names: field_key ("," field_key)*
The ON BIBLIOGRAPHY and ON DATASET alternatives use field_key (singular), not field_names. In a list, REQUIRED a, b ON BIBLIOGRAPHY would be ambiguous; the grammar removes the case.
SOURCE FIELDS
    REQUIRED lattes_id ON BIBLIOGRAPHY
    OPTIONAL region ON DATASET "interview.region"
END SOURCE FIELDS


7.3 Field Definition
field_def_block: KW_FIELD field_key KW_TYPE type_spec
                 (field_props | NEWLINE)*
                 (_INDENT (field_props | NEWLINE)* _DEDENT)?
                 KW_END KW_FIELD

type_spec: simple_type | KW_CHAIN | KW_ENUMERATED | KW_ORDERED | KW_TOPIC
simple_type: KW_QUOTATION | KW_MEMO | KW_CODE | KW_TEXT | KW_DATE | KW_SCALE

field_props: KW_SCOPE scope_type
           | KW_ROLE IDENTIFIER+
           | KW_FORMAT format_spec
           | KW_DESCRIPTION TEXT_LINE
           | KW_ARITY COMPARATOR NUMBER
           | KW_VALUES value_list KW_END KW_VALUES
           | KW_RELATIONS relation_list KW_END KW_RELATIONS
           | KW_IDENTIFIES entity_label
           | KW_REFERS KW_TO entity_label
           | KW_CONTEXT KW_FROM KW_DATASET dataset_paths
           | guidelines_block

entity_label: FIELD_NAME
dataset_paths: STRING ("," STRING)*
The grammar accepts any property on any type; the matrix is semantic:



Type
Required
Exclusive




CHAIN
ARITY
ARITY, RELATIONS


ORDERED
VALUES (with [N])
VALUES


ENUMERATED
VALUES (without [N])
VALUES


SCALE
FORMAT
FORMAT


others
—
—



DESCRIPTION, GUIDELINES and CONTEXT FROM DATASET apply to all. IDENTIFIES and REFERS TO only in SCOPE SOURCE (E078); ROLE only in SCOPE ONTOLOGY (E108). The role after ROLE is a sequence of ordinary words, checked against the compiler’s catalogue.


7.4 VALUES and RELATIONS
value_list: (value_entry | NEWLINE)+
          | NEWLINE _INDENT (value_entry | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT
          | _INDENT (value_entry | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT
value_entry: index_prefix? IDENTIFIER ":" TEXT_LINE
index_prefix: "[" NUMBER "]"

relation_list: (relation_entry | NEWLINE)+
             | NEWLINE _INDENT (relation_entry | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT
             | _INDENT (relation_entry | NEWLINE)+ _DEDENT
relation_entry: IDENTIFIER ":" TEXT_LINE
Each value is an IDENTIFIER (no spaces) followed by : and a description. The [N] prefix is required in ORDERED and forbidden in ENUMERATED (E087).


7.5 FORMAT and ARITY
format_spec: IDENTIFIER | scale_format
scale_format: "[" NUMBER ".." NUMBER "]"
FORMAT defines the range of a SCALE: [0..10], [1..5]. ARITY uses a comparator and an integer: >= 2, = 3, < 5.


7.6 GUIDELINES Block
guidelines_block: KW_GUIDELINES NEWLINE guidelines_lines KW_END KW_GUIDELINES
guidelines_lines: (_INDENT | _DEDENT | guideline_line | NEWLINE)*
guideline_line: guideline_token+ NEWLINE
guideline_token: TEXT_LINE | IDENTIFIER | FIELD_NAME | BIBREF | STRING | NUMBER | COMPARATOR
               | KW_PROJECT | KW_SOURCE | KW_ITEM | ... | KW_GUIDELINES
               | COLON | "," | "->"
It is prose inside a FIELD, so it accepts almost any token. The text is reassembled from the original tokens, with the spelling of the file.






Avoid starting a GUIDELINES line with a keyword



Words such as Include, Item, Source, Field or End at the start of a line can confuse the reading. Rephrase (“To include…” → “Add…”). # inside GUIDELINES is not a comment: the line goes to the model.

title: Language Grammar
text:
8 Tokens

8.1 Identifiers and References
BIBREF: "@" /[a-zA-Z0-9][a-zA-Z0-9_-]*/

IDENTIFIER.1: /[\p{L}_][\p{L}\p{N}_\-]*/u

FIELD_NAME.1: /(?![eE][nN][dD]\b)[\p{L}_][\p{L}\p{N}_\-]*/u

CONCEPT_NAME.0: /[^\s#\n\r][^#\n\r]*/u








Token
Accepts
Example




BIBREF
@ + letter or digit + alphanumerics/_/-
@smith2024, @WHO-2023, @001


IDENTIFIER
letter/_ + alphanumerics/_/-
demo, Social_Cohesion


FIELD_NAME
as IDENTIFIER, except END
code, citation


CONCEPT_NAME
any text up to # or end of line
Social_Cohesion









FIELD_NAME vs END



The negative lookahead (?![eE][nN][dD]\b) stops END from being read as a field name; without it, END ITEM would be a field called END.








CONCEPT_NAME and spaces



The grammar accepts spaces in the name of an ONTOLOGY block, but a concept with spaces cannot be cited in chains (E015) or used as a code (E033). Use _.




8.2 Code and Chain Elements
CHAIN_ELEMENT.2: /[\p{L}_](?:(?!->)[\p{L}\p{N}_\- ])*/u
CODE_ELEMENT.2: /[\p{L}_](?:(?!,)[\p{L}\p{N}_\- ])*/u
Both capture inner spaces and stop before their delimiter (-> or ,). Capturing the space lets the validator explain the error instead of the parser failing.


8.3 Values and Text
STRING: /"[^"]*"/
NUMBER.4: /[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?/
COMPARATOR: ">=" | "<=" | "=" | ">" | "<"
TEXT_LINE.3: /[^\s\n\r:][^\n\r]*/



Token
Accepts
Priority




STRING
text in double quotes
—


NUMBER
integer or decimal
.4


COMPARATOR
comparison operators
—


TEXT_LINE
text not starting with a space or :
.3



TEXT_LINE captures whatever more specific tokens do not. It allows scientific symbols (n=2383, p<0.05).


8.4 Special Tokens
COMMENT: "#" /[^\n]*/
NEWLINE: /(\r?\n[ \t]*)+/
%declare _INDENT _DEDENT
%ignore /[ \t]+/
%ignore COMMENT

Comments (#) are ignored by the parser, except inside GUIDELINES.
NEWLINE captures the line break and the following indentation, which feeds the SynesisIndenter.
Spaces and tabs outside that context are ignored.

title: Language Grammar
text:
9 Priorities — How Ambiguities Are Resolved








Token
Priority
Why




Keywords (KW_*)
.5
win over identifiers


NUMBER
.4
42 is a number, not text


TEXT_LINE
.3
generic text


CHAIN_ELEMENT, CODE_ELEMENT
.2
win over IDENTIFIER in values


IDENTIFIER, FIELD_NAME
.1
base for names


CONCEPT_NAME
.0
only when nothing else fits

title: Language Grammar
text:
10 Significant Indentation
Like Python, Synesis uses significant indentation. The SynesisIndenter processes the lines and emits _INDENT and _DEDENT:

Tabs are converted to 4 spaces
More indentation than the previous line → _INDENT
Less indentation → _DEDENT
Same indentation → nothing

project_body: _INDENT project_items _DEDENT
source_block: KW_SOURCE BIBREF NEWLINE (_INDENT ... _DEDENT)? KW_END KW_SOURCE






Inconsistent indentation



Closing a block at a column that matches no open level produces a syntax error with an approximate position. Avoid mixing tabs and spaces.

title: Language Grammar
text:
11 The Generated Parser
In production the compiler uses synesis_standalone.py, an LALR parser pre-generated from the .lark file (faster start-up, same grammar). Whoever changes the grammar must regenerate that file; tests compare the two.

title: Synesis
text:
Human knowledge is naturally intricate, full of nuances and deep connections. That complexity is valuable; complication arises when we lack adequate methods for organizing what we know. Synesis is a declarative domain-specific language (DSL) created for those who need more than simple notes: it provides methods of knowledge consolidation.
Synesis acts as a compiler for analytical thinking. It receives interpretations and annotations in plain text files, validates their logical consistency and turns them into canonical, rigorous structures, organized according to objectives defined in advance by the user.
By delegating logical organization to a canonical structure, Synesis shows that discipline is a form of freedom. With the structure secured, the mind stays free for what truly matters: interpretation, nuance and insight. This is possible thanks to its level of abstraction, which sets minimal structural principles — sources, meaningful excerpts and conceptual organization.
This foundation gives a high degree of flexibility, allowing it to be applied to established methodologies or to custom approaches.


Consider knowledge recorded in books, articles, web pages, interviews or analysis records. All of it can be structured in three fundamental blocks:

Sources (Block 1): The origin of the information. It may be a scientific article, a website, an interview or an original idea written in your notebook.
Items (Block 2): The meaningful excerpt taken from the source. It is the equivalent of highlighting a passage in a book. Margin notes, keywords or codes assigned to these passages express their applied meaning and make thematic retrieval easier.
Ontology (Block 3): The way items are organized into conceptual domains. In Computer Science the term refers to the formal categorization of data into sets of knowledge. This structure may evolve over time: it can start simple and fluid, stimulating discovery and creativity, or become more stable, ensuring rigour and consistency.




In short, knowledge is organized into groups containing relevant passages (items), identified by codes and keywords, and extracted from references (sources). Synesis lets you structure and restructure these annotations continuously. As knowledge matures, its ontology can be refined, expanded or reorganized without compromising the structural integrity of the whole.
This approach ranges from tacit knowledge externalized as text, hypotheses and provisional ideas to consolidated analyses. Comments, time records, versioning and explicit semantic relations can be added to items, strengthening traceability and conceptual coherence.



The same principle applies to everyday contexts — a notepad on the desk (Source) with sticky notes (Items) organized by priority or date (Ontology) — and to complex academic research workflows involving scientific articles, theses and technical documentation.
Synesis is not just an organizing system but an infrastructure for translating knowledge. It converts conceptual structures into interoperable formats — from spreadsheets (CSV, Excel) to analytical notebooks (Jupyter Lab), standard vocabularies (SKOS) and graph databases (Neo4j, ArcadeDB) — making knowledge measurable, queryable and semantically navigable, including by Large Language Models (LLMs) via MCP.

The Synesis architecture is modular and entirely based on plain text, ensuring portability, traceability, native versioning and a distraction-free environment.
The whole system is orchestrated by a project file (.synp), which acts as the coordination point and connects its main components:
Bibliographic References (.bib): gather and formally structure the original sources on which the knowledge rests.
@article{doe2026,
    author  = {Doe, John},
    journal = {Knowledge Management},
    title   = {Exploring knowledge annotation systems},
    year    = {2026},
    number  = {7},
    volume  = {1}
}
Structural Templates (.synt): the normative core of the language. The template file formally defines the structure of annotations (.syn) and ontologies (.syno). It fixes the formats, required fields, relation types and declarative rules that shape the whole body of knowledge. Fully configurable, the template determines how the ontology is organized and how annotations must be structured. Like the other components, it is a plain text file.
# ============================================
# ITEM FIELDS
# ============================================

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED text
    REQUIRED BUNDLE note, chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD text TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Textual excerpt from the bibliographic source
END FIELD

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Analytical memo explaining the interpretation and the causal mechanism identified
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Causal relation between concepts
    RELATIONS
        ENABLES: A allows B to occur
        CONSTRAINS: A limits B
    END RELATIONS
END FIELD
Annotations (.syn): analytical records structured according to the template. They are texts organized in formal blocks, following the declared rules.
SOURCE @doe2026
END SOURCE

ITEM @doe2026
    text: This study aims to assess the impacts of these transition plans on social equity in a case study of the southern coast of Iran, where the community faces severe water scarcity and there is ready access to seawater for desalination.

    note: Water scarcity creates necessary condition for desalination adoption, enabling transition pathway evaluation

    chain: Water_Scarcity -> ENABLES -> Desalination
END ITEM

ITEM @doe2026
    text: The main contribution of this research is to consider social equity as a key factor in the nexus evaluation of energy-water transition plans.

    note: Positions equity as essential evaluation criterion, constraining acceptable transition configurations

    chain: Equity -> CONSTRAINS -> Transition_Planning
END ITEM
Ontology (.syno): contains conceptual structures also defined by the template. Although they appear as structured blocks, their form and logic derive entirely from the declarations in the .synt file.
ONTOLOGY Cost
    topic: Economics
    aspect: 11
    dimension: 2
    confidence: HIGH

    reasoning: Aspect 11: Core economic factor representing financial expenditure. Mainly constrains deployment/technology development while enabling market penetration when reduced. Co-occurs with Deployment and Acceptance, indicating market-consumer relevance. Dimension 2: Directly affects investors, consumers, and market competitiveness. High frequency (96) across broad sources (66) confirms central role.

    description: Economic factor representing financial expenditure associated with energy technologies and systems. Acts as primary barrier constraining technology development, site selection, and deployment when high, while enabling market penetration, technology transition, and sustainable solutions when reduced. Influences willingness to pay, acceptance, and market competitiveness. Critical determinant of renewable energy portfolio choices and infrastructure optimization decisions.

    rgt_element_a: Low_Cost
    rgt_element_b: High_Cost
    theoretical_significance: 3
END ONTOLOGY
While annotation and ontology files resemble texts structured in blocks, it is in the template file that Synesis truly shows itself as a language. Through declarative commands, the .synt file defines the structural grammar governing the whole corpus, turning a set of texts into a formally organized body of knowledge.


When compiling these files, Synesis validates their consistency and generates exchange formats.





flowchart LR

    classDef highValue fill:#E0F7FA,stroke:#00BFA5,stroke-width:2px,color:#084C54;
    classDef defaultNode fill:#F8FAFC,stroke:#4A5568,stroke-width:1px,color:#084C84;

The result of Synesis compilation goes far beyond structured documents. The compiler converts your body of knowledge into exchange formats — such as JSON, CSV, Excel, Alpaca and SKOS — making it interoperable with other technology stacks.
More than exporting data, Synesis turns structured knowledge into computational infrastructure.


synesis-graph takes the project to Neo4j or ArcadeDB, materializing the conceptual topology of your knowledge as navigable, queryable and visually explorable graphs.



Neo4j Desktop with data generated by Synesis.





Through the MCP protocol (Model Context Protocol), your data can be connected to assistants such as Claude Desktop, enabling natural language interaction with traceable answers grounded directly in the graph database (Neo4j or ArcadeDB) — your formal source of truth.



Access to compiled data through natural language chat.





Structured datasets ready for statistical analysis in R, computational exploration in Python or interactive visualizations in Jupyter Lab.



Connection with Jupyter Lab.





Through a Language Server Protocol (LSP) server, the editor recognizes Synesis syntax and validates in real time. The environment offers structured navigation, link inspection and basic graphical views to support analysis.



Full workflow (open file + explorer + viewer).





zotero-synesis-export exports PDF highlights, comments and tags from Zotero to the Synesis format, connecting academic reading to the compilation workflow.



Export configuration in Zotero.





A VS Code extension for exegetical coding of the whole biblical text, with support for chained semantic relations (e.g. Word → ENABLES → Creation). Highlights of the canonical text can be combined through the compiler with annotations of classical, philosophical or patristic corpora, producing integrated graphs of conceptual networks.



Bible Coder view.








From the Greek σύνεσις (sýnesis):

Etymology: from συνίημι (syníēmi) — “to bring together”, “to understand”, “to make converge” — plus the nominal suffix -σις (-sis), which indicates action or process.

Classical meanings:

Confluence; union; convergence.
Understanding; discernment; intelligence.
Reflective awareness.

The original sense combines two inseparable movements: bringing together and understanding.
Synesis, as a language, embodies exactly that principle — the convergence of information fragments into an intelligible, auditable and formally structured whole.
Synesis: the confluence of information into intelligence.

title: Synesis
text:
The Synesis architecture is modular and entirely based on plain text, ensuring portability, traceability, native versioning and a distraction-free environment.
The whole system is orchestrated by a project file (.synp), which acts as the coordination point and connects its main components:
Bibliographic References (.bib): gather and formally structure the original sources on which the knowledge rests.
@article{doe2026,
    author  = {Doe, John},
    journal = {Knowledge Management},
    title   = {Exploring knowledge annotation systems},
    year    = {2026},
    number  = {7},
    volume  = {1}
}
Structural Templates (.synt): the normative core of the language. The template file formally defines the structure of annotations (.syn) and ontologies (.syno). It fixes the formats, required fields, relation types and declarative rules that shape the whole body of knowledge. Fully configurable, the template determines how the ontology is organized and how annotations must be structured. Like the other components, it is a plain text file.
# ============================================
# ITEM FIELDS
# ============================================

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED text
    REQUIRED BUNDLE note, chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD text TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Textual excerpt from the bibliographic source
END FIELD

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Analytical memo explaining the interpretation and the causal mechanism identified
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Causal relation between concepts
    RELATIONS
        ENABLES: A allows B to occur
        CONSTRAINS: A limits B
    END RELATIONS
END FIELD
Annotations (.syn): analytical records structured according to the template. They are texts organized in formal blocks, following the declared rules.
SOURCE @doe2026
END SOURCE

ITEM @doe2026
    text: This study aims to assess the impacts of these transition plans on social equity in a case study of the southern coast of Iran, where the community faces severe water scarcity and there is ready access to seawater for desalination.

    note: Water scarcity creates necessary condition for desalination adoption, enabling transition pathway evaluation

    chain: Water_Scarcity -> ENABLES -> Desalination
END ITEM

ITEM @doe2026
    text: The main contribution of this research is to consider social equity as a key factor in the nexus evaluation of energy-water transition plans.

    note: Positions equity as essential evaluation criterion, constraining acceptable transition configurations

    chain: Equity -> CONSTRAINS -> Transition_Planning
END ITEM
Ontology (.syno): contains conceptual structures also defined by the template. Although they appear as structured blocks, their form and logic derive entirely from the declarations in the .synt file.
ONTOLOGY Cost
    topic: Economics
    aspect: 11
    dimension: 2
    confidence: HIGH

    reasoning: Aspect 11: Core economic factor representing financial expenditure. Mainly constrains deployment/technology development while enabling market penetration when reduced. Co-occurs with Deployment and Acceptance, indicating market-consumer relevance. Dimension 2: Directly affects investors, consumers, and market competitiveness. High frequency (96) across broad sources (66) confirms central role.

    description: Economic factor representing financial expenditure associated with energy technologies and systems. Acts as primary barrier constraining technology development, site selection, and deployment when high, while enabling market penetration, technology transition, and sustainable solutions when reduced. Influences willingness to pay, acceptance, and market competitiveness. Critical determinant of renewable energy portfolio choices and infrastructure optimization decisions.

    rgt_element_a: Low_Cost
    rgt_element_b: High_Cost
    theoretical_significance: 3
END ONTOLOGY
While annotation and ontology files resemble texts structured in blocks, it is in the template file that Synesis truly shows itself as a language. Through declarative commands, the .synt file defines the structural grammar governing the whole corpus, turning a set of texts into a formally organized body of knowledge.


When compiling these files, Synesis validates their consistency and generates exchange formats.





flowchart LR
    %% --- NODE STYLES ---
    classDef compiler fill:#fff,stroke:#084C54,stroke-width:4px,color:#084C54,font-weight:bold;
    classDef highValue fill:#E0F7FA,stroke:#00BFA5,stroke-width:2px,color:#084C54;
    classDef defaultNode fill:#F8FAFC,stroke:#4A5568,stroke-width:1px,color:#084C84;

    %% --- DIAGRAM STRUCTURE ---
    subgraph Input ["Work Environment"]
        direction TB
        E["Ontology (.syno)"]:::defaultNode
        D["Template (.synt)"]:::defaultNode

    end

    %% The Central Engine
    C((("Synesis Compiler\nValidation & Logic"))):::compiler

    subgraph Output ["Exchange Formats"]
        direction TB

    end

    subgraph Ecosystem ["Application Ecosystem"]
        direction TB

    style Output fill:transparent,stroke:#4A5568,stroke-width:1px,stroke-dasharray: 5 5,color:#084C54

The result of Synesis compilation goes far beyond structured documents. The compiler converts your body of knowledge into exchange formats — such as JSON, CSV, Excel, Alpaca and SKOS — making it interoperable with other technology stacks.
More than exporting data, Synesis turns structured knowledge into computational infrastructure.


synesis-graph takes the project to Neo4j or ArcadeDB, materializing the conceptual topology of your knowledge as navigable, queryable and visually explorable graphs.



Neo4j Desktop with data generated by Synesis.





Through the MCP protocol (Model Context Protocol), your data can be connected to assistants such as Claude Desktop, enabling natural language interaction with traceable answers grounded directly in the graph database (Neo4j or ArcadeDB) — your formal source of truth.



Access to compiled data through natural language chat.





Structured datasets ready for statistical analysis in R, computational exploration in Python or interactive visualizations in Jupyter Lab.



Connection with Jupyter Lab.





Through a Language Server Protocol (LSP) server, the editor recognizes Synesis syntax and validates in real time. The environment offers structured navigation, link inspection and basic graphical views to support analysis.



Full workflow (open file + explorer + viewer).





zotero-synesis-export exports PDF highlights, comments and tags from Zotero to the Synesis format, connecting academic reading to the compilation workflow.



Export configuration in Zotero.





A VS Code extension for exegetical coding of the whole biblical text, with support for chained semantic relations (e.g. Word → ENABLES → Creation). Highlights of the canonical text can be combined through the compiler with annotations of classical, philosophical or patristic corpora, producing integrated graphs of conceptual networks.



Bible Coder view.

title: Synesis
text:
From the Greek σύνεσις (sýnesis):

Etymology: from συνίημι (syníēmi) — “to bring together”, “to understand”, “to make converge” — plus the nominal suffix -σις (-sis), which indicates action or process.

Classical meanings:

Confluence; union; convergence.
Understanding; discernment; intelligence.
Reflective awareness.

The original sense combines two inseparable movements: bringing together and understanding.
Synesis, as a language, embodies exactly that principle — the convergence of information fragments into an intelligible, auditable and formally structured whole.
Synesis: the confluence of information into intelligence.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
This guide shows how to connect two or more Synesis projects that describe the same entities from different sources — CVs and articles, interviews and institutional documents, profiles and publications.
Use this guide if you:

Have separate corpora referring to the same people, organizations or processes
Want to cross those corpora without merging them into one giant project
Need each corpus to keep compiling fast and being edited independently
Want to share a single conceptual vocabulary among several projects







What this guide does not do



Linking does not merge projects or create a “master project”. Each .synp remains an autonomous compilation unit. The link is resolved in an explicit command-line step and is never loaded by the editor.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
section: 3.1 When the Identifier Lives in the .bib
text:
3.1 When the Identifier Lives in the .bib
Identifiers such as ORCID or a registration number are usually source metadata, not something extracted from the text. Declare the origin with ON BIBLIOGRAPHY:
SOURCE FIELDS
    REQUIRED lattes_id ON BIBLIOGRAPHY
END SOURCE FIELDS
@misc{cv_maria,
    author    = {Silva, Maria},
    title     = {Lattes CV},
    year      = {2026},
    lattes_id = {ID-0001}
}
For structured TOML records, the equivalent is ON DATASET.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
section: 4.1 The Two Modifiers Side by Side
text:
4.1 The Two Modifiers Side by Side



Modifier
Role
Creates a graph node?
Value repeats?




IDENTIFIES <entity>
Primary key
Yes
No


REFERS TO <entity>
Foreign key
No
Yes



Both apply only to SCOPE SOURCE fields (E078).

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
7.1 Export the Aggregate
synesis compile lattes/lattes.synp abstracts/abstracts.synp \
  --json study.json --csv out/ --xls workbooks/







Option
Result




--json
aggregate in schema 3.1: kind: "link", members, entity_owners, links (edges and orphans)


--csv
links.csv with edges and orphans


--xls

--stats
per-member and aggregate statistics


--alpaca, --okf
no exporter for the aggregate: the compiler warns



links.csv:
entity,value,from_member,from_bibref,to_member,to_bibref

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
7.2 Aggregate Statistics
synesis compile lattes/lattes.synp abstracts/abstracts.synp --stats
Per-member statistics:

  PROJECT    SOURCES  ITEMS  CHAINS
  lattes           1      1       0
  abstracts        3      3       0
  ─────────  ───────  ─────  ──────
  TOTAL            4      4       0

Shared organizing model:

  1 concepts, identical in the 2 projects  (INCLUDE SHARED ONTOLOGY)
A shared ontology is counted once, not added up per member.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
8.1 Qualified Bibrefs
In the aggregate each bibref is prefixed with the alias of its project (lattes:@cv_maria). Two corpora may hold the same .bib key without being confused.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
8.2 Orphan References
A REFERS TO value without a matching IDENTIFIES becomes a warning (W083):
<link>:0:0  [WARNING]  Orphan REFERS TO `ID-9999` (researcher) in abstracts
This is often legitimate — an article citing an author with no CV in the corpus. No node is created for an orphan.

title: How to Link Independent Projects
text:
8.3 Near Matches
When the value would match only ignoring case:
<link>:0:0  [WARNING]  Orphan REFERS TO `id-0001` (researcher) — near match `ID-0001` (differs only in case)






Why the compiler does not normalize on its own



Normalizing would merge entities the source may consider distinct. The compiler detects and suggests, but never merges. Fix the value at the source, and the decision is recorded.

title: How to Export to Neo4j
text:
This guide shows how to turn your Synesis annotations into a knowledge graph in Neo4j, for network analysis, visualization and querying with AI assistants.
Use this guide if you:

Need to explore complex relations between concepts
Want to compute centrality, communities or PageRank
Want to query the corpus with an assistant over MCP







No database server?



synesis-graph can also write a local ArcadeDB database, with no server or Java to install:
pip install synesis-graph
synesis-graph arcadedb-embedded --project my_project.synp
synesis-graph serve
It also renders an HTML graph that opens in the browser. See the reference.






Python 3.10+
A Synesis project that compiles without errors
Neo4j Desktop, Neo4j Server or Neo4j Aura








Download from https://neo4j.com/download/
Create a database (DBMS) and choose a strong password
Start it (Start)







Checkpoint ✓



In Neo4j Browser, run:
RETURN "Hello, Neo4j!" AS message






Go to https://neo4j.com/cloud/aura/ and create an instance
Download the credentials file (URI, user, password) and keep it safe







Sensitive data



A cloud database receives the passages of your corpus. Check what your research ethics approval and data protection law allow.







pip install "synesis-graph[neo4j]"
synesis-graph --version
# synesis-graph, version 0.13.1






Former name



The tool used to be called synesis2graph (and before that synesis2neo4j). If you have the old version, remove it with pip uninstall synesis2graph.






Create config.toml in the folder you run the command from:
[neo4j]
uri = "bolt://127.0.0.1:7687"      # Aura: neo4j+s://xxxxx.databases.neo4j.io
user = "neo4j"
password = "YourPassword"
# database = "my_corpus"            # optional; default: PROJECT name
# fulltext_analyzer = "english"     # language-aware text search






Security



Never commit config.toml:
echo "config.toml" >> .gitignore






synesis-graph neo4j --project my_project.synp --config config.toml
config.toml is the default, so --config may be omitted. The pipeline compiles the project in memory (an error stops everything before the database is touched), connects, writes the graph, computes the metrics and writes the project context into the ProjectContext vertex.






Checkpoint ✓



MATCH (n) RETURN count(n) AS total_nodes






MATCH (n) RETURN n LIMIT 100






Labels come from your template



A concept node takes the label of the field name: a field category produces :Category; a field criterion, :Criterion. The queries below omit the label so they work on any project. To get to know the graph: MATCH (p:ProjectContext) RETURN p.template_doc.


// a concept and its relations
MATCH path = (c {name: "Cost"})-[r]->(target)
RETURN path
// annotations of a concept, with their location
MATCH (s:Source)<-[:FROM_SOURCE]-(i:Item)-[:MENTIONS]->(c {name: "Cost"})
RETURN s.bibtex, i.citation, i.source_file, i.source_line






MATCH (c)
WHERE c.mention_count IS NOT NULL
RETURN c.name AS concept, c.mention_count AS frequency, c.source_count AS sources
ORDER BY frequency DESC
LIMIT 10



MATCH (i:Item)-[:MENTIONS]->(c1), (i)-[:MENTIONS]->(c2)
WHERE c1.name < c2.name
RETURN c1.name, c2.name, count(DISTINCT i) AS co_occurrence
ORDER BY co_occurrence DESC
LIMIT 20



MATCH (c1)-[r:RELATES_TO]->(c2)
RETURN c1.name AS source, r.type AS relation, c2.name AS target, count(r) AS occurrences
ORDER BY occurrences DESC



MATCH (c)
WHERE c.betweenness IS NOT NULL
RETURN c.name AS concept, c.betweenness AS centrality
ORDER BY centrality DESC
LIMIT 10






betweenness requires the GDS plugin



Without GDS use degree, always available.







Run the same command after new annotations:
synesis-graph neo4j --project my_project.synp








--mode
What it does
When to use




rebuild (default)
wipes and rewrites the graph
always correct: mirrors the corpus exactly


update
writes only what changed
large corpus; does not remove what was deleted from the project



The graph is a derived artifact: the source of truth is the project files. After renaming or deleting material, use rebuild.




Install the Graph Data Science Library plugin on your database (Neo4j Desktop: Plugins) and restart. The pipeline detects it: with it, pagerank, betweenness and community are computed; without it, it warns and continues with the native metrics.
MATCH (c)
WHERE c.pagerank IS NOT NULL
RETURN c.name, c.degree, c.pagerank, c.betweenness, c.community
ORDER BY c.pagerank DESC
LIMIT 20

High PageRank: a concept pointed to by other relevant concepts
High betweenness: a concept linking clusters
Community (Louvain): same number, same cluster; read it according to the projection used (see the reference)





With the graph in Neo4j, the mcp-neo4j-cypher MCP server lets you query it in natural language from Claude Desktop. In claude_desktop_config.json:
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "synesis-neo4j": {
      "command": "uvx",
      "args": ["mcp-neo4j-cypher@0.5.2", "--read-only"],
      "env": {
        "NEO4J_URI": "bolt://localhost:7687",
        "NEO4J_USERNAME": "neo4j",
        "NEO4J_PASSWORD": "your_password",
        "NEO4J_DATABASE": "database_name"
      }
    }
  }
}
The file is in %APPDATA%\Claude\ (Windows) or ~/Library/Application Support/Claude/ (macOS). Keep --read-only. The repository ships a full guide in the mcp/ folder.






Neo4j is not running: click Start or run neo4j start.



Check the password in config.toml.



List the names with SHOW DATABASES and adjust database.



synesis compile my_project.synp
Fix what the compiler reports and export again.




Use --mode update when you only added material
An interrupted load leaves the graph marked as incomplete: run a rebuild

title: How to Create and Validate Chains
text:
This guide shows how to build chains to express relations between concepts in a systematic, auditable way.
Use this guide if you:

Need to express causality, influence or mediation
Want to build maps of relations between concepts
Need to validate the consistency of your chains
Want to extract relation networks for analysis or visualization




A chain is a sequence of concepts linked by ->, expressing how they relate. When the field declares relations, every link is named.
concept_a -> RELATION -> concept_b
ITEM @interview_01
    chain: high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption
END ITEM
Read: “high_cost INHIBITS adoption”.




Relations are declared in the template, in a field of type CHAIN. The field name is free; ARITY is required.
FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Relation between concepts stated by the source
    RELATIONS
        CAUSES: X directly causes Y
        INHIBITS: X reduces the likelihood or intensity of Y
        FAVORS: X promotes or eases Y
        MEDIATES: X mediates the effect on Y
        CORRELATES: X and Y occur together, with no defined causal direction
    END RELATIONS
    GUIDELINES
        Record only relations the passage states.
        Test CAUSES or FAVORS: without X, would Y not happen? Then CAUSES.
        Correct: high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption (the passage says price deters)
        Wrong: high_cost -> CAUSES -> adoption (the passage states no cause)
    END GUIDELINES
END FIELD

ARITY >= 2 accepts a single link
ARITY >= 3 requires a mediator (antecedent → mediator → outcome)

If the field declares no RELATIONS, the chain is simple (a -> b): it records the association without naming it.






ITEM @interview_01
    quote: "The high price discourages the purchase"
    memo: Economic barrier identified
    chain: high_price -> INHIBITS -> purchase_decision
END ITEM
When to use: direct relations.



ITEM @interview_01
    chain: lack_of_training -> CAUSES -> low_skill -> INHIBITS -> adoption
END ITEM
Read: “lack of training CAUSES low skill, which INHIBITS adoption”. Each consecutive pair becomes a relation (triple) in the exports.
When to use: to record mechanisms with intermediate elements.





A small, well-separated set is worth more than many overlapping relations. If two relations cannot be told apart in one sentence, they are the same.








Relation
Meaning
Example




CAUSES
X directly causes Y
software_bug -> CAUSES -> system_failure


INHIBITS
X reduces or prevents Y
high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption


FAVORS
X promotes or eases Y
training -> FAVORS -> usability


MEDIATES
X mediates
technical_support -> MEDIATES -> satisfaction


CORRELATES
they occur together, no direction
turnover -> CORRELATES -> disengagement









ITEM @doc_01
    chain: lack_of_resources -> INHIBITS -> ai_investment
    chain: lack_of_resources -> INHIBITS -> staff_training
    chain: lack_of_resources -> CAUSES -> short_term_priorities
END ITEM



ITEM @doc_02
    chain: ease_of_use -> FAVORS -> satisfaction
    chain: responsive_support -> FAVORS -> satisfaction
    chain: affordable_cost -> FAVORS -> satisfaction
END ITEM



ITEM @doc_03
    chain: capacity_building -> FAVORS -> team_skill -> FAVORS -> quality
END ITEM





A chain says a relation exists. Sources rarely say only that: they hypothesize, test, deny. Pair the chain with its qualifiers in a BUNDLE:
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quote
    OPTIONAL BUNDLE chain, status
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD status TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION How the text presents the relation right before it
    VALUES
        Asserted: presented as a finding or fact
        Hypothetical: proposed without being asserted
        Negated: the text states it does not hold
    END VALUES
END FIELD
ITEM @article_01
    quote: "Training reduced clicks but did not increase reporting."
    chain: training -> INHIBITS -> clicks
    status: Asserted
    chain: training -> FAVORS -> reporting
    status: Negated
END ITEM
Each chain: pairs by position with its status:. Without the qualifier, a hypothesis and a finding look the same in every export.






synesis compile analysis.synp --check-codes
The compiler checks:

the structure (concept → relation → concept alternation)
whether each relation is declared in the field
whether the arity is met
whether the concepts have a definition in the ontology









Message
Cause
Fix




Relation 'Y' not declared in the template
relation outside RELATIONS
use a declared one or add it to the template


Concept 'A B' contains spaces
concept with spaces
use A_B


Simple chain in 'chain' but the template requires named relations
relation missing
A -> REL -> B


Qualified chain with incorrect structure
ends in a relation or a concept is missing
concept, relation, concept

title: How to Create and Validate Chains
text:
A chain is a sequence of concepts linked by ->, expressing how they relate. When the field declares relations, every link is named.
concept_a -> RELATION -> concept_b
ITEM @interview_01
    chain: high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption
END ITEM
Read: “high_cost INHIBITS adoption”.

title: How to Create and Validate Chains
text:
Relations are declared in the template, in a field of type CHAIN. The field name is free; ARITY is required.
FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Relation between concepts stated by the source
    RELATIONS
        CAUSES: X directly causes Y
        INHIBITS: X reduces the likelihood or intensity of Y
        FAVORS: X promotes or eases Y
        MEDIATES: X mediates the effect on Y
        CORRELATES: X and Y occur together, with no defined causal direction
    END RELATIONS
    GUIDELINES
        Record only relations the passage states.
        Test CAUSES or FAVORS: without X, would Y not happen? Then CAUSES.
        Correct: high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption (the passage says price deters)
        Wrong: high_cost -> CAUSES -> adoption (the passage states no cause)
    END GUIDELINES
END FIELD

ARITY >= 2 accepts a single link
ARITY >= 3 requires a mediator (antecedent → mediator → outcome)

If the field declares no RELATIONS, the chain is simple (a -> b): it records the association without naming it.

text:

    chain: lack_of_training -> CAUSES -> low_skill -> INHIBITS -> adoption
END ITEM
Read: “lack of training CAUSES low skill, which INHIBITS adoption”. Each consecutive pair becomes a relation (triple) in the exports.
When to use: to record mechanisms with intermediate elements.

text:
A small, well-separated set is worth more than many overlapping relations. If two relations cannot be told apart in one sentence, they are the same.








Relation
Meaning
Example




CAUSES
X directly causes Y
software_bug -> CAUSES -> system_failure


INHIBITS
X reduces or prevents Y

FAVORS
X promotes or eases Y

MEDIATES
X mediates

CORRELATES
they occur together, no direction

title: How to Create and Validate Chains
text:
A chain says a relation exists. Sources rarely say only that: they hypothesize, test, deny. Pair the chain with its qualifiers in a BUNDLE:
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quote
    OPTIONAL BUNDLE chain, status
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD status TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION How the text presents the relation right before it
    VALUES
        Asserted: presented as a finding or fact
        Hypothetical: proposed without being asserted
        Negated: the text states it does not hold
    END VALUES
END FIELD
ITEM @article_01
    quote: "Training reduced clicks but did not increase reporting."
    chain: training -> INHIBITS -> clicks
    status: Asserted
    chain: training -> FAVORS -> reporting
    status: Negated
END ITEM
Each chain: pairs by position with its status:. Without the qualifier, a hypothesis and a finding look the same in every export.

title: 1 Synesis and Scripture
text:
The Bible is a remarkable book. Written over more than 1,500 years, by more than 40 authors living on three continents (Asia, Africa and Europe), in three languages (Hebrew, Aramaic and Greek), it is at once diverse and deeply cohesive. A cataloguing effort by Pastor Christoph Römhild identified 63,779 cross references in Scripture, which led to the visualization made by Chris Harrison.



Graphical representation of cross references.




Readers of Scripture have long noticed that certain themes recur throughout both Testaments. To navigate this thematic richness, tools were developed such as concordances (listing occurrences of specific terms), cross references (conceptual links between verses, connecting people, events, places and theological concepts) and systematic theology (the discipline that organizes the doctrines of the Christian faith by identifying and grouping relevant passages).
In 1890, Dr. Frank Charles Thompson, for instance, began annotating the margins of his Bible, connecting themes in a chain-reference system — a work that occupied his whole life and remains available today in the Thompson Study Bible.



Thompson Bible with markings. Source: BibleGateway





Synesis is a structured annotation language for qualitative research. It records passages from sources — texts, interviews, documents — attaching to each passage metadata such as themes, concepts and relations. Annotations are stored in a format readable by people and processable by machines, and can be exported to databases, spreadsheets or knowledge graphs.
In the context of Scripture, Synesis works as a programmable concordance: instead of consulting a fixed index, the researcher builds their own reference system, with whatever criteria and categories they wish. The result is an annotated corpus that can be queried, expanded and visualized in ways no manual system offers.
Three features make Synesis particularly suited to systematic Bible study:

Scale. A manual system like Dr. Thompson’s took a lifetime to build. With Synesis, the same kind of structure can be developed incrementally, collaboratively and verifiably.
Taxonomic flexibility. Themes and categories are defined by the researcher, with no controlled vocabulary imposed from outside. One may work with the categories of classical systematic theology, with one’s own structures, or both at once.
Interoperability. Annotations can be exported to several formats and integrated with other analysis, visualization and research tools.



Dr. Thompson’s annotation system can be represented directly in Synesis. The themes field records several keywords per item, separated by commas, working as the thematic links of chain references.
SOURCE @thompson1999
    description: Thompson study Bible with chain references
END SOURCE

ITEM @thompson1999
    passage: Pr 12.23
    quote: "A prudent man concealeth knowledge: but the heart of fools proclaimeth foolishness."
    themes: Prudence, Folly
END ITEM

ITEM @thompson1999
    passage: Pr 14.15
    quote: "The simple believeth every word: but the prudent man looketh well to his going."
    themes: Credulity, Prudence, Folly
END ITEM

ITEM @thompson1999
    passage: Pr 15.5
    quote: "A fool despiseth his father's instruction: but he that regardeth reproof is prudent."
    themes: Value_of_Reproof, Dishonoring_Parents, Prudence, Foolish_People
END ITEM




The need to organize and connect Scripture thematically did not begin with Dr. Thompson. It accompanies the history of Christian hermeneutics from the first centuries, and produced ever more sophisticated instruments over time.
In the third century Origen was already producing the Hexapla, a work of textual organization and comparison that presupposed systematic identification of parallels and variants. Jerome, in the fourth century, and the medieval monks who developed the Concordantiae — alphabetical indexes of the words of Scripture — continued the tradition. The first complete concordance of the Latin Vulgate is attributed to Hugh of Saint-Cher, in the thirteenth century, produced with the help of hundreds of copyists.



Concordantiae, organized by Hugh of Saint-Cher.


With the Reformation and the spread of vernacular translations, new tools became necessary. In 1550 John Marbeck published the first complete English concordance. But it was in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries that the project of thematically organizing Scripture reached its greatest sophistication:
Nave’s Topical Bible (1896) — Rev. Orville James Nave spent 23 years compiling this work while serving as a military chaplain. Organized by topic rather than by verse, it lists more than 20,000 themes and subthemes with their passages, over 100,000 references in all.



Nave’s Topical Bible in Synesis.


Thompson Chain-Reference Bible (1908) — Dr. Frank Charles Thompson developed a different system: instead of separate works, he integrated the references into the margins of the Bible itself, organized in numbered thematic chains that lead the reader from verse to verse across the whole canon.



Thompson Chain-Reference Bible in Synesis.


What these works share is the problem they try to solve: Scripture forms a dense network of thematic, typological and theological relations that no reader can map entirely from memory. Each system is a manual solution to this problem — and each carries the limits of the medium in which it was built. A printed book cannot be queried by several criteria at once, cannot be updated without a new edition and cannot be integrated with other analysis systems.
Synesis starts exactly here: the tradition has already established that the problem is worth solving. What changes is the medium.


The annotations can be exported to several formats and used for thematic analysis. It is even possible to generate graphical visualizations similar to Chris Harrison’s, showing the structure of connections among the annotated passages.




Notably, both concordances and modern qualitative coding answer the same epistemological challenge: how to extract patterns from a large, heterogeneous textual corpus while preserving the link between each pattern and its source text.
In both cases the researcher needs to:

(1) read the text,
(2) identify units of meaning,
(3) assign categories to those units, and
(4) later retrieve every passage associated with a category.

The structure of the process is identical.
Qualitative coding and the systematic organization of Scripture share a deep common structure: identifying units of meaning in a textual corpus, assigning categories and retrieving connections.
Synesis does not apply research methods to a new domain — it recognizes a continuity that always existed between these two traditions and offers a formal instrument for both.

title: 1 Synesis and Scripture
section: 2.1 The Potential of Synesis for Theology
text:
2.1 The Potential of Synesis for Theology
The relevant question is not technical — it is about what the format makes it possible to think.

2.1.1 Convergence of Heterogeneous Sources
Nave’s and Thompson were born as parallel projects, by different authors, with different structures, in different decades. In print it was not simple to ask: on which verses about Faith do Nave’s and Thompson agree? — because the sources sat in separate silos.
In Synesis both works can be adapted to share the same data model. A query like that then becomes trivial.


2.1.2 The chain Field as a Tool for Systematic Theology
Systematic theology works with relations between doctrinal concepts — and Synesis has formal primitives to represent them:
SOURCE @systematic_theology2026
    description: "Fundamental doctrinal relations"
END SOURCE

ITEM @systematic_theology2026
    memo: Relation between grace, faith and justification in Pauline soteriology
    chain: Grace -> PRODUCES -> Faith -> PRODUCES -> Justification
END ITEM

ITEM @systematic_theology2026
    memo: Structural tension between the paradigms of Law and Gospel
    chain: Law -> CONTRASTS_WITH -> Gospel
END ITEM
Synesis offers a data model that expresses the relational chaining of theological concepts precisely and easily, with open and traceable data.


2.1.3 Controlled Theological Vocabulary
Ontologies allow a structured theological thesaurus, with hierarchical navigation by area of theology:
ONTOLOGY Justification
    description: "Act by which God declares the sinner righteous on the basis of the work of Christ"
    group: Soteriology
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY Sanctification
    description: "Progressive process of conformity to the image of Christ"
    group: Soteriology
END ONTOLOGY
This allows questions Bible indexing systems never offered in structured form: show all concepts mapped under Soteriology, or which Nave’s passages deal with concepts of that group?


2.1.4 Doctrinal Tensions as Comparable Data
The most significant potential lies in modelling interpretive disagreements. Different theological traditions assign different meanings to the same texts. With Synesis this can be represented explicitly:
SOURCE @calvin_institutes
    description: "Institutes of the Christian Religion, John Calvin"
END SOURCE

ITEM @calvin_institutes
    quote: "Jn 6:37 — All that the Father giveth me shall come to me"
    memo: Proof of divine sovereignty in unconditional election
    chain: Divine_Sovereignty -> PRODUCES -> Unconditional_Election
END ITEM

SOURCE @arminius_works
    description: "Complete Works, Jacobus Arminius"
END SOURCE

ITEM @arminius_works
    quote: "Jn 6:37 — All that the Father giveth me shall come to me"
    memo: Election is grounded in divine foreknowledge of future faith
    chain: Divine_Foreknowledge -> PRODUCES -> Conditional_Election
END ITEM
The same passage, two theological systems, structured and comparable data.

Synesis does not turn the sacred text into data — it turns the inspired human work of interpretation into data. Thompson and Nave are the indexing layer. What is built above it — commentaries, doctrinal relations, interpretive traditions — is where the language shows its full potential.

title: Synesis Language
text:
Knowledge modelling and the annotation of qualitative corpora face a classic architectural dilemma: the tension between human ergonomics (the fluency a researcher needs to write and think) and computational formal rigor (the strict structure machines need to compile, validate and export the data).
Synesis was designed as a declarative Domain-Specific Language (DSL) precisely to resolve this dilemma, turning interpretive annotations into canonical structures while keeping both human readability and formal rigor. To understand the design decisions of the language, it helps to look at how other knowledge representation paradigms handle the same tension.


Historically, approaches that prioritize mechanical validation and data structure sacrifice human readability.
The TEI/XML paradigm: the XML-based Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) is the gold standard of digital humanities. It offers absolute ontological rigor, but writing in it is exhausting. The constant nesting of opening and closing tags clutters the document, drains the researcher’s cognitive energy and hinders fluent reading of the analytical text.
The RDF/Turtle paradigm (Semantic Web): designed to build knowledge graphs, RDF expresses data as triples (Subject → Predicate → Object). It is excellent for network analysis, but it is a data modelling language hostile to deep qualitative analysis. Placing long excerpts or dense analytical memos among RDF statements breaks the natural flow of the hermeneutic process.



On the other side, Personal Knowledge Management (PKM) tools such as Obsidian or Logseq popularized Markdown with YAML front matter for agile annotation (Zettelkasten).
The illusion of structure: Markdown offers an unbeatable, light writing experience. But it lacks a strict compiler. Since the format essentially accepts any free text, no validation engine stops the researcher from using inconsistent field names or leaving out required metadata.
The extraction problem: without strict rules, extracting reliable tabular data, relationship matrices or consistent graphs from Markdown notes often becomes expensive data wrangling.



Synesis finds its place by combining the readability of plain text with the predictability of a strongly typed programming language. The balance rests on three design invariants:

Separation of rules and data: unlike Markdown, the language splits the responsibilities of a project. Validation rules (which fields are required or optional) are isolated in the Template file (.synt), while the researcher concentrates on interpretation in the Annotation files (.syn).
Text and graphs as first-class citizens: the language lets dense blocks of human text — source excerpts (QUOTATION) or analytical notes (MEMO) — coexist cleanly with topological connectors (CHAIN). Semantic chains reproduce graph logic, joining codes and relations, with a fluent syntax.
Deterministic compilation: the compiler does not try to “guess” formats, so the same input always produces the same output. A full compilation produces rigorous structured artifacts (JSON, CSV, Excel) or fails instructively, reporting diagnostics with context and exact file, line and column. Validation covers the form and consistency of what was annotated; whether the interpretation holds remains the researcher’s judgement.

title: Synesis Language
text:
Knowledge modelling and the annotation of qualitative corpora face a classic architectural dilemma: the tension between human ergonomics (the fluency a researcher needs to write and think) and computational formal rigor (the strict structure machines need to compile, validate and export the data).
Synesis was designed as a declarative Domain-Specific Language (DSL) precisely to resolve this dilemma, turning interpretive annotations into canonical structures while keeping both human readability and formal rigor. To understand the design decisions of the language, it helps to look at how other knowledge representation paradigms handle the same tension.


Historically, approaches that prioritize mechanical validation and data structure sacrifice human readability.
The TEI/XML paradigm: the XML-based Text Encoding Initiative (TEI) is the gold standard of digital humanities. It offers absolute ontological rigor, but writing in it is exhausting. The constant nesting of opening and closing tags clutters the document, drains the researcher’s cognitive energy and hinders fluent reading of the analytical text.
The RDF/Turtle paradigm (Semantic Web): designed to build knowledge graphs, RDF expresses data as triples (Subject → Predicate → Object). It is excellent for network analysis, but it is a data modelling language hostile to deep qualitative analysis. Placing long excerpts or dense analytical memos among RDF statements breaks the natural flow of the hermeneutic process.



On the other side, Personal Knowledge Management (PKM) tools such as Obsidian or Logseq popularized Markdown with YAML front matter for agile annotation (Zettelkasten).

title: Knowledge Graphs and GraphRAG
text:
When you export your Synesis annotations to a graph database (Neo4j or ArcadeDB, through synesis-graph), you are not just “saving data in another format”. You are turning structured text into navigable knowledge — a fundamental change in how we interact with qualitative analyses.



A knowledge graph is a representation of information where:

Nodes (vertices) represent entities (concepts, codes, annotations, sources)
Edges (relationships) represent connections between those entities
Properties store attributes of nodes and edges



Tables (CSV/Excel):
| Code        | Frequency   |
|-------------|-------------|
| Cost        | 15          |
| Adoption    | 23          |
You know “Cost” appears 15 times, but not how it relates to “Adoption”.
Graphs:
(Cost)-[INHIBITS {frequency: 8}]->(Adoption)
You know not only that they exist, but how they connect and how strongly.







In tables, relations are implicit (you join them mentally or in SQL). In graphs, relations are explicit and navigable.
Practical example:
You want to know: “Which codes are affected by ‘Lack of Infrastructure’?”
In CSV you need to:

Open chains.csv
Filter rows where from_code = "Lack_of_Infrastructure"
List the unique values of to_code
Check transitive chains by hand

In a graph:
MATCH (origin {name: "Lack_of_Infrastructure"})-[r:RELATES_TO*1..3]->(affected)
RETURN DISTINCT affected.name AS affected_code, length(r) AS distance
ORDER BY distance
Result: the database walks direct and indirect connections (up to 3 hops). An indirect path, assembled from chains of different sources, is a hypothesis to examine: no single source need have asserted the whole path.



Network metrics that are trivial in graphs (and nearly impossible in tables):








Metric
What It Reveals
Use in Research




Degree centrality
How many connections a node has
The most connected codes — candidates for central concepts in the theory


Betweenness centrality
How often a node lies on paths between other nodes
Codes that “bridge” thematic clusters


PageRank
Importance based on important connections
Codes connected not only widely, but to other important codes


Community detection
Densely connected groups of nodes
Thematic clusters emerging from the data (themes, subdimensions)



Practical insight:
In an analysis of resistance to technology you might find:

High degree: “Trust” has 23 connections → central concept
High betweenness: “Digital Literacy” links the “Technology” and “Social Exclusion” clusters → important mediator
Same community: “Cost”, “Infrastructure” and “Access” form a cohesive cluster → “Structural Barriers” dimension

These patterns are emergent — you did not program them; they emerge from the structure of your annotations.





RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) is a technique in which LLMs (such as Claude or GPT) look up information in databases before answering. GraphRAG uses graphs instead of plain text.


Traditional (vector) RAG:

Retrieves semantically similar texts
Works well for document retrieval
Limitation: does not understand structural relations

GraphRAG:

Retrieves explicit relations between concepts
Can follow reasoning paths (A → B → C)
Advantage: auditable, traceable answers




Question to Claude Desktop (with MCP connected to the graph):

“Why does ‘Technological Distrust’ hinder telemedicine adoption?”

Answer with GraphRAG:

“According to your project’s knowledge graph:

‘Technological Distrust’ appears in 8 annotations
Of these, 6 establish the relation: Distrust -> INHIBITS -> Adoption
The most representative annotation is @interview_mrs_maria, item 1:

Quotation: “How will they know what I have without touching me?”
Memo: “The participant links diagnostic quality to physical presence”


‘Technological Distrust’ also co-occurs frequently with: - ‘Preference for In-person Contact’ (5 times) - ‘Lack of Information’ (3 times)
You may want to explore whether distrust softens when local health agents mediate (see the chain in @interview_mr_joao, item 3).”

Notice:

The answer is traceable (it cites specific sources)
It includes frequencies (quantification over qualitative data)
It suggests further analyses based on graph patterns
You can check every claim by running the query and reading the source

Purely vector RAG returns similar passages without the relational structure that allows these counts and paths. The two complement each other: see Vector Embeddings and GraphRAG. An assistant’s answer can still be wrong; the advantage is that each claim can be checked in the graph and in the source text.





When a project is exported, the graph structure is:
(Item)-[:FROM_SOURCE]->(Source)
(Item)-[:MENTIONS]->(Concept)
(Concept)-[:RELATES_TO {type: "INHIBITS"}]->(Concept)
(Concept)-[:GROUPED_BY]->(Theme)
(Concept)-[:KIND_OF]->(Concept)        # with ROLE HIERARCHY










Type
Content
Example




Source
bibliographic reference and SOURCE fields
interview, article, document


Item
quotation, interpretation, ITEM fields and file location
coded unit


Concept (label = field name)
name, definition and ontology fields
:Code, :Factor, :Second_order


Taxonomy (label = field name)
groupings such as TOPIC
:Topic, :Group


ProjectContext
project description, template and GUIDELINES
one per graph













Type
Meaning




FROM_SOURCE
the item comes from that source


MENTIONS
the item mentions the concept


RELATES_TO
relation stated in a chain, with its type


GROUPED_BY, QUALIFIED_BY, BELONGS_TO
classification of the concept


IS_LINKED_TO
coupling between categories


KIND_OF, PART_OF, INSTANCE_OF
hierarchy adopted in the .syno






The graph structure is derived from the template (.synt). Add an ITEM field FIELD context TYPE TEXT and it becomes a property of the Item nodes. That is why the same tool serves any domain.





Graphs are no panacea. Do not use a graph database if:

Your focus is pure quantitative analysis (frequencies, descriptive statistics)

Use CSV + R/Python. Simpler and faster.

You have few explicit relations (isolated codes, no chains)

Excel is enough. A graph adds needless complexity.

You need complex longitudinal temporal analyses

Temporal graphs exist, but time-series databases (InfluxDB, TimescaleDB) are more efficient.

You have no Cypher background

There is a learning curve. If you only want it to “look nice”, use CSV visualizers (RAWGraphs, Flourish).


Use a graph database when:

You have many chains (more than 20% of annotations)
You want network metrics (centrality, communities)
You will integrate with AI systems (GraphRAG, MCP)
You want to publish interactive, navigable visualizations





Neo4j Graph Data Science is a library of optimized graph algorithms. A few examples:


// What is the shortest path between "Cost" and "Satisfaction"?
MATCH path = shortestPath((a {name:"Cost"})-[:RELATES_TO*]-(b {name:"Satisfaction"}))
RETURN path
Insight: if there is a direct or indirect path, you can trace it conceptually.



// Which concepts are structurally similar to "Trust"?
// (requires the GDS plugin and a projection called 'myGraph')
CALL gds.nodeSimilarity.stream('myGraph')
YIELD node1, node2, similarity
WHERE gds.util.asNode(node1).name = "Trust"
RETURN gds.util.asNode(node2).name AS similar_code, similarity
ORDER BY similarity DESC
LIMIT 10
Insight: codes with similar connection patterns may be candidates for merging or related categories.



// Pairs that appear together in many items but were never linked by a chain
MATCH (i:Item)-[:MENTIONS]->(a), (i)-[:MENTIONS]->(b)
WHERE a.name < b.name AND NOT (a)-[:RELATES_TO]-(b)
RETURN a.name, b.name, count(DISTINCT i) AS together
ORDER BY together DESC
LIMIT 20
Use: point to where rereading pays off. Appearing together does not mean a relation exists; the decision goes back to the text.





Synesis currently works with text. The graph architecture allows future extensions:

Images: Image nodes connected to Item (annotations on images in visual research)
Audio: AudioSegment nodes with timestamps (oral interview analysis)
Video: VideoFrame nodes (analysis of recorded interactions)
Geo: lat, lon properties on Source for spatial analysis

The graph structure accommodates these naturally — new node types are added while relations stay consistent.







Neo4j Graph Academy — free Cypher courses
The Practitioner’s Guide to Graph Data — free book





Model Context Protocol — connecting assistants to databases
Microsoft GraphRAG — original research





How to export to Neo4j — hands-on guide
synesis-graph — also ArcadeDB (no server) and HTML


Closing thought: graphs do not replace analytical thinking — they amplify patterns already implicit in your data. Just as Synesis does not replace interpretation (it makes it traceable), a graph does not replace analysis (it makes it navigable).
