title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
An honest answer about when Synesis makes sense — and when it does not



“If the final result is a spreadsheet, why learn a language? Why not write everything straight into Excel?”

This question is not cynical. It is methodologically healthy.
Every tool has to justify its cost.




If your project is small, simple and individual: use Excel.
Excel is an extraordinary tool. Flexible, accessible, powerful and universal.
Synesis does not exist to replace Excel. It exists to solve problems that appear when your spreadsheet:

Turns into a web of internal links that is hard to maintain.
Holds information so dense that it becomes visually exhausting.
Needs version control.
Must avoid conflict errors from real-time collaboration.

The difference is not technical. It is structural.




The question is not “which tool is more powerful”.
It is:

Where is the structure that organizes your thinking?

In Excel, structure is implicit. In Synesis, structure is explicit and validated.
The difference seems small at first. It becomes decisive as the project grows.






In Excel you can record:



Code
Relation
Code




Cost
influences
Adoption


cost
INFLUENCES
adoption


Price
affects
Acceptance



Are these three ways of saying the same thing? Or different concepts? Excel does not know. Neither will you remember six months from now.
Excel does not know. It was not built to know.
Yes, you can create a code sheet, use data validation, drop-down lists, cross references. It works. But as the project grows, keeping that discipline becomes manual and fragile.
The Synesis compiler does not depend only on the researcher’s memory or care. It validates content against a declared ontology.
That is not bureaucracy. It is syntactic and semantic control.



In Excel a typical structure is:



Quotation
Code




“The price is too high”
Economic Barrier



But:

Why is this not “Value Perception”?
Was the decision debated?
Did it change over time?
Can you reconstruct the reasoning a year from now?

Yes, you can add note columns. You can create a separate codebook. You can document method decisions. But those layers end up scattered. There is no structural guarantee that interpretation and evidence stay traceably linked.
Synesis can be configured to require interpretation as part of the record — not as an optional comment.
That makes analysis auditable, not merely organized.



Excel can do:

Filters
VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP
Pivot tables
Power Query

It is technically capable.
The problem is not computing power. It is architecture.
Once you add dozens of sources, several researchers and successive revisions, questions appear:

Who changed this code?
In which version was this quotation different?
Why did two spreadsheets diverge?
How to reconcile conflicting classifications?

Excel was not designed as a versionable system.
Synesis works with structured text files. That allows version control, full history and merging of parallel contributions.
For a three-month project this is overkill. For a three-year project it is methodological survival.



Try to represent formally:
Falta de Informação → GERA → Desconfiança → INIBE → Adoção
In Excel this becomes:

Multiple columns
Concatenated strings
Structures to be interpreted later

Nothing stops you. But nothing guarantees structural integrity.
Synesis treats causal chains as formal entities, not descriptive text.
That allows export to:

network analysis
knowledge graphs
automatic validation of relational consistency






It is not learning syntax. It is accepting that:

Concepts must be defined
Relations must be formalized
Interpretations must be justified
Structure must be explicit

Excel lets you postpone these decisions. Synesis makes you take them early. And that is uncomfortable.




Use Excel when:

Data volume is small
Conceptual complexity is low
The project is exploratory
No team is collaborating
Formal traceability is not required
Methodological risk is low

Excel is excellent for exploration, initial organization and visualization. There is no virtue in needless sophistication.




Consider Synesis when:

The vocabulary must be strictly controlled
Several people code at once
The project will continue or be reused
You need to defend method decisions
Causal relations are central to the analysis
Structural integrity is part of the result
You integrate large volumes of AI-generated data (Big Qual)

In these cases the issue is not immediate efficiency. It is the accumulated cost of inconsistency.







Low entry cost
High hidden cost of structural maintenance
Silent errors
Heavy dependence on human discipline





Higher initial cost
Explicit structure from the start
Errors detected early
Methodological scalability






It is not:

“Can I do this in Excel?”

You probably can.
It is:

“What is the cost of inconsistency in this project?”

If the cost is low, Excel will do. If the cost is high, structure is not a luxury — it is epistemological protection.




Synesis does not replace Excel.
Excel is excellent as:

a visualization tool
a means of sharing
an exploration environment
an export format

That is why one of the export formats of the Synesis compiler is precisely Excel. The difference lies in where the source of truth is.
If the source of truth is the spreadsheet, you depend on manual discipline.
If the source of truth is a structured, checkable system, the spreadsheet becomes just an interface.




Synesis is not for everyone. And that is not a flaw — it is focus.
It makes sense when:

Structure matters more than initial speed
Rigor matters more than convenience
Scalability matters more than improvisation


The best tool is the one whose structural cost is proportional to the risk of your project. Sometimes it is Excel. Sometimes it is not.

The Synesis compiler does not depend only on the researcher’s memory or care. It validates content against a declared ontology.
That is not bureaucracy. It is syntactic and semantic control.



In Excel a typical structure is:



Quotation
Code




“The price is too high”
Economic Barrier



But:

Why is this not “Value Perception”?
Was the decision debated?
Did it change over time?
Can you reconstruct the reasoning a year from now?

Yes, you can add note columns. You can create a separate codebook. You can document method decisions. But those layers end up scattered. There is no structural guarantee that interpretation and evidence stay traceably linked.
Synesis can be configured to require interpretation as part of the record — not as an optional comment.
That makes analysis auditable, not merely organized.



Excel can do:

Filters
VLOOKUP / XLOOKUP
Pivot tables
Power Query

It is technically capable.
The problem is not computing power. It is architecture.
Once you add dozens of sources, several researchers and successive revisions, questions appear:

Who changed this code?
In which version was this quotation different?
Why did two spreadsheets diverge?
How to reconcile conflicting classifications?

Excel was not designed as a versionable system.
Synesis works with structured text files. That allows version control, full history and merging of parallel contributions.
For a three-month project this is overkill. For a three-year project it is methodological survival.



Try to represent formally:
Falta de Informação → GERA → Desconfiança → INIBE → Adoção
In Excel this becomes:

Multiple columns
Concatenated strings
Structures to be interpreted later

Nothing stops you. But nothing guarantees structural integrity.
Synesis treats causal chains as formal entities, not descriptive text.
That allows export to:

network analysis
knowledge graphs
automatic validation of relational consistency

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
It is not learning syntax. It is accepting that:

Concepts must be defined
Relations must be formalized
Interpretations must be justified
Structure must be explicit

Excel lets you postpone these decisions. Synesis makes you take them early. And that is uncomfortable.

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
Use Excel when:

Data volume is small
Conceptual complexity is low
The project is exploratory
No team is collaborating
Formal traceability is not required
Methodological risk is low

Excel is excellent for exploration, initial organization and visualization. There is no virtue in needless sophistication.

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
Consider Synesis when:

The vocabulary must be strictly controlled
Several people code at once
The project will continue or be reused
You need to defend method decisions
Causal relations are central to the analysis
Structural integrity is part of the result
You integrate large volumes of AI-generated data (Big Qual)

In these cases the issue is not immediate efficiency. It is the accumulated cost of inconsistency.

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
Low entry cost
High hidden cost of structural maintenance
Silent errors
Heavy dependence on human discipline





Higher initial cost
Explicit structure from the start
Errors detected early
Methodological scalability

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
It is not:

“Can I do this in Excel?”

You probably can.
It is:

“What is the cost of inconsistency in this project?”

If the cost is low, Excel will do. If the cost is high, structure is not a luxury — it is epistemological protection.

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
Synesis does not replace Excel.
Excel is excellent as:

a visualization tool
a means of sharing
an exploration environment
an export format

That is why one of the export formats of the Synesis compiler is precisely Excel. The difference lies in where the source of truth is.
If the source of truth is the spreadsheet, you depend on manual discipline.
If the source of truth is a structured, checkable system, the spreadsheet becomes just an interface.

title: 1 Why Not Just Do It in Excel?
text:
Synesis is not for everyone. And that is not a flaw — it is focus.
It makes sense when:

Structure matters more than initial speed
Rigor matters more than convenience
Scalability matters more than improvisation


The best tool is the one whose structural cost is proportional to the risk of your project. Sometimes it is Excel. Sometimes it is not.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
Who is this document for?



Developers and technical readers who want to understand what happens inside when the Synesis compiler processes a project. No prior knowledge of the source code is needed.
For a high-level overview, see The Compilation Flow. To understand how the compiler connects to the editor through LSP, see The LSP Interface.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
1 What the Compiler Does
The Synesis compiler takes a set of text files with their own syntax (.synp, .synt, .syn, .syno, .bib) and:

Reads and validates each file
Checks consistency between them (e.g. does every code used exist in the dictionary?)
Links the pieces (sources, excerpts, codes, ontology) into a semantic graph
Exports the result as JSON, CSV, Excel and other formats

To follow each stage with concrete examples we use the Basic project — a minimal but complete project.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
2 The Example Project
Before diving into the compiler, look at the files to be processed. They are deliberately simple — they serve as reference throughout the document.

2.1 project.synp — Entry point
PROJECT demo
    TEMPLATE "template.synt"
    INCLUDE BIBLIOGRAPHY "references.bib"
    INCLUDE ANNOTATIONS "annotations.syn"
    INCLUDE ONTOLOGY "ontology.syno"
END PROJECT
This is the “project file”. It says which other files exist and how they relate.


2.2 template.synt — Field schema
SOURCE FIELDS
    OPTIONAL description
END SOURCE FIELDS

FIELD description TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
END FIELD

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED citation, note, code
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD citation TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
END FIELD

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
END FIELD

FIELD code TYPE CODE
    SCOPE ITEM
END FIELD

ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED definition, group
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD definition TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
END FIELD

FIELD group TYPE TOPIC
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
END FIELD
Defines which fields exist, which are required and of what type. It is the contract the rest of the project must respect.


2.3 references.bib — Bibliography
@article{smith2024,
    author = {Smith, Jane},
    title  = {Understanding Community Resilience},
    journal = {Journal of Social Research},
    year   = {2024},
    volume = {12},
    pages  = {45--67}
}
Lists the bibliographic references. Each key (smith2024) identifies a data source.


2.4 annotations.syn — Coded data
SOURCE @smith2024
    description: Qualitative study on community resilience
        strategies in urban contexts.
END SOURCE

ITEM @smith2024
    citation: "People here look out for each other. When the flood
        came, nobody waited for official help — neighbors just
        organized themselves."

    note: Participant describes spontaneous collective action as a
        primary resilience mechanism, bypassing formal institutions.
        Suggests strong bonding social capital.

    code: Social_Cohesion, Collective_Action
END ITEM
Contains the data excerpts and the researcher’s annotations. Each ITEM references a SOURCE through the @bibref key.


2.5 ontology.syno — Code dictionary
ONTOLOGY Social_Cohesion
    definition: The degree to which community members trust,
        support, and cooperate with one another. Applies when
        participants describe solidarity, mutual aid, or a shared
        sense of belonging.
    group: Community_Resilience
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY Collective_Action
    definition: Coordinated efforts by community members to address
        shared challenges without formal institutional direction.
        Applies when groups self-organize in response to a problem
        or crisis.
    group: Community_Resilience
END ONTOLOGY
Defines the meaning of each code used in annotations. It is the project’s controlled vocabulary.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
3 Pipeline Overview
The compiler runs 8 stages in sequence. Each stage receives data from the previous one and produces a richer structure:





flowchart TB
    classDef stage fill:#E0F7FA,stroke:#084C54,stroke-width:2px,color:#084C54,font-weight:bold;
    classDef data fill:#F8FAFC,stroke:#4A5568,stroke-width:1px,color:#084C84;

    S1["1. Project parsing"]:::stage
    D1["ProjectNode"]:::data

    S2["2. Template loading"]:::stage
    D2["TemplateNode"]:::data

    S3["3. Bibliography loading"]:::stage
    D3["Dict of BibEntry"]:::data

    S4["4. Ontology parsing"]:::stage
    D4["List of OntologyNode"]:::data

    S5["5. Annotation parsing"]:::stage
    D5["Lists of SourceNode + ItemNode"]:::data

    S6["6. Semantic validation"]:::stage
    D6["ValidationResult"]:::data

    S7["7. Linking"]:::stage
    D7["LinkedProject"]:::data

    S8["8. Export"]:::stage
    D8["JSON / CSV / Excel ..."]:::data

    S1 --> D1 --> S2 --> D2 --> S3 --> D3 --> S4 --> D4 --> S5 --> D5 --> S6 --> D6 --> S7 --> D7 --> S8 --> D8

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
4 Stage 1 — Project Parsing
Where: compiler.py → SynesisCompiler.parse_project()

4.1 Input
The path of project.synp, passed when creating the compiler.


4.2 What happens

parse_file("project.synp") reads the file and runs the Lark parser — an LALR(1) parser that turns the raw text into a concrete syntax tree (lark.Tree).
SynesisTransformer.transform(tree) walks that tree and builds a typed Python object: the ProjectNode.



4.3 Output
ProjectNode(
    name          = "demo",
    template_path = Path("template.synt"),
    includes      = [
        IncludeNode(include_type="BIBLIOGRAPHY", path="references.bib"),
        IncludeNode(include_type="ANNOTATIONS",  path="annotations.syn"),
        IncludeNode(include_type="ONTOLOGY",      path="ontology.syno"),
    ],
    metadata    = {},
    description = None,
    location    = SourceLocation(file="project.synp", line=1, column=1)
)
The compiler then checks the project structure: files in the directory that were not included, declared files that are not found, a missing template and invalid dates.






SourceLocation — full traceability



Every AST node carries a SourceLocation with the file, line and column it came from. This lets error messages point to the exact place in the source — even in projects with dozens of files.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
5 Stage 2 — Template Loading
Where: parser/template_loader.py → load_template()

5.1 Input
The path of template.synt, taken from ProjectNode.template_path.


5.2 What happens

The .synt file is parsed the same way as the .synp — via Lark + Transformer.
A TemplateNode is built, organizing the fields into categories:

field_specs — dictionary with all field definitions (name, type, scope)
required_fields — which fields are required per scope (SOURCE, ITEM, ONTOLOGY)
optional_fields — which are optional
forbidden_fields — which are forbidden
bundled_fields — which must appear together

validate_template() checks structural inconsistencies — for instance, a field listed as REQUIRED without a FIELD definition.

If the template does not exist or cannot be parsed, compilation ends here: without a contract there is nothing to validate.


5.3 Output
TemplateNode(
    name = "",               # the example has no TEMPLATE line
    field_specs = {
        "description": FieldSpec(type=TEXT,      scope=SOURCE),
        "citation":    FieldSpec(type=QUOTATION, scope=ITEM),
        "note":        FieldSpec(type=MEMO,      scope=ITEM),
        "code":        FieldSpec(type=CODE,      scope=ITEM),
        "definition":  FieldSpec(type=TEXT,       scope=ONTOLOGY),
        "group":       FieldSpec(type=TOPIC,      scope=ONTOLOGY),
    },
    required_fields = {
        SOURCE:   [],
        ITEM:     ["citation", "note", "code"],
        ONTOLOGY: ["definition", "group"],
    },
    optional_fields = {
        SOURCE: ["description"],
        ITEM:     [],
        ONTOLOGY: [],
    },
)
The template works as a contract: from here on, all validation is based on it.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
6 Stage 3 — Bibliography Loading
Where: parser/bib_loader.py → load_bibliography()

6.1 Input
The path of the .bib file.


6.2 What happens
Uses the bibtexparser library to parse BibTeX. It lower-cases all keys, ensuring case-insensitive comparison. Several INCLUDE BIBLIOGRAPHY lines add up; for a repeated key the first occurrence wins. When the project declares INCLUDE DATASET, the TOML records are loaded at this same point.


6.3 Output
{
    "smith2024": {
        "ID":            "smith2024",
        "ENTRYTYPE":     "article",
        "author":        "Smith, Jane",
        "title":         "Understanding Community Resilience",
        "journal":       "Journal of Social Research",
        "year":          "2024",
        "_original_key": "smith2024"
        # ... other fields of the entry
    }
}






Why normalize the keys?



So that @Smith2024, @smith2024 and @SMITH2024 are treated as the same reference. The _original_key field preserves the original spelling for use in exports.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
7 Stage 4 — Ontology Parsing
Where: compiler.py → SynesisCompiler.parse_ontologies()

7.1 Input
List of .syno paths, taken from the IncludeNodes of the ProjectNode.


7.2 What happens
For each .syno file, the same process as the previous stages:

parse_file() produces a lark.Tree
SynesisTransformer.transform() converts it into Python objects

Ontology files are read one after another, in INCLUDE order.


7.3 Output
[
    OntologyNode(
        concept     = "Social_Cohesion",
        description = "",   # filled only by a field called "description"
        fields      = {"definition": "The degree to which community members trust...",
                       "group": "Community_Resilience"},
        field_names = ["definition", "group"],
        location    = SourceLocation("ontology.syno", line=1, column=1)
    ),
    OntologyNode(
        concept     = "Collective_Action",
        description = "",
        fields      = {"definition": "Coordinated efforts by community members...",
                       "group": "Community_Resilience"},
        field_names = ["definition", "group"],
        location    = SourceLocation("ontology.syno", line=9, column=1)
    ),
]

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
8 Stage 5 — Annotation Parsing
Where: compiler.py → SynesisCompiler.parse_annotations()

8.1 Input
List of .syn paths.


8.2 What happens
Same process as Stage 4. A .syn file may contain several SOURCE and ITEM blocks, which the compiler separates into distinct lists. With more than three annotation files, parsing is distributed across up to four processes (ProcessPoolExecutor).






ITEMs are not nested in SOURCEs — yet



At this stage ITEMs are returned in a flat list, separate from SOURCEs. The ITEM → SOURCE link happens only in Stage 7 (Linking), based on the shared @bibref key. This allows SOURCE and ITEM to live in different files.




8.3 Output
# SourceNode
SourceNode(
    bibref   = "@smith2024",       # as written; comparisons use the normalized form
    fields   = {"description": "Qualitative study on community resilience..."},
    items    = [],                 # empty now — filled in Stage 7
    location = SourceLocation("annotations.syn", line=1, column=1)
)

# ItemNode
ItemNode(
    bibref           = "@smith2024",
    quote            = "",         # the QUOTATION field named "citation" lives in extra_fields
    codes            = ["Social_Cohesion", "Collective_Action"],
    notes            = ["Participant describes spontaneous..."],
    chains           = [],
    extra_fields     = {"citation": '"People here look out for each other..."'},
    code_locations   = {"code": [SourceLocation(...), SourceLocation(...)]},
    field_names      = ["citation", "note", "code"],
    location = SourceLocation("annotations.syn", line=6, column=1)
)

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
9 Stage 6 — Semantic Validation
Where: semantic/validator.py → SemanticValidator

9.1 Input
All parsed nodes: ProjectNode, TemplateNode, Dict[BibEntry], lists of SourceNode, ItemNode and OntologyNode.
It also receives a norm_cache: dict — a shared dictionary that memoizes string normalization results, avoiding repeated conversions.


9.2 What happens
SemanticValidator walks every node and applies rules beyond syntax. Concrete examples with the Basic project:



Check
Result in Basic
If it failed




Does @smith2024 exist in the .bib?
Yes
E001: UnregisteredSource (error)


Does Social_Cohesion exist in the ontology?
Yes
E090: summary of undefined codes (warning); with --check-codes, one E004 per occurrence


Are the required fields (citation, note, code) present in the ITEM?
Yes
E020: MissingRequiredField (error)


Is there a field not declared in the template?
No
E022: UnknownFieldName (error)


Do the values respect the declared type (list, scale, chain)?
Yes
Type-specific error





9.3 Output
ValidationResult(
    errors   = [],    # blocks export
    warnings = [],    # does not block, but is reported
    info     = [],    # purely informative
)
In the Basic project everything is correct — the three lists come out empty.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
10 Stage 7 — Linking
Where: semantic/linker.py → Linker.link()
This is the most important stage: it turns a collection of loose nodes into a coherent semantic graph.

10.1 Input
All node lists, the project and the template. Whatever problems the Linker finds are added to the ValidationResult of Stage 6.


10.2 What happens — step by step

ORDERED normalization — the materialized value is always the index, as an integer.
Duplicate bibref check across SOURCE blocks (E070).
ITEM → SOURCE association — each ITEM is linked to the SOURCE with the same bibref, and the SourceNode.items list is filled. An ITEM without a SOURCE is an error (E002); a SOURCE without ITEMs, a warning (E003).
Duplicate concepts and descriptions in the ontology (E068).
Building ontology_index — dictionary {normalized_code → OntologyNode}, with values already interpreted by declared type.
Deprecated terms — with the USE role, mentions of the old term count toward the adopted term.
Building code_usage — dictionary {code → [ItemNode, ...]} answering: “which items used this code?”
Triple extraction — chains such as A -> B -> C become triples (A, relation, B), (B, relation, C), indexed in relation_index.
Building topic_index — ontology TOPIC fields become {topic → [codes]}.
Hierarchy — fields with ROLE HIERARCHY produce role_hierarchy.



10.3 Output
LinkedProject(
    project = ProjectNode(...),

    # Sources now with their items
    sources = {
        "smith2024": SourceNode(
            bibref = "@smith2024",
            items  = [ItemNode(...)]   # filled!
        )
    },

    # Code → definition lookup
    ontology_index = {
        "social_cohesion":   OntologyNode(concept="Social_Cohesion", ...),
        "collective_action": OntologyNode(concept="Collective_Action", ...),
    },

    # Which ITEMs used each code
    code_usage = {
        "social_cohesion":   [ItemNode(...)],
        "collective_action": [ItemNode(...)],
    },

    # CHAIN triples (empty in Basic)
    all_triples    = [],
    relation_index = {},

    # Topics → codes (from the ontology TOPIC field)
    topic_index = {
        "Community_Resilience": ["Social_Cohesion", "Collective_Action"]
    },

    hierarchy      = {},     # older route, via "parent"/"is_a" fields
    role_hierarchy = None,   # filled by fields with ROLE HIERARCHY
    aliases        = {},     # deprecated → adopted (USE role)
)

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
11 Stage 8 — Export
Where: exporters/

11.1 Input
The complete LinkedProject + TemplateNode + bibliography.


11.2 What happens
Each exporter walks the LinkedProject and serializes the data into the target format. On the command line, export only happens if there are no errors (or with --force).


11.3 Output








Format
Module
Content




JSON
json_export.py
Project, template, bibliography, indices, ontology and corpus


CSV
csv_export.py
sources.csv, items.csv, ontologies.csv and, if there are chains, chains.csv


Excel
xls_export.py
Workbook with sheets matching the CSV tables


Alpaca
alpaca_export.py, alpaca_mapped.py
Fine-tuning data


OKF (experimental)
okf_export.py
File-based knowledge bundle


SKOS
skos_export.py
SKOS vocabulary, declared by an EXPORT block in the .synp



Linking several projects (synesis compile p1.synp p2.synp) is a later step, in semantic/link_step.py: see Linking Projects.

title: Inside the Compiler
text:
12 The Orchestrator
Where: compiler.py → SynesisCompiler
The compiler is the conductor — it calls each stage in order and decides what to do with errors:
# Simplified for clarity
def compile(self) -> CompilationResult:
    project, pv = self.parse_project()                      # Stage 1
    sv = self.validate_project_structure(project)
    template, tv = self._safe_load_template(project)        # Stage 2
    if template is None:
        return CompilationResult(success=False, ...)        # ends here
    validate_template(template)
    bibliography = self.load_bibliography(project)          # Stage 3
    dataset, dv = self.load_dataset_index(project, template)
    ontologies, ov = self.parse_ontologies(project)         # Stage 4
    sources, items, av = self.parse_annotations(project)    # Stage 5
    validation = self.validate_all(...)                     # Stage 6
    linked = self.link_all(..., validation_result=validation)  # Stage 7
    # partial results (pv, sv, tv...) are merged into `validation`
    # Stage 8 is triggered by the caller: result.to_json(), etc.

    return CompilationResult(
        success           = not validation.has_errors(),
        linked_project    = linked,
        validation_result = validation,
        stats             = self._compute_stats(linked, sources, items, ontologies),
        template          = template,
        bibliography      = bibliography,
        dataset           = dataset,
    )
The final result is a CompilationResult with all the information:
CompilationResult(
    success = True,
    linked_project    = LinkedProject(...),
    validation_result = ValidationResult(errors=[], warnings=[], info=[]),
    stats = CompilationStats(
        source_count   = 1,
        item_count     = 1,
        ontology_count = 2,
        code_count     = 2,
        chain_count    = 0,
        triple_count   = 0,
    ),
    template     = TemplateNode(...),
    bibliography = {"smith2024": {...}},
    dataset      = None,
)

title: Inside the Compiler
section: 13 Behind the Scenes: the Lark Parser
text:
13 Behind the Scenes: the Lark Parser
All parsing stages (1, 2, 4, 5) share the same internal mechanism.

13.1 How Text Becomes a Tree
Raw text (.syn, .synt, etc.)
        │
        ▼
  SynesisIndenter        ← counts each tab as 4 columns and
        │                   emits INDENT/DEDENT tokens (like Python)
        ▼
  LALR(1) lexer          ← tokenizes: KEYWORD, STRING, IDENTIFIER, NEWLINE...
        │
        ▼
  LALR(1) parser         ← applies the grammar (synesis.lark)
        │
        ▼
  lark.Tree              ← concrete syntax tree
        │
        ▼
  SynesisTransformer     ← turns the tree into typed AST nodes
        │
        ▼
  ProjectNode / SourceNode / ItemNode / OntologyNode / ...
Synesis uses Lark — a Python parsing library that accepts EBNF grammars and generates efficient LALR(1) parsers. The compiler uses a standalone parser generated from synesis.lark. The complete grammar, explained rule by rule, is in Language Grammar.


13.2 How the Tree Becomes Python Objects
SynesisTransformer extends lark.Transformer. Each method corresponds to a grammar rule:
class SynesisTransformer(Transformer):

    def source_block(self, items) -> SourceNode:
        # Extracts the bibref, builds the field dict
        # Returns SourceNode

    def item_block(self, items) -> ItemNode:
        # Separates fields (quote, notes, codes, chains, extra_fields)
        # Preserves raw tokens in field_line_tokens
        # Returns ItemNode

    def ontology_block(self, items) -> OntologyNode:
        # Builds OntologyNode with concept, description and extra fields


13.3 Field Name Normalization
_normalize_field_name("CODE")     # → "code"    (all caps → lowercase)
_normalize_field_name("citation") # → "citation" (unchanged)
_normalize_field_name("MyField")  # → "MyField"  (mixed → unchanged)
This ensures CODE and code in .syn files are treated as the same field.


13.4 Syntax Errors
When the parser finds an error, parse_string() intercepts the Lark exception and raises a SynesisSyntaxError with:

Precise location — file, line and column
Pedagogical message — via create_pedagogical_error(), which turns Lark tokens into readable suggestions
Expected tokens — what the parser expected at that point

text:
16 Most Common Errors



Code
Name
Severity
When it happens




E001

error

The complete list is in the Error Guide.

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text: This document shows how to use Synesis to structure a Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis (PSD) — a process that combines technical data and community perceptions to assess the sustainability of a place. The proposed template integrates qualitative coding, SWOT analysis and dimensions of sustainability in a single compilable structure.

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
2.1 Sources: who said it
SOURCE FIELDS
    REQUIRED ref_type
END SOURCE FIELDS

FIELD ref_type TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Type of reference used
    VALUES
        pri: Primary reference, interviews
        sec: Secondary reference, blogs, newspapers, magazines, podcasts
        ref: Scientific articles, official documents
    END VALUES
END FIELD
Distinguishing pri, sec and ref makes it possible to filter results by type of evidence. Data from community workshops (pri) can be analyzed separately from technical reports (ref).

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
section: 2.2 Items: what was said and how it is interpreted
text:
2.2 Items: what was said and how it is interpreted
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quote, summary, factor, swot, importance
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD quote TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Textual excerpt from the bibliographic source
END FIELD

FIELD summary TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Analytical memo explaining the interpretation
END FIELD

FIELD factor TYPE CODE
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Thematic keyword
END FIELD

FIELD swot TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Elements of the SWOT matrix
    VALUES
        st: Strength (internal perspective)
        we: Weakness (internal perspective)
        op: Opportunity (external perspective)
        th: Threat (external perspective)
    END VALUES
END FIELD

FIELD importance TYPE SCALE
    SCOPE ITEM
    FORMAT [0..2]
    DESCRIPTION Importance of the factor (0=none or low, 1=moderate, 2=high)
END FIELD
Each item combines five field types: QUOTATION (raw data), MEMO (interpretation), CODE (thematic factor linked to the ontology), ENUMERATED (SWOT classification) and SCALE (significance).






Integer scoring



A SCALE declared with integer bounds, such as [0..2], accepts only integer values. That is why importance uses 0, 1 and 2.

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
2.3 Ontology: what each factor means
ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED description, sustainability_dimension
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD description TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Description of the factor
END FIELD

FIELD sustainability_dimension TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Dimensions of sustainability
    VALUES
        environmental: Ecosystems, natural resources, fauna, flora
        sociocultural: Quality of life, cultural values, intergenerational continuity
        economic: Investment, trade, employability
        governance: Infrastructure, legal sustainability, social justice
    END VALUES
END FIELD






Composing types



This template uses 5 field types in a single project: QUOTATION, MEMO, CODE, ENUMERATED and SCALE. Together they express the complete pipeline of our diagnosis: extraction → interpretation → coding → classification → scoring.

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
4.1 Strength
ITEM @workshop_coqueiros2026
    quote: "Small-scale fishing here supports more than half
            of the families. My grandfather already fished in
            this same spot, so did my father."

    summary: Artisanal fishing is the community's main
             economic activity, with intergenerational
             continuity that strengthens both the local
             economy and cultural identity.

    factor: Artisanal_Fishing
    swot: st
    importance: 2
END ITEM
Positive internal factor: artisanal fishing supports families and carries cultural meaning. High importance (2).

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
4.2 Weakness
ITEM @workshop_coqueiros2026
    quote: "People throw rubbish into the mangrove because
            there is no collection. The city hall doesn't
            come here."

    summary: Lack of waste collection leads to improper
             disposal in the mangrove ecosystem, causing a
             direct environmental impact.

    factor: Waste_Disposal
    swot: we
    importance: 1
END ITEM
Negative internal factor: a local practice of improper disposal, aggravated by the absence of a public service. Moderate importance (1).

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
4.3 Opportunity
ITEM @coast_news2026
    quote: "A federal community-based tourism programme has
            selected five coastal villages to receive
            training and infrastructure."

    summary: A government programme may diversify the local
             economy and give value to the community's
             cultural assets.

    factor: Community_Tourism
    swot: op
    importance: 2
END ITEM
Positive external factor: an opportunity for economic diversification coming from public policy. High importance (2).

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
4.4 Threat
ITEM @environmental_report2025
    quote: "Monitoring identified an accelerated rate of
            siltation at the mouth of the Coqueiros river,
            with a 30% reduction in the depth of the main
            channel over the last five years."

    summary: Siltation compromises navigability and fish
             stocks, threatening the community's main
             economic activity.

    factor: Siltation
    swot: th
    importance: 2
END ITEM
Negative external factor: an environmental process independent of the community’s actions that directly affects its sustainability. High importance (2).

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
4.5 More Items
The factors Cultural_Heritage and Basic_Sanitation, present in the ontology, also appear as items:
ITEM @workshop_coqueiros2026
    quote: "The Saint Peter festival and the manioc flour
            gatherings are an old tradition. Everyone takes
            part, even those who left the village come back
            for it."

    summary: Traditional festivities and collective
             production practices reinforce the community's
             social cohesion and cultural identity.

    factor: Cultural_Heritage
    swot: st
    importance: 1
END ITEM

ITEM @workshop_coqueiros2026
    quote: "There is no sewage network. Each one handles it
            their own way --- cesspit, ditch, or straight
            into the river."

    summary: Lack of sewage services produces improvised
             solutions with a risk of water contamination.

    factor: Basic_Sanitation
    swot: we
    importance: 2
END ITEM

title: Participatory Socio-environmental Diagnosis
text:
6.1 Local Sustainability Scale
After exporting the data, the importance points can be combined into a sustainability scale from 0 to 10, where 0 is very unfavourable and 10 very favourable. The formula normalizes the ratio between positive and negative factors:
\[
\text{Scale} = \frac{(S + O) - (W + T)}{(S + O) + (W + T)} \times 5 + 5
\]
Where \(S\), \(O\), \(W\) and \(T\) are the sums of the importance points of strengths, opportunities, weaknesses and threats.
Properties of the formula:

If all factors are positive (\(W + T = 0\)): result = 10
If all are negative (\(S + O = 0\)): result = 0
If positives and negatives balance (\(S + O = W + T\)): result = 5
The result always lies in the interval [0, 10]


6.1.1 Example with the Vila dos Coqueiros data
Adding up the importance points of the items shown:

Importance points by SWOT category







Category
Factors
Importance




Strengths (S)
Artisanal_Fishing (2) + Cultural_Heritage (1)
3


Opportunities (O)
Community_Tourism (2)
2


Weaknesses (W)
Waste_Disposal (1) + Basic_Sanitation (2)
3


Threats (T)
Siltation (2)
2



Applying the formula:
\[
\text{Scale} = \frac{(3 + 2) - (3 + 2)}{(3 + 2) + (3 + 2)} \times 5 + 5 = \frac{0}{10} \times 5 + 5 = 5.0
\]
The result 5.0 places Vila dos Coqueiros in the Stagnation band — positive and negative factors balance out.

Limitations of the formula



The formula requires at least one factor to have been identified (\(S + O + W + T > 0\)), otherwise there is a division by zero. In addition, the result is sensitive to the number of factors: a community with many scored factors tends to converge to 5, while communities with few factors may swing more. For comparisons between communities, it is important to keep consistent coding criteria.

fig.text(0.5, 0.90, current_class,
         ha="center", va="top", fontsize=11, color="#7F8C8D")

title: 1 How Did Synesis Come About?
text:
The original problem

Synesis arose from a concrete study: research on the social acceptance of offshore energy technologies, carried out within OTIC (Offshore Technology Innovation Centre) at the University of São Paulo (USP). The goal was to identify and organize the factors that shape public perception of technological innovations in the context of the energy transition — a problem at once empirical and interpretive.
Addressing it required an integrated workflow combining bibliometric techniques, qualitative coding and artificial intelligence. Tools such as RStudio, the Bibliometrix package and VOSviewer were used to identify the most relevant scientific articles by citation count, exported from databases such as Web of Science and Scopus. Zotero centralized reference management and also served as the initial qualitative annotation environment.


Zotero was not designed for qualitative analysis. Even so, it proved useful for a first phase of open coding: PDFs could be annotated with highlights and comments, tags attached to passages, and the annotations exported in a custom format.
For that, Zotero was configured with custom templates in its advanced preferences. Each exported annotation followed a structure with specific delimiters:
[-begin_header-]
referencia_bibtex: burke2018
descricao: Explores the relationship between renewable energy systems and political power distribution, examining energy democracy as a framework for energy transitions.
modelo_epistemico: Energy democracy, political power theory
metodo: Conceptual review
[-end_header-]

[-begin-][@burke2018@][!Distributed energy-politics posits that distributed energy sources and technologies enable and organize distributed political power and vice versa.!][%Distributed energy systems can reorganize political power structures%][#Energy System#][&correlates-with&][#Governance#][-end-]
The format worked for small, manually reviewed volumes. But it already carried a structural weakness: the delimiters were textual conventions, not a formal grammar. And the human researcher depended on the same informal format to record interpretations.



As the corpus grew — hundreds of abstracts exported as BibTeX and converted to CSV by the bib2csv.py script — processing everything by hand became unfeasible. The solution was to bring in language models through an API to automate the extraction of factors and relations.
The abstract_processor9.py script sent each abstract to the model, with a prompt structured in five parts (system_prompt, task, instructions, relation_types, critical_reminders), and received back the same tag format already used in Zotero. Scale grew. So did the problem.
Language models produce probabilistic text. Regular expressions assume stable patterns. Small variations in the output — an extra space, a badly closed tag, a relation chain out of the expected order — broke parsing. Each adjustment required new regular expressions. The system depended on an ever more fragile balance between model stability, format discipline and the growing complexity of annotations.



To work around the limitations, the toolkit kept growing. editor.py appeared as a visual interface to review and fix the .txt files generated by AI by hand — with right-click support to edit factors, relations and chains. compare_annotations.py was created to measure the distance between what the AI produced and what the researcher meant, using Levenshtein similarity, word overlap and block counts:
INFO: burke2018:
INFO:   Exact Match: 60.0%
INFO:   Levenshtein Similarity: 99.8%
INFO:   Word Overlap: 98.2%
INFO:   Blocks: File1=5, File2=4
docs2txt.py widened the scope beyond scientific abstracts: PDFs, Word documents and HTML pages could now be converted and processed by the same flow — interviews, technical reports, web content. An interactive menu, menu_txt.py, was created just to coordinate the order of the other scripts.
When it became necessary to build a tool only to measure the distance between the AI output and the researcher’s intention, the diagnosis was undeniable: the problem was not technical. It was structural.



As the analysis advanced, the data stopped being tabular records. They came to include semantic chains:
A → influences → B → enables → C
Representing them in a relational database became artificial. Moving to a graph database was natural. But even with suitable storage the problem persisted: the input was still fragile text, not formal structure. The graph was robust; the language feeding it was not.



AI-generated analysis was structured but rigid. Human annotation was flexible but informal. New fields had to be added, interpretations recorded, codes revised, chains expanded, the ontology evolved. The tag-based system made that evolution hard: every structural change required modifying parsing, storage and often the prompt.
The problem became clear: how to integrate structured analysis generated by AI with organic human annotation without sacrificing consistency or flexibility?



The answer was not a better database, nor more sophisticated regular expressions. What was needed was explicit syntax, formal parsing, semantic validation and a separation between language and configuration.
Hence the idea of turning the annotation format into a language proper, a domain-specific language (DSL):
SOURCE @burke2018
    descricao: Explores the relationship between renewable energy systems and political power distribution, examining energy democracy as a framework for energy transitions.
    modelo_epistemico: Energy democracy, political power theory
    metodo: Conceptual review
END SOURCE

ITEM @burke2018
    text: Distributed energy-politics posits that distributed energy sources and technologies enable and organize distributed political power and vice versa.

    note: Distributed energy systems can reorganize political power structures

    chain: Energy_System -> influences -> Governance
END ITEM
This new approach let human and AI-generated annotation pass through the same text and the same rules, checked by a compiler.



Synesis is not a middle layer between AI and database.
It is the point where two processes converge: structured, scalable generation by AI, and contextual, evolving human interpretation. Both operate in the same language.
AI can produce annotations in Synesis. The researcher can edit, extend and reinterpret them. The compiler guarantees consistency and traceability.
Structure does not eliminate interpretation. It organizes it.



Synesis answers a contemporary problem: AI models generate structured text, but text is not reliable structure. Without grammar, validation and a controlled ontology, analysis becomes hard to maintain, version and audit.
Synesis formalizes that structure without preventing evolution.
It was born from practical friction — in a real research problem, with real data, in a workflow that grew until its own patches became the obstacle. And it keeps evolving from that same friction.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text: AI-assisted qualitative coding depends critically on the language model used. Different models produce annotations with distinct levels of relational precision, thematic coverage and syntactic conformity. This document presents a comparative evaluation of five LLMs applied to the same scientific abstract, using a manually reviewed gold-standard annotation as reference.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
1.1 Original Abstract (in full)

Electric vehicles are regarded as energy transition technology towards more sustainable and environment-friendly transportation systems. Despite the benefits of reducing the dependence on fossil fuels and greenhouse gas emissions, the adoption of electric vehicles faces several obstacles ranging from financing issues, government policies, and public acceptance. This study aims to identify the economic, environmental, and social impact of the adoption of electric vehicles for public transportation. Using the Philippines as a case study, the findings highlight the economic advantage of investing in electric public transportation with high public acceptance. The results further identify significant decrease in air pollution, reduction of greenhouse gas emissions and encourage lowering the reliance on imported fossil fuels by shifting the public transport from conventional to electric transport system. This study recommends stricter implementation of government policies on modernized public transportation, stronger government support on financing mechanisms, establishment of charging stations in public and private terminals, and boosting programs for developing local-made electric vehicles. To make electric vehicle more environment-friendly, the government must accelerate the energy transition by increasing the electricity share from renewable sources and investing in more sustainable sources of energy.

This abstract was chosen because it contains multiple causal mechanisms — barriers to adoption, enabling relations, environmental effects and policy recommendations — offering a rich test field for assessing each model’s analytical capability.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.1 Variation Is Not Error
Qualitative research and, consequently, the pursuit of objectivity and rigour involve a series of questions. First, the fact that there are different highlights and codings does not invalidate the effort of qualitative analysis. One of the main points, as we will see below, is the transparency and traceability of data. Just as all research — qualitative or quantitative — requires constant review cycles, AI-assisted qualitative coding is not exempt from the same approach.
Analysis of the items extracted by the models reveals a sophisticated effort to translate the text into chains of causal and logical relations, following the instructions in the prompt (GUIDELINES) to look for causal relations. However, although extraction captures the themes of the abstract, analytical precision varies. At several points the interpretation goes beyond the original text, forcing causal and sequential relations where the text presents only correlation or parallel lists.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.2 The Problem of Ontological Granularity
Ideally, the codes (factors) assigned to the text would keep the same wording used in the original context. In an extensive corpus, however, this would produce a high degree of factor granularity, making analysis infeasible. Here topic modelling techniques are essential to group semantically close concepts under labels that preserve meaning without proliferating indefinitely.
In Synesis the template defines granularity control rules (Factor Granularity Control) that guide both the human researcher and the AI model on when to preserve a term’s specificity and when to generalize it. Even so, as the results show, each model draws that line differently.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.3 Coding as an Interpretive Process
According to Saldaña (2009, p. 3), “a code in qualitative inquiry is most often a word or short phrase that symbolically assigns a summative, salient, essence-capturing, and/or evocative attribute for a portion of language-based or visual data.” It is in this sense that we use the term factor in Synesis.
Crucially, the coding process is directly influenced by each researcher’s analytical lens; the same data set can be coded in many different ways (Saldaña, 2009, pp. 7–8). This applies equally to AI models: each has its own interpretive biases affecting excerpt selection, concept naming and relation choice.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.4 Factors as Fuzzy Concepts
Fuzzy set logic, introduced by Zadeh (1965), offers a theoretical basis for understanding why variation in coding is not arbitrary. According to Zadeh, the classes of objects encountered in the real physical world do not have precisely defined criteria of membership (Zadeh, 1965, p. 338). Unlike Boolean algebra (where an element either belongs to a set or not), in fuzzy logic the degree of membership is a continuum.
In qualitative coding, similar terms — such as bathing use, beach access, sea bathing — may be associated with the same factor (Bathing_Quality) with varying degrees of affinity without that being arbitrary. Ragin (2008), applying this logic to sociology, argues that qualitative analysis is fundamentally about establishing relations (Ragin, 2008, p. 2) between theoretical sets, and that attention to consistent connections is the cornerstone of the technique commonly known as analytic induction (Ragin, 2008, p. 2).
This is directly relevant to the present comparison: when two models give different names to the same concept (e.g. Financial_Barrier vs Financing), the question is not which name is “right”, but which better preserves the concept’s function within the project’s network of relations.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.5 Rigour Criteria for AI-assisted Coding
Shenton (2004) sets out four criteria for grounding qualitative research, adapted from the traditional criteria of the natural sciences:

Credibility (instead of validity): how congruent are the findings with reality? In AI-assisted coding this shows in the traceability of each chain to the source text — none of the models tested hallucinated, which is a positive indicator of credibility.
Transferability (instead of generalization): are the results applicable to other contexts? Comparison across multiple models shows that the structural findings (barriers, enablers, environmental effects) are consistent across models, even if granularity varies.
Dependability (instead of reproducibility): is the process explicit enough to be replicated? Standardized prompts, declarative templates and documented command lines support procedural dependability.
Confirmability (instead of objectivity): do the findings reflect the data and not the researcher’s bias? In Shenton’s words, the beliefs underpinning decisions made and methods adopted should be acknowledged within the research report (Shenton, 2004, p. 72). In the AI context this translates into the audit trail — the record of each interpretive decision, which in Synesis is materialized by the note field of each ITEM.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
section: 2.6 The Audit Trail as a Differentiator
text:
2.6 The Audit Trail as a Differentiator
The audit trail is central to giving coding its rigour:

Qualitative researchers use the audit trail to establish a study’s rigour by providing the details of data analysis and some of the decisions that led to the findings. […] This record provides evidence that the raw data went through a process of analysis, reduction and synthesis. (Wolf, 2003, p. 175)

In Synesis the audit trail operates at several levels: in the note field of each ITEM (justifying the interpretation), in factor memos (documenting merges and splits) and in the ontology (recording the modal classification of each concept). This means that even when two models produce different annotations, both are auditable — the researcher can trace each decision and evaluate it critically.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
2.7 Technical Limitations
AI-assisted coding applies advanced LLMs that still need calibration for specific domains. A future strategy might involve building corpora extensively reviewed by competent researchers and using them to calibrate models, yielding significant gains in hermeneutic accuracy. It is therefore necessary to acknowledge the quality achieved while seeking constant improvement.






Implication for reading the results



Quantitative differences between models (number of ITEMs, chain coverage) should be read in light of this discussion: more ITEMs does not necessarily mean better analysis, just as fewer chains does not necessarily mean worse coverage. The decisive criterion is interpretive quality — the ability to identify correct causal mechanisms, select appropriate relations and produce analytical notes that add value for the researcher.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
8.1 Relation Selection
The most important differentiator between models is the choice of relation (CONSTRAINS vs ENABLES vs INFLUENCES vs RELATES-TO). The reference uses:

CONSTRAINS for the three barrier factors (financing, policy, public acceptance)
RELATES-TO for the economic benefit ↔︎ social acceptance association (generic, non-causal association)
INFLUENCES for the effects of electrification on the environment
ENABLES for the enablers and the energy chain

Opus reproduced this selection exactly. The other models made polarity errors:








Model
Error
Impact




Haiku
Public_Acceptance -> INFLUENCES (should be CONSTRAINS)
Loses the barrier semantics


Sonnet
Economic_Benefit -> INFLUENCES (reference uses RELATES-TO)
Imposes causality where there is association


Gemma4
Public_Acceptance -> ENABLES (should be CONSTRAINS)
Reverses the meaning of the source text


Qwen
Public_Acceptance -> ENABLES -> Investment
Captures a different mechanism (valid, but not matching the reference)

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
8.2 Parallel Decomposition vs Compression
The reference decomposes parallel factors into separate ITEMs — three ITEMs for the barriers (Axis 1) and four for the enablers (Axis 4). This follows the template GUIDELINES, which instruct:

PARALLEL (X,Y,Z→A): Create SEPARATE ITEM blocks when multiple factors independently affect the same outcome.


Opus: complete decomposition (12 ITEMs) — identical to the reference
Qwen: partial decomposition — decomposed barriers (3 ITEMs) but not enablers
Gemma4: partial decomposition — decomposed barriers but with a relational error
Haiku and Sonnet: compressed everything into 5 ITEMs — not decomposed

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
8.3 Format and Encoding
Two models produced output with format problems:

Sonnet: added double quotes ("...") to the text field, which alters the value stored by the compiler. It also showed corrupted em-dash characters (ÔÇö instead of ---).
Gemma4: added single quotes ('...') to the text field, inconsistent with Synesis convention.







UTF-16 encoding



All output files from the Anthropic models were encoded as UTF-16LE with BOM. This is an artefact of PowerShell redirection (>>), not of the model itself.

title: Comparing AI Models for Qualitative Coding
text:
10.1 Practical Recommendations

For production (final corpus): Claude Opus 4.6 — superior relational precision and structural coverage.
For quick drafting / triage: Claude Haiku 4.5 — clean format, high speed, low cost; requires human review of relations and decomposition.
For environments without a commercial API: Qwen 3.5:397b — best open-weight model tested, with good barrier decomposition; requires review of the enabler axes.

title: How the Benchmark Was Run
text:
What this page is



It is the methodological appendix of Vector Embeddings and GraphRAG, for those who want to audit the experiment instead of accepting the numbers. Here are the complete gold standard of 40 questions, the description of the scripts, the exact queries sent to the database and the question-by-question results.
You do not need to read this to use the feature. You need to read it to check that it does what we say.

title: How the Benchmark Was Run
text:
1 Summary for the Reviewer







Corpus
Social_Acceptance — 1,388 concepts on social acceptance of energy transition technologies


Database
ArcadeDB 26.7.3, database social_acceptance, queried through the HTTP API


Embedding model
sentence-transformers/all-mpnet-base-v2, 768 dimensions, local


Indexes
FULL_TEXT (Lucene/BM25) and LSM_VECTOR (cosine, INT8 quantization)


Sample
40 concepts drawn with fixed seed 20260817


Gold standard
One question per concept, frozen before any search


Depth
top-10; RRF with the standard constant k = 60


Measurement date
17 August 2026









Where the numbers come from



All values on this page come from the run of 17 August 2026 against a real ArcadeDB database. The gold standard, the scripts and the raw output live in the case-studies/benchmark_rrf folder of this documentation project, which is not yet published in a public repository. The page reads the results directly from the file generated by the measurement, so the result tables and charts are not typed by hand.

title: How the Benchmark Was Run
section: 2 The Design, and What It Protects Against
text:
2 The Design, and What It Protects Against
The central trap in any search comparison is writing the question after seeing what each method returned. Whoever does that can prove anything. The design below exists to make that impossible.





flowchart TB
    classDef stageA fill:#E8F5E9,stroke:#2E7D32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1B5E20,font-weight:bold;
    classDef frozen fill:#FFF3E0,stroke:#E65100,stroke-width:2px,color:#E65100,font-weight:bold;
    classDef stageB fill:#E0F7FA,stroke:#084C54,stroke-width:2px,color:#084C54,font-weight:bold;

    S["1 · Draw of 40 concepts<br/>fixed seed 20260817"]:::stageA
    Q["2 · One question per concept<br/>deliberately disjoint vocabulary"]:::stageA
    F["3 · Gold standard frozen in a file<br/>questions.json"]:::frozen
    R["4 · Only then: the three searches<br/>BM25 · Vector · RRF"]:::stageB
    M["5 · Metrics computed<br/>results.json"]:::stageB

    S --> Q --> F --> R --> M






Step 3 is what gives value to steps 4 and 5: the gold standard is a separate file, written before any search.






Where this design comes from





Nothing here was invented for the occasion. The design follows the established standard for evaluation in Information Retrieval, described in Manning et al. (2008) — the canonical reference of the field, freely accessible.

The test collection structure (documents + information needs + relevance judgements) is that of chapter 8.2, the same as the Cranfield collection and the TREC rounds. Our equivalent: the 1,388 concepts, the 40 questions and the target concept of each.
Freezing the judgements before running the searches is what separates a test collection from a demonstration — the alternative (judging after seeing the output) measures the evaluator, not the system.
The metrics (Recall@k, MRR, nDCG) are those of chapter 8.4. The logarithmic discount of nDCG, 1/log₂(1+position), is used here exactly as defined there; with a single relevant item per question, the ideal ranking is worth 1 and DCG is already nDCG.
The BM25 that ArcadeDB runs is the probabilistic model of chapter 11.4.3, with frequency saturation (k₁) and document length normalization (b) — formalized in Robertson & Zaragoza (2009).
RRF fusion comes from Cormack et al. (2009), including the constant k = 60.

Where our design diverges from the standard, this is declared in Design limitations — above all regarding who wrote the questions and the adoption of a single answer per question.




2.1 Step 1 — the draw
Simple random sampling over the 1,388 concepts, with a fixed seed and deterministic ordering before the draw (without it, file reading order would change the sample between runs).
#| eval: false
SEED, N = 20260817, 40

names = sorted(concepts)          # deterministic order BEFORE drawing
rng = random.Random(SEED)
sample = sorted(rng.sample(names, N))
Full script: case-studies/benchmark_rrf/sample_concepts.py. Running it again with the same seed produces exactly the same sample.


2.2 Step 2 — the questions
For each concept drawn, one natural-language question following a single verifiable rule:

No content word of the concept name may appear in the question.

The aim is to simulate the researcher who describes the phenomenon in their own words because they did not memorize the ontology’s controlled vocabulary. The rule was checked by code, not by eye — and the check caught a real violation (Technology_Uptake × “technology”), fixed before any search ran:


Show code
import json, re
from pathlib import Path

BASE = Path("../../case-studies/benchmark_rrf")
gold_standard = json.loads((BASE / "questions.json").read_text(encoding="utf-8"))

STOP = {"the","a","an","of","to","in","and","or","that","is","are","how","what","for",
        "not","it","on","who","which","by","from","with","as","at","all","just","out",
        "up","so","be","do","does","get","gets","has","have","they","their","you","we",
        "its","into","than","then","only","more","most","some","several","through",
        "over","about","before","after","when","where","whether","while","why"}

def words(text):
    return {w for w in re.findall(r"[a-z]+", text.lower()) if w not in STOP and len(w) > 2}

violations = [
    p["gold"] for p in gold_standard["pairs"]
    if words(p["gold"].replace("_", " ")) & words(p["question"])
]
print(f"questions: {len(gold_standard['pairs'])}")
print(f"rule violations: {len(violations)} {violations}")


questions: 40
rule violations: 0 []




2.3 Step 3 — the three searches
All run inside ArcadeDB, with no reimplementation in Python. That is the difference between measuring the product and measuring an approximation of it.
Keyword search (BM25) — FULL_TEXT index, ordered by the Lucene score:
SELECT name, $score as s FROM Chain
WHERE SEARCH_INDEX('Chain[search_name,ontology_description,reasoning,
                    rgt_element_a,rgt_element_b,theoretical_significance]',
                   '<question>') = true
ORDER BY s DESC LIMIT 10
Search by meaning — LSM_VECTOR index, nearest neighbours of the question vector:
SELECT expand(vector.neighbors('Chain[embedding]', :v, 10))
The vector :v is generated locally with the same model that embedded the corpus. Using different models on the two sides would produce meaningless neighbours — a silent failure, because the database accepts the vector and returns wrong results without complaint.
Fusion (RRF) — the standard formula of the IR (Information Retrieval, the field that studies search systems) literature, adding the two lists without normalizing scales:


Show code
def fuse_rrf(rank_lists, k=10, RRF_K=60):
    scores = {}
    for ranking in rank_lists:
        for position, name in enumerate(ranking, start=1):
            scores[name] = scores.get(name, 0.0) + 1.0 / (RRF_K + position)
    return [n for n, _ in sorted(scores.items(), key=lambda kv: -kv[1])][:k]


The constant 60 was not tuned to favour the result: it is the value proposed in the article that introduced the method (Cormack et al., 2009), kept untuned precisely to avoid introducing one more degree of freedom. That work already showed the effect we find again here — rank fusion outperforms individual methods, including learning-to-rank methods.

3.1 The Three Findings


Show code

r10_bm, r10_rrf = M["bm25"]["Recall@10"], M["rrf"]["Recall@10"]
mrr_bm, mrr_rrf = M["bm25"]["MRR"], M["rrf"]["MRR"]

**1. Fusion wins on all seven metrics.** That was not guaranteed: if one method were superior
on its own, fusion would be cost without return. The average position of the right answer

hit rate goes from {pct(r10_bm)} to {pct(r10_rrf)}.

**2. Meaning alone does not dominate.** For 1st place, vector search
({num(M['vector']['Recall@1'])}) falls **below** keyword search ({num(M['bm25']['Recall@1'])}).
A corpus of 1,388 concepts has many semantic neighbours, and choosing between

**{o['so_bm25']}** only exact word ranks 1st and **{o['so_vetor']}** only meaning does.

1. Fusion wins on all seven metrics. That was not guaranteed: if one method were superior on its own, fusion would be cost without return. The average position of the right answer rises from 0.421 to 0.552 (+31%), and the top-10 hit rate goes from 57.5% to 87.5%.
2. Meaning alone does not dominate. For 1st place, vector search (0.325) falls below keyword search (0.350). A corpus of 1,388 concepts has many semantic neighbours, and choosing between near-synonyms is exactly where vectors hesitate.
3. The errors do not overlap — and that is what makes fusion work. Of the 40 cases, only 5 are ranked 1st by both methods; 9 only exact word ranks 1st and 8 only meaning does. That is, 17 questions are solved by exactly one of the two. Methods that failed together would have nothing to gain from fusion.

title: How the Benchmark Was Run
section: 5 What Went Wrong, and Was Not Hidden
text:
5 What Went Wrong, and Was Not Hidden

5.1 Fusion Can Lose a Target One of the Methods Found


Show code
losses = [r for r in res["por_pergunta"]
          if r["rrf"]["rank"] is None and (r["bm25"]["rank"] or r["vector"]["rank"])]
print(f"In **{len(losses)} of the 40 questions**, the target appeared in the top-10 of a single method "
      f"but vanished from the fusion top-10:\n")
for r in losses:
    b = r["bm25"]["rank"] or "—"
    v = r["vector"]["rank"] or "—"
    print(f"- `{r['gold']}` — word: {b} · meaning: {v} · fusion: outside the top-10")

In 3 of the 40 questions, the target appeared in the top-10 of a single method but vanished from the fusion top-10:

Benefit — word: — · meaning: 10 · fusion: outside the top-10
Capital_Cost — word: — · meaning: 6 · fusion: outside the top-10
Energy_Transformation — word: — · meaning: 6 · fusion: outside the top-10


This is not an implementation defect: it is how RRF works. When the target is deep in only one list (6th to 10th position) and the other method contributes ten different candidates, the sum of weights pushes the target past the cut-off. It is the price of fusing without normalizing scales — and the reason fusion wins in aggregate without winning on every individual question.


5.2 Generic Concepts Are Intrinsically Ambiguous
Four sampled targets — Context, Driver, Benefit and Time — are generic labels in a corpus of 1,388 items. The question “the surrounding circumstances that frame how everything else is interpreted” legitimately matches dozens of concepts.
They were kept in the sample. Removing them after seeing that they give poor results would be exactly the contamination the frozen gold standard exists to prevent. They drag the metrics down, and that is honest.


5.3 Design Limitations
1. Whoever wrote the questions knew the answer. The 40 questions were written by a language model (Claude Opus 5) looking at the description of each concept. Even with the disjoint vocabulary rule, someone who knows the target tends to describe it in a retrievable way. This is the most serious limitation of this measurement — and the literature is explicit about it: Manning, Raghavan and Schütze recommend that information needs be designed by domain experts and warn against using random combinations of query terms as a substitute for real needs (2008, ch. 8.5). Questions collected from real researchers without access to the ontology would be more faithful — and would probably produce worse numbers.
2. One corpus, one language. Everything here is Social_Acceptance, in English, with all-mpnet-base-v2. Another language, model or conceptual density changes the numbers. Measure on your project before assuming the same gain.
3. A single answer per question. The gold standard allows only one correct concept. A good share of the “errors” are neighbours a researcher would accept in a conversation. A gold standard with multiple valid answers would give higher and more realistic numbers — at the cost of a subjective judgement about what counts as acceptable. The problem is well known: human relevance judgement is not a device that reliably reports a gold standard, being quite idiosyncratic and variable (2008, ch. 8.5), which is why reference collections usually measure inter-judge agreement (the kappa statistic) instead of assuming a single obvious gold standard.
4. Forty questions show a pattern, not a distribution. The qualitative conclusion (errors do not overlap) is robust; the decimals should not be treated as constants of the system. For calibration: the early rounds of TREC — the reference in the field — used 50 information needs each (2008, ch. 8.2). With 40, this experiment is of the same order of magnitude as established collections, but at the lower end; more questions would give more stable estimates.

The files below belong to the case-studies/benchmark_rrf folder mentioned above, not yet published.

text:
7 References
The design, the metrics and the two search methods follow the established Information Retrieval literature. For those who want to check the definitions at the source:
Manning et al. (2008) — Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press. Freely available at nlp.stanford.edu/IR-book. The chapters that support this experiment:








Chapter
What it covers
Where it is used here




6 — Scoring, term weighting & the vector space model
Vector space model
Conceptual basis of search by meaning


8.2 — Standard test collections
Test collection structure; TREC with 50 needs per round
The gold standard design and the sample size discussion


8.4 — Evaluation of ranked retrieval results
Precision@k, MAP, nDCG and its logarithmic discount
The metrics used

Variability of human judgement, inter-judge agreement (kappa)

11.4.3 — Okapi BM25

What ArcadeDB’s FULL_TEXT index runs



Robertson & Zaragoza (2009) — full treatment of the probabilistic relevance framework and BM25 by the authors of the model.
Cormack et al. (2009) — the article that introduced Reciprocal Rank Fusion, the source of the formula and the constant k = 60 used here.






What the literature corroborates, and what it does not



Corroborates: the test collection structure, the requirement to freeze judgements before measuring, the three metrics and their interpretation, the two search methods and the fusion formula. None of these elements is a local invention.
Does not corroborate — and could not: the values obtained. No reference predicts performance on a specific corpus; the result from one corpus does not transfer to another. That is why the practical recommendation remains to measure on your own project.

title: About Synesis
text:
How can the data of a qualitative study with hundreds of sources, dozens of concepts and complex relations among them be organized rigorously and replicably?
That question followed the same researcher for more than a decade — and each attempt to answer it became a step in building what is today the Synesis language.
The language was formally born in 2026, but its history did not begin that year. Its architecture, domain vocabulary and methodological requirements result from a path started decades earlier, along which two lines of experience advanced until they converged: the practice of software development and qualitative research. BDM, SocioAtlas, the socio-environmental diagnosis pipeline, SocioAtlas for Google Sheets and DGT7 were not disconnected projects but successive implementations of one same effort. Each solved part of the problem, revealed new limits and left conceptual or technical components that would be incorporated into Synesis.
