The meaning of each code is in the Error Guide.





This specification details features under consideration for a future version of the Synesis language. The focus is to evolve the language from a linear annotation system into a knowledge management system (Zettelkasten), and to introduce native support for canonical loci (sacred texts).




An addressing system specialized for sacred texts that use the Locus pattern (Book, Chapter, Verse). To keep the grammar intact, canonical addressing would be implemented through a specific field type (TYPE PERICOPE), leaving the standard block structure untouched.
Today the same address can be recorded in a TYPE TEXT field, without format validation.


No block is replaced. The SOURCE block is still used to reference the bibliographic work (the specific translation or manuscript via BibTeX). The analytical unit (ITEM) receives a field typed as PERICOPE to identify the exact passage.
Syntax in the .syn file:
SOURCE @niv2011
    translation_type: Dynamic equivalence
END SOURCE

# The ITEM references the translation and gives the locus in a field
ITEM @niv2011
    passage: ROM 8:28-30, 32a
    quote: "And we know that in all things God works for the good..."
    code: Providence
END ITEM



The parser would apply strict rules to identify books, with ergonomic flexibility in verse punctuation:

USX code (strict): exactly 3 capital letters for the book (e.g. MAT, GEN, ROM). Full names would not be accepted, to avoid ambiguity.
Chapter separator (flexible): both colon (:) and period (.) separate chapter and verse (e.g. ROM 8:1 or ROM 8.1). The syntax tree (AST) normalizes the variation.
Verses and subdivisions: hyphen - for ranges and comma , for lists, with lowercase letters attached to numbers for exegetical subdivisions (e.g. 6a, 6b).




In the .synt file the field would be declared with type PERICOPE and scope ITEM.
TEMPLATE biblical_exegesis

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED passage, quote
    OPTIONAL code
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD passage TYPE PERICOPE
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Canonical locus address (Book Chap:Verses)
END FIELD

FIELD quote TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Textual excerpt from the bibliographic source
END FIELD



Sketch of how the value of a PERICOPE field would be processed by the language rules:
// The strict rule that processes the Locus field value
pericope_value: usx_code WS INT separator verse_list

// USX codes (strictly 3 capital letters)
usx_code: UCASE_LETTER~3

// The separator (accepts both common academic formats)
separator: ":" | "."

// Verse list with commas and optional spaces
verse_list: verse_node ("," WS? verse_node)*

// A node may be a single verse or a range
verse_node: verse_single | verse_single "-" verse_single

// The verse: a number followed by an optional lowercase letter (e.g. 6a)
verse_single: INT /[a-z]?/



In the compiler:

Template parser: add PERICOPE to the list of field types, alongside TEXT, QUOTATION, MEMO, CHAIN etc.
Lark grammar: create the pericope_value rule.
Transformer (Python): split the string into a dictionary (book, chapter, verses).

The relation between ITEM and SOURCE, BibTeX validation and BUNDLE validation would not change; exporters would treat the new field like any field defined in the template.
In the VS Code extension:

Syntax highlighting: a regular expression for the canonical pattern (e.g. \b[A-Z]{3}\s\d+[:.]\d+[\d\-,a-z\s]*\b).
Snippets: autocomplete the ITEM block with the locus field already in place.
Code Actions (optional): convert “Romans 8, 1 to 3” into ROM 8:1-3 as a quick-fix suggestion, without touching the compiler.






There is a converter from the proprietary Logos annotation format to Markdown text:

Logos Bible Software notes to Markdown converter

From there, converting Markdown annotations into Synesis is simple.




Synesis offers structural flexibility to researchers who need to compare manuscripts or translations of the same passage. Since an ITEM belongs to exactly one SOURCE, there are two approaches, depending on how the data will be used later. The examples use the proposed PERICOPE type; today, declare these fields as TEXT.


Prioritizes bibliographic rigour. Each base text (e.g. the Greek original and an English translation) is treated as a separate work in a SOURCE block. The annotation blocks correlate because the locus field acts as a relationship key.
SOURCE @na28
    language: "grc"
END SOURCE

ITEM @na28
    passage: ROM 8:1
    quote: "Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα..."
END ITEM

SOURCE @niv2011
    language: "en"
END SOURCE

ITEM @niv2011
    passage: ROM 8:1
    quote: "Therefore, there is now no condemnation..."
END ITEM
Analytical advantage: produces normalized flat tables suited to Data Science workflows — translations can be grouped in Python (Pandas) or queried in graph databases, connecting nodes through the locus property.



If the focus is visual and hermeneutical juxtaposition, and the base text is an interlinear or parallel Bible, use the BUNDLE modifier, which guarantees positional correspondence between version and excerpt.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED passage
    REQUIRED BUNDLE version, quote  # Fields tied by position
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD passage TYPE PERICOPE
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Canonical address
END FIELD

FIELD version TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Abbreviation of the bibliographic translation
    VALUES
        NA28: Nestle-Aland (Greek)
        NIV: New International Version
        ESV: English Standard Version
    END VALUES
END FIELD

FIELD quote TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Excerpt matching the version
END FIELD
In the annotation (.syn):
ITEM @interlinear_bible2025
    passage: ROM 8:1

    # -- Bundle pair 1 --
    version: NA28
    quote: "Οὐδὲν ἄρα νῦν κατάκριμα..."

    # -- Bundle pair 2 --
    version: NIV
    quote: "Therefore, there is now no condemnation..."
END ITEM
Analytical advantage: keeps the comparison cohesive in one block. The compiler raises an error if a version is annotated without its excerpt, or the reverse, and ENUMERATED accepts only the versions declared in VALUES.





The Synesis ecosystem is agnostic about the research domain. Configurable field types allow modelling the complexity of legal texts (legislation and case law) without changing the SOURCE and ITEM block structure.


Normative texts require structured, non-linear addressing.

Suggested field type: TYPE LEGAL_LOCUS
Parser behaviour: capture and structure the topography of the law (act, article, paragraph, item, sub-item). Example target syntax (Brazilian law): CF/88 Art. 5, inc. X.




Court decisions have strict categories, which can already be enforced today with ENUMERATED.

Common categories: Ratio Decidendi (main thesis), Obiter Dictum (side remark) and Headnote (official summary).




Mapping how decisions relate over time can use qualified chains (CHAIN). The proposal adds the use of bibliographic references as chain nodes.



TEMPLATE legal_analysis

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED locus, quote
    OPTIONAL legal_concept, chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD locus TYPE LEGAL_LOCUS
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Normative or case-law topographic address
END FIELD

FIELD legal_concept TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Structural classification of the court decision
    VALUES
        RATIO: Ratio Decidendi (main thesis)
        OBITER: Obiter Dictum (side argument)
        HEADNOTE: Official summary
    END VALUES
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    RELATIONS
        OVERRULES: A higher court overturns the previous thesis
        CITES_PRECEDENT: Decision grounded in a previous case
        DISTINGUISHES: Current case distinguished from the general rule
    END RELATIONS
END FIELD
SOURCE @stj_petition_1234
    access_date: 2026-02-17
END SOURCE

ITEM @stj_petition_1234
    locus: CF/88 Art. 5, inc. X
    legal_concept: RATIO
    quote: "intimacy, private life, honor and image of persons are inviolable..."

    # Precedent graph between bibliographic works (rulings)
    chain: @stj_petition_1234 -> OVERRULES -> @tj_decision_999
END ITEM
Expected advantage: exported to relational (CSV) or graph formats, the project would give the researcher the precedent network with its legal topology and traceability to the text.
For the modelling that already works today, see Synesis for Legal Professionals.





Introduces “Permanent Notes” that synthesize knowledge. To preserve the language invariants, the Zettelkasten would not be a new block but a set of specialized fields inside the ITEM.


Since every ITEM belongs to a SOURCE, a BibTeX entry representing the author’s note repository is recommended (e.g. @zettel_vault).
# The "Source" is the researcher's own repository
SOURCE @zettel_vault
    access_date: 2026-02-17
END SOURCE

# The ITEM acts as the Permanent Note (Zettel)
ITEM @zettel_vault
    zettel_id: 2026011401
    title: "The Principle of Atomicity"
    body: "A DSL should force concepts to be broken down..."

    # Explicit connections
    links: 2026011205, 2025123001

    # Metadata and traceability
    topic: DSL_Design
    origin: @turing1936
END ITEM



New types would support the graph topology of a Zettelkasten, with cross-validation at the linking stage:

ZETTEL_ID: unique note identifier (usually a timestamp); the compiler would guarantee there are no duplicate IDs.
ZETTEL_LINK: creates directed edges between notes; the compiler would check that referenced IDs exist.
BIB_REF: references an external source directly in the field, creating a citation edge.

TEMPLATE zettel_knowledge_base

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED zettel_id, title, body
    OPTIONAL links, topic, origin
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD zettel_id TYPE ZETTEL_ID
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Unique chronological identifier of the Zettel
END FIELD

FIELD links TYPE ZETTEL_LINK
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Connections to other Zettels (comma-separated IDs)
END FIELD

FIELD origin TYPE BIB_REF
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Bibliographic reference that inspired the permanent note
END FIELD



// The generic field rule absorbs the new types
field_value: text_value
           | chain_value
           | zettel_id_value
           | zettel_link_value
           | bib_ref_value

// The ID is a strictly numeric string (e.g. YYYYMMDDHH)
zettel_id_value: INT

// Comma-separated list of IDs
zettel_link_value: INT ("," WS? INT)*

// Citation format with '@'
bib_ref_value: "@" LCASE_LETTER+ DIGIT+



With zettel_link and bib_ref as ITEM field types, the JSON export would carry clean lists of links and the BibTeX key in origin, enough to build the note network in a graph database.





The compiler would scan the ontology for concepts with similar spelling, preventing fragmentation of the knowledge graph. Today part of this need is met in assisted coding, by the normalize command of synesis-coder.

Algorithm: Levenshtein / Jaro-Winkler distance.
Behaviour: warning during compilation.
Detection example: SocialInteraction vs Social_Interaction.







Logical invariants to ensure the methodological consistency of annotations.
CONSTRAINT
    # Mutual exclusion: an item cannot have both codes at once
    FORBID Code "Sentiment: Positive" WITH Code "Risk: Critical"

    # Logical dependency: code B requires code A
    REQUIRE Code "Solution" IF Code "Problem" PRESENT
END CONSTRAINT



Formalizes rhetorical relations between bibliographic sources, independently of internal annotations.
CROSSREF
    @smith2019 -> REFUTES -> @doe2018
    @jones2020 -> EXTENDS -> @smith2019
END CROSSREF

title: The LSP Interface
text:
Who is this document for?



Developers and technical readers who want to understand how the Synesis compiler connects to VS Code (or any LSP-compatible editor) to offer real-time validation, autocomplete, navigation and much more. No prior knowledge of the source code is needed.
If you want to understand the compiler itself, see Inside the Compiler.

title: The LSP Interface
text:
1 What Is LSP?
The Language Server Protocol is an open standard created by Microsoft that separates a language’s intelligence (validation, autocomplete, navigation) from the editor itself. Instead of reimplementing everything for each editor, you build a language server that any compatible editor can use.





flowchart LR
    VS["VS Code"]
    EX["Synesis Explorer\n(extension)"]
    LSP["LSP server\nsynesis-lsp"]
    COMP["Synesis\ncompiler"]

    VS --> EX
    EX -- "JSON-RPC STDIO\n(standard protocol)" --> LSP
    EX -- "synesis/loadProject\nsynesis/getCodes...\n(custom commands)" --> LSP
    LSP -- "direct Python\ncalls" --> COMP






Synesis Explorer is the VS Code extension that ties everything together. Inside it, SynesisLspClient (built on vscode-languageclient) manages the connection to the server: it starts the Python process, keeps the STDIO channel open and dispatches editor events (file opened, key typed, file saved). For features beyond the standard protocol — such as listing codes and relations — the Explorer sends custom commands over the same channel.

title: The LSP Interface
text:
2 General Architecture
The ecosystem involves three distinct components: Synesis Explorer (VS Code extension), synesis-lsp (Python server) and the Synesis compiler. Internally the server is organized in three layers:





flowchart TB
    classDef extension fill:#E8F5E9,stroke:#2E7D32,stroke-width:2px,color:#1B5E20,font-weight:bold;
    classDef protocol fill:#E0F7FA,stroke:#084C54,stroke-width:2px,color:#084C54,font-weight:bold;
    classDef adapter fill:#F8FAFC,stroke:#4A5568,stroke-width:1px,color:#084C84;
    classDef compiler fill:#FFF3E0,stroke:#E65100,stroke-width:2px,color:#E65100,font-weight:bold;

The Synesis compiler knows nothing about LSP. The bridge is the lsp_adapter.py module, which lives inside the compiler itself and exposes a simplified interface for single-file validation.

title: The LSP Interface
text:
3 The Two Modes of Operation
The LSP works in two distinct modes, depending on what the editor needs:

3.1 Mode 1: Per-file validation (real time)
Used on every keystroke. Fast, light, focused on the open file.





sequenceDiagram
    participant E as Editor
    participant S as server.py
    participant A as lsp_adapter
    participant P as Lark parser
    participant V as Semantic validator

    E->>S: textDocument/didChange
    Note over S: 300ms debounce
    S->>A: validate_single_file(source, uri)
    A->>A: discover_context(uri)
    Note over A: Per-workspace cache<br/>(file mtimes)
    A->>P: parse_string(source)
    P-->>A: AST nodes
    A->>V: validate_source/item/ontology
    V-->>A: ValidationResult
    A-->>S: errors + warnings
    S->>S: build_diagnostics()
    S->>E: publishDiagnostics






In this mode lsp_adapter does the heavy lifting:

Discovers the context — finds the workspace .synp, loads template and bibliography
Parses — turns the text into AST nodes through Lark
Validates — applies semantic rules with the SemanticValidator
Returns — a list of errors and warnings with precise locations







Why not compile the whole project on every keystroke?



Full compilation reads every project file from disk and may take several seconds on large projects. That is unworkable for real-time feedback. lsp_adapter solves this by validating only the open file, using cached context (template, bibliography, ontology).




3.2 Mode 2: Full compilation (on demand)
Used when Synesis Explorer needs complete data — codes, relations, graphs.





sequenceDiagram
    participant X as Synesis Explorer
    participant S as server.py
    participant C as SynesisCompiler
    participant CA as WorkspaceCache

    X->>S: synesis/loadProject
    S->>CA: get(workspace_key)
    alt Valid cache (fingerprint match)
        CA-->>S: CachedCompilation
    else Cache miss
        S->>C: SynesisCompiler(synp).compile()
        C-->>S: CompilationResult
        S->>CA: put(workspace_key, result)
    end
    S-->>X: stats + diagnostics
    Note over X: Can now call<br/>getCodes, getRelations etc.






In this mode the server invokes the full compiler (SynesisCompiler.compile()) and caches the CompilationResult. Subsequent Explorer requests (getCodes, getRelations, getRelationGraph) read this cache without recompiling.

title: The LSP Interface
text:
4 The Adapter: lsp_adapter.py
lsp_adapter is the bridge between the two worlds. It lives in the synesis package (not in synesis-lsp) because it needs internal access to the parser, the transformer and the validator.

4.1 What It Exposes
from synesis.lsp_adapter import (
    validate_single_file,   # Validates in-memory text, returns errors
    discover_context,       # Finds the workspace template/bib/ontology
    find_workspace_root,    # Detects the workspace root (looks for .synp, .git)
    invalidate_cache,       # Forces the context to reload
)


4.2 How Discovery Works
When the editor opens a .syn file, the adapter must find the project context:

Finds the workspace root — walks up the directory tree looking for a .synp, .git or .vscode
Parses the .synp — extracts the template, bibliography and ontology paths
Loads the context — reads template (.synt), bibliography (.bib) and ontology (.syno)
Caches — stores the context with the mtime of the watched files

On the next validation the cache is checked: if no context file changed, the previous context is reused. If any mtime changed, the cache is invalidated and the context rebuilt.






Two caches, two purposes



The lsp_adapter cache stores the context (template + bibliography + ontology) for fast per-file validation. The server’s WorkspaceCache stores the full compilation result (LinkedProject with all sources, items and relations) to serve Synesis Explorer. They are independent caches with different life cycles.

text:
5 How Errors Travel
An error’s path — from detection by the compiler to the red underline in the editor — goes through several transformations:
 Compiler                      LSP                        Editor
┌──────────────────┐        ┌──────────────┐          ┌──────────────┐
│ ValidationError  │──────▶│  Diagnostic  │─────────▶│  Red /       │
│  .severity       │        │  .severity   │          │  yellow      │
│  .location       │        │  .range      │          │  underline   │
│  .to_diagnostic()│        │  .message    │          │              │
└──────────────────┘        └──────────────┘          └──────────────┘

Pedagogical messages



For syntax errors, the compiler’s error_handler enriches the message with context and suggestions. This is done by create_pedagogical_error(), which translates internal Lark tokens into readable language. Compiler and server messages are written in English; the Error Guide explains each diagnostic.








Undefined codes



A code used in annotations and absent from the ontology produces a warning, not an error. By default the editor does not mark every occurrence: the extension setting synesisExplorer.diagnostics.checkCodes, off by default, turns on the per-occurrence diagnostic (E004). When the option changes, the server recompiles the cached projects and republishes the diagnostics.

6.5 The LSP ↔︎ Extension Contract

The gain is that a format change in the server does not reach the user as an empty panel or an obscure error in the editor: it breaks the CI of both repositories at once, at the moment of the change.

title: The LSP Interface
text:
7 Performance Strategies
The LSP must answer in milliseconds while the compiler works in seconds. Four strategies resolve that tension:

7.1 1. Layered Cache
Layer 1: lsp_adapter     → context (template, bib, ontology)
                            Invalidation: file mtimes
                            Avoids: reloading the template on every validation

Layer 2: WorkspaceCache  → full CompilationResult
                            Invalidation: fingerprint {count}:{max_mtime}
                            Avoids: recompiling the project on every Explorer request

Layer 3: FileState       → per-document dirty flags
                            Invalidation: content hash + context version
                            Avoids: revalidating an unchanged file

Layer 4: Feature caches  → per-feature results (symbols, tokens)
                            Invalidation: source hash
                            Avoids: recomputing tokens for the same content


7.2 2. Debounce + Cancellation
Inspired by Pyright:

300ms timer — each key restarts the timer; validation happens only after a pause
Task cancellation — if a validation is running and the user types again, the old one is cancelled before the new one starts
Result: 10 keys = 1 validation, not 10



7.3 3. Focused File First
When the context changes (e.g. the template was edited and saved), all open files must be revalidated. The server validates the focused file first (immediate feedback) and then the others in the background, yielding the event loop between files (asyncio.sleep(0)).


7.4 4. Workspace Fingerprint
Instead of computing the SHA1 of every project file, WorkspaceCache uses a simple fingerprint: {file_count}:{latest_mtime}. That is enough to detect changes in most cases and costs microseconds instead of milliseconds.

title: The LSP Interface
section: 8 The Case of the Shared Ontology
text:
8 The Case of the Shared Ontology
The introduction of INCLUDE SHARED ONTOLOGY — an ontology living outside the project folder — broke two premises the LSP assumed. It is worth documenting because the solution involved reversing an earlier architectural decision.

8.1 The Broken Premise: Projects Are Self-contained
The file watchers (FileSystemWatcher) had been removed from the project as redundant: onDidSaveTextDocument already triggered revalidation, and everything a project read was inside its own folder.
INCLUDE SHARED ONTOLOGY invalidates that premise. The save event fires only for documents open in the editor. A shared ontology changed by git pull, by another VS Code window or by another process never triggered anything — the project including it became stale silently.
The extension installed watchers again, now scoped: one per external target, using the reverse index target → projects returned by the server. When a target changes, only the projects declaring it are reloaded, with a 300ms debounce — a git pull may rewrite the file several times in a row.






A deliberate reversal, not a regression



The original removal of the watchers was correct for the premise of the time. What changed was the premise, not the quality of the decision. The reintroduction is scoped to external targets, not a broad watcher over the whole workspace — the original performance gain is kept where it still applies.




8.2 The Broken Premise: Everything That Matters Is Under the Workspace Root
There was a second, subtler defect that the watcher alone would not solve. The workspace fingerprint (Section 7) walked only the workspace root. The shared ontology, living outside it, simply did not enter the calculation — editing it did not invalidate the cache.
The result would be a useless watcher: it would trigger the reload, which would consult the cache, which would return old data. Fixing the fingerprint is a prerequisite of the watcher, not a later refinement.
Today the INCLUDE SHARED targets are part of the fingerprint, and a purely external edit correctly reaches the server context.

9 Life Cycle of a File
To consolidate, this is the full cycle when the user works with a .syn file:

    Validating --> Diagnosed: publish_diagnostics

    Diagnosed --> Editing: did_change

    Debounce --> Editing: new key (timer reset)
    Debounce --> Validating: timer expired

    Saved --> CacheInvalidated: if .synp/.synt/.bib

Opening — immediate validation, context discovered or loaded from cache
Editing — 300ms debounce, dirty flag updated, previous task cancelled

title: The LSP Interface
text:
11 Relationship with the Compiler
synesis-lsp depends on the compiler, but the compiler does not depend on the LSP. This asymmetry is intentional:
synesis (compiler)
  ├── lsp_adapter.py     ← Interface for the LSP
  ├── compiler.py        ← Full pipeline
  ├── parser/            ← Lark + transformer
  ├── semantic/          ← Validator + linker
  └── exporters/         ← JSON, CSV, Excel, Alpaca, OKF, SKOS

synesis-lsp (server)
  ├── server.py          ← Imports from synesis.lsp_adapter
  ├── converters.py      ← Imports from synesis.ast
  └── features/          ← Import from synesis.*
lsp_adapter.py was placed inside the compiler (and not in the LSP) because it needs internal access to the parser, the transformer and the validator — components that are not part of the compiler’s public API. It works as an internal façade: it exposes validate_single_file() as an atomic operation that hides the complexity of the pipeline.

11.1 The Boundary of the Multi-project Aggregate
There is one compiler capability the LSP deliberately does not use: the link step between projects (synesis compile p1.synp p2.synp, see Linking Projects).
The server always works with isolated projects. If it kept the aggregate in memory, every save of a .syn would recompile the whole study — exactly the cost the two-mode architecture (Section 3) exists to avoid. A study with six large corpora would be unusable in the editor.
The practical effect is that resolved edges do not appear in the editor. This is acceptable because they are an analysis result, produced at export time — not something consulted while annotating. A project declaring REFERS TO receives, in isolated compilation, only an informational note (SYNESIS_I080), never a recurring error or warning.
The shared ontology is the opposite case and worth contrasting: it is loaded by the server, with autocomplete and code validation, because it is part of the editing context of each project individually (Section 8).






For contributors



To add a new LSP feature (e.g. folding ranges), the pattern is:

Create a module in synesis_lsp/ (e.g. folding.py)
Implement the main function (e.g. compute_folding_ranges())
Register the handler in server.py with @server.feature(TEXT_DOCUMENT_FOLDING_RANGE)
The data come from the WorkspaceCache (full compilation) or from compile_string (fast parse of the source)

title: Why Structured Annotation Matters
text:
The first reaction of many researchers on seeing Synesis is:

“Why should I follow such strict rules? Won’t that limit my analytical creativity?”

It is a legitimate question. And the short answer is: no, the opposite is true. Structure does not limit creativity — it releases it. But to understand why, we first need to understand the problem that structured annotation solves.



Free annotations (PDF highlights, notes in Word, sticky notes) have an obvious advantage: speed. You capture thoughts in the moment, without interruption, without thinking about format. That is valuable.
But this freedom has a hidden cost that only shows later:


You note “Cost” in an interview. Three months later, reviewing, you cannot remember:

Cost of what? Acquisition? Maintenance? Opportunity?
Perceived cost or actual cost?
Is it a barrier, or just a descriptive mention?

Free annotation does not force you to decide in the moment. You push the decision into the future, when your memory will be weaker and the context less clear.



Over a project you call the same concept in slightly different ways:

“High cost”
“Expensive price”
“Financial barrier”
“Prohibitive investment”

Synonyms? Nuances? Free annotation does not make you decide. The result is a conceptual vocabulary that looks rich but is merely disorganized.



When you finally need to justify an interpretation (to an advisor, a reviewer, or yourself), you must return to the original evidence. But how?

Where was that quotation about “organizational resistance”?
Did I really code 15 cases as “Cultural Barrier”, or am I fooling myself?
Is this causal chain I propose really supported by the data?

Free annotation keeps no automatic two-way links between interpretation and evidence. You waste time (a lot of time) searching, or worse, you trust memory and make mistakes.





Synesis, as a structured annotation system, is not about bureaucracy. It is about externalizing cognitive decisions into a reliable system so that your mind is free for the work that really matters: interpreting, reflecting, theorizing.


When you write:
ITEM @interview_01
    quote: "The price is too high"
    note: The interviewee expresses an economic barrier to adoption
    code: Acquisition_Cost
    chain: Acquisition_Cost -> INHIBITS -> Adoption_Decision
END ITEM
You are forced to decide, at the moment of annotation:

What is the literal evidence? (quote)
What is my interpretation? (note)
How do I categorize it conceptually? (code)
Which causal relation am I inferring? (chain)

That looks laborious, but consider the alternative: you will have to make these decisions anyway — either while annotating (with fresh context) or three months later (without it). Structure only brings the inevitable forward.



The Synesis compiler checks that:

If you use the code Acquisition_Cost, it is defined in the ontology (otherwise the compiler warns; with --strict it refuses)
If you rename a code, you update the definition or use an alias
If you cite a bibliographic source, it exists in the .bib file

This is not bureaucracy, it is automatic auditing. It is the difference between:

Fragile system: you forget that you renamed “Cost” to “Acquisition Cost” in some annotations and not in others. Your final analysis is inconsistent and you do not even notice.
Robust system: the compiler points exactly to the problem. You fix it once and move on.




With Synesis you can answer immediately:

Given a concept, which quotations support it?
# In items.csv: filter rows where the concept appears in chains
grep "Acquisition_Cost" output/items.csv
Given a quotation, which causal relations were assigned?
# In chains.csv: filter the triples tied to that source
grep "@interview_01" output/chains.csv
Given a causal relation, what is the original evidence?
# In chains.csv: filter all triples with the relation INHIBITS
grep ",INHIBITS," output/chains.csv

If you prefer a visual interface, the Synesis Explorer extension for VS Code offers two-way traceability in a click: select a concept in the editor and see all associated quotations and relations at once, without the command line.
This is not magic, it is structure. When you name fields (quote, code, chain) you create natural indices that tools can exploit.





A common objection:

“But if I have to predefine codes and relations, am I not imposing a theoretical structure before seeing the data? Doesn’t that violate the principles of qualitative research?”

It is a legitimate confusion, but it comes from a misunderstanding of what “structure” means in Synesis.


Synesis does not force you to define ALL codes in advance. You can:

Start with an empty ontology
Annotate freely, creating codes as they emerge
Periodically consolidate: “These three codes are actually the same concept”
Update the ontology
Recompile to check consistency

The structure is not in the specific codes (those may emerge inductively). The structure is in the contract: if you use a code, it must be documented in the ontology with an explicit definition.




Pseudo-freedom: no rules about terminology. Result: you are stuck trying to remember what each term means three months later.
Real freedom: a system that checks your consistency automatically. Result: your mind is free for interpretive work, trusting that the system looks after structural integrity.

An analogy: jazz musicians improvise freely — but over well-defined harmonic structures (II-V-I, 12-bar blues). Structure does not limit creativity, it channels it.










Aspect
Free Annotation
Synesis

Slightly slower


Consistency

Checked automatically


Traceability

Automatic and two-way


Scalability

Grows linearly


Auditability
Hard to justify
Fully transparent



Conclusion: free annotation is better for initial exploration (first readings, brainstorms). Synesis is better for systematic consolidation (formal analysis, articles, reports).






Aspect

Synesis

Plain-text files

Conclusion: CAQDAS tools are excellent for researchers who prefer visual interfaces and guided workflows. Synesis is better for those who value portability, reproducibility and integration with data science tools.






Aspect

Conclusion: spreadsheets are better for already structured data and simple quantitative analyses. Synesis is better for modelling complex relations and ensuring conceptual consistency. (See also: Why not Excel?)





The deepest reason to use structured annotation is not immediate efficiency — it is long-term sustainability.


Without structure your knowledge is scattered across:

Zotero highlights
Comments in Word documents
Notes in paper notebooks
Unrecorded memories

Result: five years later, when you want to write a second article on the same topic, you start almost from scratch. Your past knowledge is inaccessible.



Research is not individual — it is cumulative. How will another researcher (or you, years from now) understand your analytical decisions if they exist only in your head or in proprietary formats?
Structured annotations in plain text are:

Versionable (Git shows how your interpretations evolved)
Portable (they work on any OS, now and in 20 years)
Auditable (analytical decisions are explicit, not implicit)
Reusable (others can extend them without reinventing the wheel)




The reproducibility crisis is not only in experimental sciences — it exists in qualitative research too. How do you show that your conclusions are supported by the data if the process is opaque?
Synesis produces audit trails:
{
  "interpretation": "Cost is the main barrier",
  "supporting_evidence": [
    {"source": "@interview_01", "quote": "The price is prohibitive"},
    {"source": "@interview_03", "quote": "It doesn't fit the budget"},
    {"source": "@report_2025", "quote": "Unfeasible investment"}
  ]
}
Anyone can check: “This interpretation is justified by these three pieces of evidence”. That is methodological transparency.
The exported JSON can be consumed directly by Python or R scripts or Data Science pipelines — or reprocessed by AI tools. For more traditional workflows, the compiler also exports the same data as CSV (separate tables by type: items.csv, chains.csv, ontologies.csv) and Excel (sheets organized by block type), ready for spreadsheets, dashboards or statistical software.





Synesis is not for everyone nor for every phase. Do not use structured annotation when:

You are exploring: first readings, you do not yet know what you are looking for. Use free highlights.
You are brainstorming creatively: wild connections, free association. Use mind maps.
You have very little data: for a single short interview, structure is needless overhead.
You will not revisit the data: for a throwaway analysis (a single, non-reusable report), the investment does not pay.

Use structured annotation when:

You have a lot of data: 10+ interviews, dozens of documents
You need consistency: long project, several collaborators
You will publish formally: articles, dissertations, reports requiring rigorous justification
You want advanced integration: Neo4j, R, Python, interactive dashboards





The philosopher Andy Clark argues that external tools (paper, calculators, computers) are not mere aids — they are extensions of the mind. When you write a to-do list you are not just “recording” what was in your head; you are externalizing cognitive processes so that your finite mind can handle greater complexity.
Structured annotations are cognitive extensions.
When you define a code in the ontology with an explicit definition, you are not “creating bureaucracy” — you are externalizing categorization decisions so that, three months later, you need not rely on fragile memory.
When you write an explicit chain (A -> INHIBITS -> B), you are not “complicating” — you are externalizing causal inferences so that, on review, you can ask: “Do I really have evidence for this?”
Structure does not replace thinking — it amplifies it. As a pianist practises scales (rigid structure) in order to improvise freely, a researcher structures annotations in order to theorize freely.
In the end, the question is not:

“Why should I limit myself with structure?”

The right question is:

“Why would I trust a system that does not check my consistency?”

title: Why Structured Annotation Matters
text:
Free annotations (PDF highlights, notes in Word, sticky notes) have an obvious advantage: speed. You capture thoughts in the moment, without interruption, without thinking about format. That is valuable.
But this freedom has a hidden cost that only shows later:


You note “Cost” in an interview. Three months later, reviewing, you cannot remember:

Cost of what? Acquisition? Maintenance? Opportunity?
Perceived cost or actual cost?
Is it a barrier, or just a descriptive mention?

Free annotation does not force you to decide in the moment. You push the decision into the future, when your memory will be weaker and the context less clear.



Over a project you call the same concept in slightly different ways:

“High cost”
“Expensive price”
“Financial barrier”
“Prohibitive investment”

Synonyms? Nuances? Free annotation does not make you decide. The result is a conceptual vocabulary that looks rich but is merely disorganized.



When you finally need to justify an interpretation (to an advisor, a reviewer, or yourself), you must return to the original evidence. But how?

Where was that quotation about “organizational resistance”?
Did I really code 15 cases as “Cultural Barrier”, or am I fooling myself?
Is this causal chain I propose really supported by the data?

Free annotation keeps no automatic two-way links between interpretation and evidence. You waste time (a lot of time) searching, or worse, you trust memory and make mistakes.

title: Why Structured Annotation Matters
text:
Synesis, as a structured annotation system, is not about bureaucracy. It is about externalizing cognitive decisions into a reliable system so that your mind is free for the work that really matters: interpreting, reflecting, theorizing.


When you write:
ITEM @interview_01
    quote: "The price is too high"
    note: The interviewee expresses an economic barrier to adoption
    code: Acquisition_Cost
    chain: Acquisition_Cost -> INHIBITS -> Adoption_Decision
END ITEM
You are forced to decide, at the moment of annotation:

What is the literal evidence? (quote)
What is my interpretation? (note)
How do I categorize it conceptually? (code)
Which causal relation am I inferring? (chain)

That looks laborious, but consider the alternative: you will have to make these decisions anyway — either while annotating (with fresh context) or three months later (without it). Structure only brings the inevitable forward.



The Synesis compiler checks that:

If you use the code Acquisition_Cost, it is defined in the ontology (otherwise the compiler warns; with --strict it refuses)
If you rename a code, you update the definition or use an alias
If you cite a bibliographic source, it exists in the .bib file

This is not bureaucracy, it is automatic auditing. It is the difference between:

Fragile system: you forget that you renamed “Cost” to “Acquisition Cost” in some annotations and not in others. Your final analysis is inconsistent and you do not even notice.
Robust system: the compiler points exactly to the problem. You fix it once and move on.




With Synesis you can answer immediately:

Given a concept, which quotations support it?
# In items.csv: filter rows where the concept appears in chains
grep "Acquisition_Cost" output/items.csv
Given a quotation, which causal relations were assigned?
# In chains.csv: filter the triples tied to that source
grep "@interview_01" output/chains.csv
Given a causal relation, what is the original evidence?
# In chains.csv: filter all triples with the relation INHIBITS
grep ",INHIBITS," output/chains.csv

If you prefer a visual interface, the Synesis Explorer extension for VS Code offers two-way traceability in a click: select a concept in the editor and see all associated quotations and relations at once, without the command line.
This is not magic, it is structure. When you name fields (quote, code, chain) you create natural indices that tools can exploit.

title: Why Structured Annotation Matters
text:
A common objection:

“But if I have to predefine codes and relations, am I not imposing a theoretical structure before seeing the data? Doesn’t that violate the principles of qualitative research?”

It is a legitimate confusion, but it comes from a misunderstanding of what “structure” means in Synesis.


Synesis does not force you to define ALL codes in advance. You can:

Start with an empty ontology
Annotate freely, creating codes as they emerge
Periodically consolidate: “These three codes are actually the same concept”
Update the ontology
Recompile to check consistency

The structure is not in the specific codes (those may emerge inductively). The structure is in the contract: if you use a code, it must be documented in the ontology with an explicit definition.




Pseudo-freedom: no rules about terminology. Result: you are stuck trying to remember what each term means three months later.
Real freedom: a system that checks your consistency automatically. Result: your mind is free for interpretive work, trusting that the system looks after structural integrity.

An analogy: jazz musicians improvise freely — but over well-defined harmonic structures (II-V-I, 12-bar blues). Structure does not limit creativity, it channels it.

title: Why Structured Annotation Matters
text:
The deepest reason to use structured annotation is not immediate efficiency — it is long-term sustainability.


Without structure your knowledge is scattered across:

Zotero highlights
Comments in Word documents
Notes in paper notebooks
Unrecorded memories

Result: five years later, when you want to write a second article on the same topic, you start almost from scratch. Your past knowledge is inaccessible.



Research is not individual — it is cumulative. How will another researcher (or you, years from now) understand your analytical decisions if they exist only in your head or in proprietary formats?
Structured annotations in plain text are:

Versionable (Git shows how your interpretations evolved)
Portable (they work on any OS, now and in 20 years)
Auditable (analytical decisions are explicit, not implicit)
Reusable (others can extend them without reinventing the wheel)




The reproducibility crisis is not only in experimental sciences — it exists in qualitative research too. How do you show that your conclusions are supported by the data if the process is opaque?
Synesis produces audit trails:
{
  "interpretation": "Cost is the main barrier",
  "supporting_evidence": [
    {"source": "@interview_01", "quote": "The price is prohibitive"},
    {"source": "@interview_03", "quote": "It doesn't fit the budget"},
    {"source": "@report_2025", "quote": "Unfeasible investment"}
  ]
}
Anyone can check: “This interpretation is justified by these three pieces of evidence”. That is methodological transparency.
The exported JSON can be consumed directly by Python or R scripts or Data Science pipelines — or reprocessed by AI tools. title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
This document presents the features of the Synesis language one by one. Each example shows first the configuration in the template (.synt) and then an example block using the feature.
All examples belong to one fictitious study: barriers to telemedicine adoption in rural communities.

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
1.1 TEXT in SOURCE
The TEXT type stores free text. Here we use it to record the context of the interview.
In the template (.synt):
SOURCE FIELDS
    OPTIONAL context
END SOURCE FIELDS

FIELD context TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Context or circumstances of data collection
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
SOURCE @interview_mrs_maria2026
    context: Interview at the participant's home, rural area, without internet access
END SOURCE

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
1.2 DATE in SOURCE
The DATE type records dates. Useful to keep track of when a source was accessed or collected.
In the template (.synt):
SOURCE FIELDS
    OPTIONAL collection_date
END SOURCE FIELDS

FIELD collection_date TYPE DATE
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Date the data were collected
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
SOURCE @interview_mrs_maria2026
    collection_date: 2026-01-15
END SOURCE

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
1.3 ENUMERATED in SOURCE
The ENUMERATED type restricts a value to a predefined closed list. Here we classify the type of source.
In the template (.synt):
SOURCE FIELDS
    REQUIRED source_type
END SOURCE FIELDS

FIELD source_type TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Type of data source
    VALUES
        interview: Individual or group interview
        document: Textual or audiovisual document
        observation: Field observation
    END VALUES
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
SOURCE @interview_mrs_maria2026
    source_type: interview
END SOURCE






Note



If the researcher writes a value outside the list (for instance source_type: questionnaire), the compiler rejects it with an error message pointing to the allowed values.

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.1 QUOTATION in ITEM
The QUOTATION type stores the textual excerpt from the source. It is typically the most basic required field.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quotation_text
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD quotation_text TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Textual excerpt from the source
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
END ITEM

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.2 MEMO in ITEM
The MEMO type records the researcher’s interpretation or analytical note on the excerpt.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED note
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Analytical interpretation by the researcher
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    note: The participant expresses technological distrust linked to the lack of in-person contact
END ITEM

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.3 CODE in ITEM
The CODE type assigns conceptual labels to the excerpt. Each code must exist as a concept in the project ontology. One item may receive several codes.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    OPTIONAL code
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD code TYPE CODE
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Conceptual label for categorization
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    code: Technological_Distrust, In_Person_Preference
END ITEM






Multiple codes



Separate codes with commas on one line, or repeat the field on separate lines:
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    code: Technological_Distrust
    code: In_Person_Preference
END ITEM
Both forms are equivalent.

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.4 Simple CHAIN in ITEM
The CHAIN type expresses relations between concepts. When the template does not define RELATIONS, the chain uses implicit relations — just concepts separated by ->.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    OPTIONAL chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Relation between concepts
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    chain: Technological_Distrust -> Telemedicine_Resistance
END ITEM
Here the relation between the concepts is implicit: the researcher knows there is a connection but does not need to name it.

title: What Synesis Can Express
section: 2.5 Qualified CHAIN with BUNDLE in ITEM
text:
2.5 Qualified CHAIN with BUNDLE in ITEM
When the template defines RELATIONS, every relation in the chain must be named. The BUNDLE modifier guarantees that note and chain always appear together, in positional pairs.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED quotation_text
    REQUIRED BUNDLE note, chain
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Analytical interpretation by the researcher
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Causal chain between ontology concepts
    ARITY >= 2
    RELATIONS
        INFLUENCES: Direct causal effect
        INHIBITS: Limits or prevents
        ENABLES: Makes possible or eases
    END RELATIONS
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"

    note: Distrust of technology produces direct resistance
    chain: Technological_Distrust -> INHIBITS -> Telemedicine_Uptake

    note: Low digital literacy reinforces the distrust
    chain: Low_Digital_Literacy -> INFLUENCES -> Technological_Distrust -> INHIBITS -> Telemedicine_Uptake
END ITEM






What BUNDLE guarantees




note and chain must appear in equal numbers (here, 2 of each)
The first note pairs with the first chain, the second with the second
With 2 notes and 1 chain, the compiler reports an error









ARITY



The ARITY >= 2 property requires each chain to contain at least 2 concepts. A chain with only 1 concept would be rejected.

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.6 SCALE in ITEM
The SCALE type records a numeric value within a range defined by FORMAT.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    OPTIONAL confidence
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD confidence TYPE SCALE
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Researcher's confidence in the interpretation
    FORMAT [1..5]
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    note: Distrust of technology produces direct resistance
    confidence: 5
END ITEM
If the researcher writes confidence: 7, the compiler rejects it because the value is outside [1..5].

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.7 ENUMERATED in ITEM
ENUMERATED can also be used in ITEM blocks — for instance, to classify the sentiment expressed in each excerpt.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    OPTIONAL sentiment
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD sentiment TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Predominant sentiment of the excerpt
    VALUES
        positive: Favorable sentiment
        negative: Unfavorable sentiment
        neutral: No evident emotional charge
        ambivalent: Mixed or contradictory sentiments
    END VALUES
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    sentiment: negative
END ITEM

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
2.8 ORDERED in ITEM
The ORDERED type works as a list with an explicit hierarchy. Each value has a numeric index that defines the order.
In the template (.synt):
ITEM FIELDS
    OPTIONAL relevance
END ITEM FIELDS

FIELD relevance TYPE ORDERED
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Relevance of the excerpt to the research question
    VALUES
        [1] low: Tangentially related
        [2] medium: Contributes to understanding
        [3] high: Central to the research question
    END VALUES
END FIELD
In the annotation file (.syn):
ITEM @interview_mrs_maria2026
    quotation_text: "I don't trust this computer business for talking to a doctor"
    relevance: 3
END ITEM
In an ORDERED field you write the index (3), not the label; writing high produces an error whose message gives the right index. The editor shows the label next to the number.






ORDERED vs. ENUMERATED



The difference is hierarchy: in ORDERED, high > medium > low has ordinal meaning. In ENUMERATED, values are unranked categories (such as positive, negative, neutral).

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
3.1 TEXT in ONTOLOGY
The TEXT type in the ontology stores the concept definition.
In the template (.synt):
ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED definition
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD definition TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Textual definition of the concept
END FIELD
In the ontology file (.syno):
ONTOLOGY Technological_Distrust
    definition: Resistance or scepticism towards digital technologies mediating essential services
END ONTOLOGY

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
3.2 TOPIC in ONTOLOGY
The TOPIC type creates dynamic grouping categories. Unlike ENUMERATED there is no closed list — the researcher creates categories freely while defining concepts.
In the template (.synt):
ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED definition
    OPTIONAL theme
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD theme TYPE TOPIC
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Thematic domain of the concept
END FIELD
In the ontology file (.syno):
ONTOLOGY Technological_Distrust
    definition: Resistance to digital technologies
    theme: Cultural_Factors
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY Low_Digital_Literacy
    definition: Insufficient digital skills to use health platforms
    theme: Cultural_Factors
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY Poor_Infrastructure
    definition: Absent or insufficient connectivity and equipment
    theme: Structural_Factors
END ONTOLOGY
The themes Cultural_Factors and Structural_Factors emerge from the analysis — they need not be predefined in the template.

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
3.3 ORDERED in ONTOLOGY
ORDERED in the ontology classifies concepts in an explicit hierarchy.
In the template (.synt):
ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED definition
    OPTIONAL priority
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD priority TYPE ORDERED
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Priority of the concept for intervention
    VALUES
        [1] low: Secondary factor
        [2] medium: Relevant factor
        [3] high: Critical factor for intervention
    END VALUES
END FIELD
In the ontology file (.syno):
ONTOLOGY Technological_Distrust
    definition: Resistance to digital technologies
    priority: 3
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY In_Person_Preference
    definition: Preference for face-to-face medical care
    priority: 2
END ONTOLOGY

title: What Synesis Can Express
text:
4.1 Beyond Fields

Other features


Feature
Purpose




ROLE
gives an ontology field a function (label, definition, hierarchy, consolidation) — see The Organizing Model


IDENTIFIES / REFERS TO
link independent projects — see How to Link Projects


QUESTIONS, PHASE, EXPORT
in the .synp: research questions, production plan and artifacts — see the Reference

title: Synesis for Legal Professionals
text: Human knowledge is naturally intricate, full of nuance and deep connections. In the course of their work, legal professionals accumulate contract analyses, read and annotated opinions, case law, meeting notes and hearing records — plus a vast amount of qualitative knowledge.

title: Synesis for Legal Professionals
section: 1 A Language That Both People and Computers Understand
text:
1 A Language That Both People and Computers Understand
Legal professionals already live with specialized languages. Legal Latin is the clearest example: expressions absent from everyday speech, with a rich vocabulary and their own rules of use, which any jurist understands precisely.
Synesis is a computer Domain-Specific Language (DSL) that plays an analogous role for textual knowledge. Its grammar is recognized by both people and computers. It imposes structure on annotations so that the computer can check automatically whether they conform to a pre-established contract — the template.
The template is flexible enough to serve completely different configurations, defined according to each professional’s or team’s needs. A lawyer may create a configuration to organize cases and documents, classify them into categories and establish explicit connections among them. In a case database, for instance, it is possible to identify themes, recurring concepts and relations between the parties involved.
Synesis records not only what — a fact, an argument, a doctrinal position — but also why and how it connects to other things. A legal professional may document, for example, that the absence of objective good faith in a contractual relationship tends to compromise performance — and link that interpretation directly to the contract passage that supports it, the scholarly article that informed it and the precedent that confirms it. This web of causal and conceptual relations, previously scattered across documents and memory, comes to exist explicitly, verifiably and shareably.

title: Synesis for Legal Professionals
text:
2 The Synesis Ecosystem
The language itself is only the starting point. The Synesis ecosystem is the set of tools that makes the process practical, covering several stages of knowledge governance.
Creating and validating annotations. A dedicated editing environment assists the professional while annotating: it checks in real time whether required fields are filled in, whether values are correct and whether references between documents are consistent. Problems are flagged immediately, before they pile up.
Organizing and exporting knowledge. Accumulated knowledge can be converted into the formats most used in professional data work — spreadsheets, specialized structured formats — and becomes available for analysis, sharing or integration with other tools. For larger projects, the whole network of concepts and relations built along the way can be visualized.
Natural language querying. The compiled collection becomes queryable as a conversation. A professional can ask which decisions deal with a theme, which concepts connect to a specific precedent or how an understanding evolved over time — and obtain answers traceable to the original sources.

title: Synesis for Legal Professionals
text:
3 What Synesis Is Not
It is also important to say what Synesis is not. A compiler validates structure — it ensures that required fields are present and declared values are valid. The intellectual content — interpreting a ruling, identifying a ratio decidendi, building a line of argument — is and remains human work.
Annotations are stored as plain text files, readable in any editor, with no dependence on a platform or proprietary format. Annotations may nonetheless be produced with the help of Artificial Intelligence, speeding up knowledge curation in a process that people can easily audit.
For a law firm, this means that the knowledge built by an experienced partner over decades is not trapped in their memory or lost in disorganized files. It becomes institutional heritage, auditable and evolving.

title: Synesis for Legal Professionals
text:
4 Practical Examples
The examples use Brazilian law and keep the original Portuguese legal terms where they are part of the data.

4.1 The Structure of an Annotation
A Synesis annotation consists of three blocks which together capture all the knowledge produced about a document. The following example starts from a ruling of the Brazilian Superior Court of Justice (STJ) on the right to privacy.
SOURCE block — the traceable origin
Records the source document with all its metadata. No ITEM exists without a corresponding SOURCE — traceability is structurally enforced.
SOURCE @stj_petition_1234
    access_date: 2026-02-17
    document_type: RULING
    court: STJ
    case_number: 1234/2025
    reporting_judge: Justice John Doe
    judgment_date: 2025-11-10
    publication_date: 2025-11-20
    judging_body: Third Panel
    outcome: GRANTED
    url: https://processo.stj.jus.br/processo/pesquisa/?tipoPesquisa=tipoPesquisaNumeroRegistro&termo=1234
END SOURCE
ITEM block — the passage and its interpretation
Records the relevant passage, the professional’s interpretation and the connections with other concepts. The chain field expresses explicit relations between concepts — not only that two themes appear in the same document, but how one prevails over the other.
ITEM @stj_petition_1234
    locus: Federal Constitution, art. 5, item X
    quote: "intimacy, private life, honor and image of persons are inviolable"
    note: The provision enshrines privacy as an absolute fundamental right, the ratio decidendi of the appealed decision.
    chain: Right_to_Privacy -> OVERRULES -> Unauthorized_Exposure
END ITEM
ONTOLOGY block — the controlled vocabulary
Defines the concepts used in annotations. It ensures that every team member uses the same terms with the same meaning — removing fragmentation by synonymy at the root.
ONTOLOGY Right_to_Privacy
    topic: Personality_Rights
    description: Fundamental individual right securing control over one's intimate sphere, personal data and private life, barring unconsented interference by third parties or the State. Basis: Federal Constitution, art. 5, item X; Civil Code, art. 21; General Data Protection Law, art. 2, I.
END ONTOLOGY


4.2 The Template — the Contract Governing the Whole Analysis
The template defines which fields are required, which are optional and which values are accepted. It is what lets the compiler validate each annotation automatically. Although its syntax looks technical, a template is usually defined once at the start of a project — with specialist support or with the help of artificial intelligence.
TEMPLATE privacy_case_law version: "1.0"

SOURCE FIELDS
    REQUIRED document_type, court, case_number
    REQUIRED judgment_date, outcome
    OPTIONAL reporting_judge, judging_body, publication_date
    OPTIONAL url, access_date
END SOURCE FIELDS

ITEM FIELDS
    REQUIRED locus, quote, note
    OPTIONAL chain
END ITEM FIELDS

ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED description
    OPTIONAL topic
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD document_type TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Type of legal document
    VALUES
        RULING:    Appellate ruling
        JUDGMENT:  First-instance judgment
        OPINION:   Legal opinion
        STATUTE:   Normative text
    END VALUES
END FIELD

FIELD outcome TYPE ENUMERATED
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Outcome of the judgment
    VALUES
        GRANTED:        Appeal granted
        DENIED:         Appeal denied
        PARTIAL:        Partially granted
        NOT_ADMITTED:   Appeal not admitted
    END VALUES
END FIELD

FIELD court TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Court or body issuing the document
END FIELD

FIELD case_number TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Case identification number
END FIELD

FIELD judgment_date TYPE DATE
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Date of judgment
END FIELD

FIELD reporting_judge TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Name of the reporting justice or judge
END FIELD

FIELD judging_body TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Panel, chamber or body responsible for the judgment
END FIELD

FIELD publication_date TYPE DATE
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Date the decision was published
END FIELD

FIELD url TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Address of the document in the court system
END FIELD

FIELD access_date TYPE DATE
    SCOPE SOURCE
    DESCRIPTION Date the document was accessed
END FIELD

FIELD locus TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Location of the passage within the norm or decision
END FIELD

FIELD quote TYPE QUOTATION
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Passage quoted literally from the document
END FIELD

FIELD note TYPE MEMO
    SCOPE ITEM
    DESCRIPTION Professional's interpretation and analysis of the passage
END FIELD

FIELD chain TYPE CHAIN
    SCOPE ITEM
    ARITY >= 2
    DESCRIPTION Relation between legal concepts identified in the passage
    RELATIONS
        OVERRULES:        Thesis prevails over a previous understanding
        CITES_PRECEDENT:  Decision grounded in a previous case
        DISTINGUISHES:    Current case distinguished from the general rule
    END RELATIONS
END FIELD

FIELD description TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Definition of the legal concept, including normative basis
END FIELD

FIELD topic TYPE TOPIC
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Branch or legal domain the concept belongs to
END FIELD
This is only one of countless possible configurations. A labour lawyer may structure a case-law base completely differently. A corporate legal department may create one template for contract management, another for regulatory monitoring and another for internal opinions. A legal scholar may map the doctrinal evolution of a concept over decades.
The grammar is the same. What changes is what each professional decides to build within it.

title: How to Define an Ontology
text:
This guide shows how to create and organize ontologies (.syno) to structure your conceptual vocabulary in a systematic, auditable way.






ONTOLOGY blocks are organizing principles



ONTOLOGY blocks do not commit you to a formal ontology: they are the organizing principles of the project, and the compiler calls the whole the organizing model. The same mechanism serves a flat list of concepts, a vocabulary with synonyms, a taxonomy or a multi-relation taxonomy exported as SKOS — the degree is a research decision. The function of each field (label, definition, hierarchy, consolidation) is declared with ROLE in the template. See The Organizing Model.


Use this guide if you:

Need to define reusable concepts
Want to organize concepts into thematic groups
Want terminological consistency in the project




The fields of an ONTOLOGY block are declared in the template. The example below is used throughout this guide; the field names are yours.
ONTOLOGY FIELDS
    REQUIRED definition
    OPTIONAL group, used_for, kind_of
END ONTOLOGY FIELDS

FIELD definition TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    ROLE NOTE DEFINITION
    DESCRIPTION Definition of the concept and application criterion
    GUIDELINES
        Say what the concept is and when to apply it.
        Correct: Barrier linked to purchase price; excludes maintenance cost.
        Wrong: Things about money.
    END GUIDELINES
END FIELD

FIELD group TYPE TOPIC
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    DESCRIPTION Theme that groups the concept (a term without spaces)
END FIELD

FIELD used_for TYPE TEXT
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    ROLE LABEL ALTERNATIVE
    DESCRIPTION Synonyms used by the sources
END FIELD

FIELD kind_of TYPE CODE
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    ROLE HIERARCHY KIND
    DESCRIPTION Broader concept, when there is one
END FIELD
The ROLE lines are optional. Without them the fields are just text; with them the compiler validates labels and hierarchy.




Each block defines one concept:
ONTOLOGY cost
    definition: Factors related to price, budget and economic viability
    group: adoption_barriers
END ONTOLOGY
A concept name has no spaces. Use letters (accents are accepted), digits, _ and -. Matching with the codes of the annotations ignores case.






Prefer plain names



Accented characters are allowed, but plain names are easier to type, search and use in other tools.






ONTOLOGY cost
    definition: Factors related to price, budget and economic viability
    group: adoption_barriers
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY technical_complexity
    definition: Perceived difficulty of use or need for specialist knowledge
    group: adoption_barriers
END ONTOLOGY


When different sources use different terms for the same concept, keep one canonical name and record the variants as alternative labels:
ONTOLOGY organizational_resistance
    definition: Cultural or structural opposition to change
    group: contextual_factors
    used_for: institutional inertia, resistance to change
END ONTOLOGY
A label belongs to a single concept (E115). When a code used in annotations is a registered label, the compiler suggests the right concept.



Declare the broader concept with a ROLE HIERARCHY field:
ONTOLOGY infrastructure
    definition: Technical resources available to operate the system
    group: technology_factors
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY network_infrastructure
    definition: Network and broadband capacity
    group: technology_factors
    kind_of: infrastructure
END ONTOLOGY
The compiler requires the parent to have a block, accepts several parents and refuses cycles. There are three species of hierarchy: kind (KIND), part (PART) and instance (INSTANCE). Subtree counts appear in the JSON, the graph and the editor.






Adopted hierarchy and stated relations



What is in the .syno is what the project adopts. What sources state stays in the chains of the annotations, with evidence.







A TOPIC field groups concepts with no predefined list: use the same value for what belongs together.


ONTOLOGY upfront_cost
    definition: Investment required to implement
    group: economic_dimension
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY staff_acceptance
    definition: Degree of staff buy-in to the change
    group: social_dimension
END ONTOLOGY



A template may ask for several classifications, including closed scales (ORDERED, where the index is stored):
ONTOLOGY Public_Acceptance
    topic: Social
    aspect: 10
    dimension: 1
    confidence: HIGH
    reasoning: Community and collective dynamics central to acceptance;
        co-occurs with stakeholder engagement and trust.
    description: The degree to which local communities support or oppose
        energy transition projects.
END ONTOLOGY



ONTOLOGY awareness
    definition: Knowledge that the technology exists
    group: pre_adoption
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY satisfaction
    definition: Perception of expectations met after adoption
    group: post_adoption
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY usability
    definition: Ease of everyday operation
    group: user_perspective
END ONTOLOGY





Chain relations are declared in the template (.synt), in the CHAIN field, not in the ontology. See How to Create Chains.
ITEM @source_01
    chain: high_cost -> INHIBITS -> adoption
END ITEM




ITEM @source_01
    quote: "The price is too high"
    code: cost
END ITEM
Every concept used in a CODE field or in a chain should exist in the ontology. A concept without a block raises a warning (summarized in one line, or detailed with --check-codes); with --strict, compilation fails.




synesis check ontology.syno                        # only the syntax of the file
synesis compile project.synp --check-codes         # consistency of the project








Message
Cause
Fix




Concept `X` duplicated
two blocks for the same concept
merge the blocks


Required field `definition` missing in ONTOLOGY block
a required field is missing
fill it in


Identifier `X` contains the invalid character
name with a disallowed character
use letters, digits, _, -


Code `X` is not defined in the organizing model
code without a block
create the block or fix the code


Concepts `A` and `B` have identical descriptions
likely duplicate
differentiate or consolidate



At the end, the compiler describes the profile of the model (flat list, vocabulary, taxonomy…). With ROLE, it also warns about concepts with no evidence and no descendant with evidence (E120).




With the corpus annotated, synesis-coder proposes definitions grounded in the use of each concept:
synesis-coder ontology --project project.synp --output ontology.syno --update
Review the result: a definition is a proposal. To produce definitions, synonyms and taxonomy in stages, declare PHASE blocks.







add the ONTOLOGY block to the .syno
compile with --check-codes




With a ROLE USE field in the template, the deprecated name counts as the other one without editing the annotations:
FIELD use TYPE CODE
    SCOPE ONTOLOGY
    ROLE USE
END FIELD
ONTOLOGY voice_phishing
    use: vishing
END ONTOLOGY
synesis-coder consolidate project.synp voice_phishing --into vishing moves labels and parents, with a manifest, and is undone with --revert.



Rename the block and update the .syn files: in VS Code, F2 on the code renames it across the project. If the vocabulary has been published (SKOS), prefer USE, so that the old address keeps resolving.



ONTOLOGY acquisition_cost
    definition: Initial purchase price
    group: economic_factors
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY maintenance_cost
    definition: Recurring operating expenses
    group: economic_factors
END ONTOLOGY
Then review each annotation that used the original concept and decide which one applies. To find the occurrences, use the Codes panel in VS Code or the source_file and source_line columns of the CSV tables.







ONTOLOGY lived_experience
    definition: First-hand accounts of personal experience
    group: descriptive_themes
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY apparent_contradiction
    definition: Tension between perspectives on the same phenomenon
    group: analytical_themes
END ONTOLOGY



ONTOLOGY implementer
    definition: Agent responsible for carrying out the policy
    group: actors
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY equity
    definition: Fair distribution of benefits across groups
    group: evaluation_dimensions
END ONTOLOGY



ONTOLOGY integration
    definition: Communication with external systems
    group: functional_requirements
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY security
    definition: Data protection and authentication
    group: non_functional_requirements
END ONTOLOGY





Use comments in the .syno files themselves:
# DECISION 2026-02-04: we split "cost" into two concepts after
# finding ambiguity in interviews 15 to 20

ONTOLOGY operating_cost
    # NOTE: includes training, support and recurring licences
    definition: Recurring maintenance and operating expenses
    group: economic_factors
END ONTOLOGY




For large projects, split by domain; a whole folder can be included:
ontology/
├── actors.syno
├── processes.syno
└── outcomes.syno
PROJECT my_analysis
    TEMPLATE "template.synt"
    INCLUDE BIBLIOGRAPHY "references.bib"
    INCLUDE ANNOTATIONS "annotations"
    INCLUDE ONTOLOGY "ontology"
END PROJECT
For a vocabulary shared by several projects, use INCLUDE SHARED ONTOLOGY.

The Organizing Model
How to create chains
Getting Started


Questions? Check GitHub Discussions or open an issue.
