title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
A guide for decision makers and knowledge professionals



We live in an era summed up by the acronym VUCA: Volatility, Uncertainty, Complexity and Ambiguity. In this context, making effective decisions takes more than intuition — it requires integrating and analysing multiple data sources, identifying not just correlations but cause-and-effect relations among the observed phenomena.
As recent research on Causal Knowledge Graphs highlights, mere correlation between data can lead to wrong conclusions. The classic example: there is a statistical correlation between chocolate consumption and the number of Nobel laureates across countries — but it would be absurd to conclude that handing out chocolate will increase an organization’s scientific output.
The real challenge is capturing causal relations, not just superficial correlations.




Synesis is a structured language for the systematic capture of causal knowledge from documentary sources and qualitative observations.
While automated systems such as statistical causal discovery work on numerical data, much organizational knowledge is scattered across:

Reports and technical documents
Interviews and qualitative surveys
Specialized literature and manuals
Incident records and lessons learned
Engagement and organizational climate surveys

Synesis offers a standard way to extract, document and structure causal relations from these textual sources, making them processable and integrable with other analysis systems.






When a causal relation is extracted from a document (for instance, “lack of training causes operating errors”), it is purely qualitative. There is no way to predict the probability or magnitude of the effect.
How Synesis helps: by structuring these relations systematically, they can later be integrated with numerical data to quantify causal effects.



Statistical causal discovery algorithms applied to biased or incomplete data may derive relations whose causal direction is inverted.
How Synesis helps: knowledge documented in Synesis works as prior knowledge to validate or correct statistical findings.



Traditional causal discovery works on a single dataset. It cannot combine observations from different departments, periods or conditions.
How Synesis helps: the standard structure allows knowledge from several sources to be integrated in a common vocabulary.







Scenario: HR needs to recommend initiatives to improve engagement, but each department has different characteristics.
With Synesis:

Document causal relations from the organizational behaviour literature
Record engagement survey observations with structured interpretations
Identify which factors (career opportunities, clarity of vision, teamwork) cause which outcomes (motivation, satisfaction, retention)
Recommend initiatives based on documented evidence

SOURCE @engagement_survey_q4_2024_sales
    access_date: 2024-12-15
END SOURCE

ITEM @engagement_survey_q4_2024_sales
    quote: "I feel there are no growth opportunities for me here"
    memo: The employee expresses frustration with limited career paths and links the lack of progression to lower motivation.
    chain: lack_of_career_opportunities -> INHIBITS -> motivation
END ITEM



Scenario: an operations team needs to find root causes of failures in complex systems.
With Synesis:

Extract causal relations from technical manuals and troubleshooting guides
Document each incident with the causal chain identified
Build a knowledge base that speeds up future diagnoses

SOURCE @incident_report_2024_0892
    access_date: 2024-11-10
END SOURCE

ITEM @incident_report_2024_0892
    quote: "Intermittent disconnection during file downloads"
    memo: Pattern consistent with a MAC configuration error; reproducible under the same network conditions.
    chain: mac_configuration_error -> INHIBITS -> stable_connectivity
END ITEM



Scenario: a sales team wants to understand why some negotiations succeed and others do not.
With Synesis:

Record observations from each negotiation (meetings, objections, decisions)
Identify causal patterns between actions and results
Combine with engagement data to understand how internal factors affect external performance

SOURCE @negotiation_review_2024_156
    access_date: 2024-10-22
END SOURCE

ITEM @negotiation_review_2024_156
    quote: "The client mentioned trust in the technical team as the deciding factor"
    memo: Showing technical competence during the proposal shaped perceived trust, which in turn enabled the deal.
    chain: technical_competence -> FAVORS -> client_trust -> FAVORS -> deal_closing
END ITEM







SOURCE @engagement_survey_2024
    access_date: 2024-12-15
END SOURCE
All knowledge is traceable to its origin — a document, an interview, a report.



ITEM @engagement_survey_2024
    quote: "I don't know where the company is heading"
    memo: The employee expresses a lack of clarity about strategic direction
    chain: lack_of_strategic_clarity -> INHIBITS -> engagement
END ITEM
Each item connects textual evidence with your interpretation and the causal relation identified.



ONTOLOGY engagement
    description: The employee's level of commitment and emotional connection with the organization.
    group: organizational_outcomes
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY lack_of_strategic_clarity
    description: Absence of clear communication about the organization's direction, goals or vision.
    group: organizational_factors
END ONTOLOGY
Concepts are defined explicitly, keeping the project consistent over time.



The Synesis compiler:

Checks annotations against the defined model (the template)
Produces structured formats (JSON, CSV, spreadsheets)
Enables integration with analysis systems and graph databases

Field names and allowed relations are defined by the organization itself. To get started with an assistant, see the Synesis Skill for Claude Desktop; to code large volumes with AI and human review, synesis-coder.







Every conclusion can be traced to the original evidence. When someone asks “why do you recommend this?”, the answer is documented.



Specialist knowledge, which usually exists only in people’s heads, is recorded and available to the organization.



Causal relations documented qualitatively can be combined with statistical analyses for cross-validation.



Organizations investing in Causal Knowledge Graphs need structured knowledge as input. Synesis provides that structure from documentary sources.



Instead of decisions based on guesswork or superficial correlations, the organization works with documented, verifiable causal relations.














Approach
Data source
Type of relation
Limitation




Traditional statistics
Numerical
Correlation
Does not tell cause from effect


Statistical causal discovery
Numerical
Causal (estimated)
Needs large volumes; may get direction wrong


Traditional qualitative research
Textual
Qualitative
Unstructured; hard to integrate


Synesis
Textual
Causal (documented)
Needs human analysis; complements statistics



The ideal combination: Synesis to structure qualitative knowledge, statistical causal discovery for numerical data, and both integrated into a Causal Knowledge Graph.




Imagine a company that wants to improve at the same time:

The success rate of sales negotiations
Employee engagement
Project delivery quality

Flow with Synesis:

Structured collection

Engagement surveys documented in Synesis
Negotiation reviews documented in Synesis
Quality reports documented in Synesis

Finding connections

Statistical discovery identifies: Engagement → Delivery Quality
Synesis documents: Teamwork → Engagement (from the literature)
Synesis documents: Delivery Quality → Client Trust (from negotiations)

Integrated graph

Teamwork → Engagement → Quality → Trust → Negotiation Success

Grounded recommendation

Investing in teamwork initiatives has a documented cascade effect up to commercial results









Pick a pilot domain — HR, operations or sales are good starting points
Define the initial vocabulary — which concepts matter for your decisions?
Train the analysts — the syntax is readable; the main effort is defining concepts well
Integrate with existing processes — Synesis complements current tools, it does not replace them
Protect data — remove personal data before using AI services





Try a small project — a literature review, a set of interviews
Focus on causal relations — always ask “what causes what?”
Stay consistent — use the same terms for the same concepts
Document your interpretations — the annotation matters as much as the quotation








No. Synesis works with qualitative knowledge and integrates with quantitative tools. It is a complement, not a substitute.



The syntax is simple and readable. Research, analysis and management professionals can learn it quickly. No programming is required.



AI systems that reason about causes need structured knowledge. Synesis helps build it from textual sources, with a trail that lets people check what the AI or the analyst recorded.



Spreadsheets have no consistency validation, do not structure causal relations natively and do not guarantee traceability. Synesis was designed for capturing causal knowledge.





In a world where decisions need to rest increasingly on data, qualitative knowledge cannot be left out. Synesis offers a bridge between expert knowledge — scattered across documents, reports and observations — and the analysis systems that support decisions.
Combining structured causal knowledge with statistical analysis is the next step in organizational intelligence: decisions based not only on data, but on a causal understanding of phenomena.

Synesis: turning scattered knowledge into actionable intelligence.

The classic example: there is a statistical correlation between chocolate consumption and the number of Nobel laureates across countries — but it would be absurd to conclude that handing out chocolate will increase an organization’s scientific output.
The real challenge is capturing causal relations, not just superficial correlations.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
Synesis is a structured language for the systematic capture of causal knowledge from documentary sources and qualitative observations.
While automated systems such as statistical causal discovery work on numerical data, much organizational knowledge is scattered across:

Reports and technical documents
Interviews and qualitative surveys
Specialized literature and manuals
Incident records and lessons learned
Engagement and organizational climate surveys

Synesis offers a standard way to extract, document and structure causal relations from these textual sources, making them processable and integrable with other analysis systems.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
When a causal relation is extracted from a document (for instance, “lack of training causes operating errors”), it is purely qualitative. There is no way to predict the probability or magnitude of the effect.
How Synesis helps: by structuring these relations systematically, they can later be integrated with numerical data to quantify causal effects.



Statistical causal discovery algorithms applied to biased or incomplete data may derive relations whose causal direction is inverted.
How Synesis helps: knowledge documented in Synesis works as prior knowledge to validate or correct statistical findings.



Traditional causal discovery works on a single dataset. It cannot combine observations from different departments, periods or conditions.
How Synesis helps: the standard structure allows knowledge from several sources to be integrated in a common vocabulary.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
Scenario: HR needs to recommend initiatives to improve engagement, but each department has different characteristics.
With Synesis:

Document causal relations from the organizational behaviour literature
Record engagement survey observations with structured interpretations
Identify which factors (career opportunities, clarity of vision, teamwork) cause which outcomes (motivation, satisfaction, retention)
Recommend initiatives based on documented evidence

SOURCE @engagement_survey_q4_2024_sales
    access_date: 2024-12-15
END SOURCE

ITEM @engagement_survey_q4_2024_sales
    quote: "I feel there are no growth opportunities for me here"
    memo: The employee expresses frustration with limited career paths and links the lack of progression to lower motivation.
    chain: lack_of_career_opportunities -> INHIBITS -> motivation
END ITEM



Scenario: an operations team needs to find root causes of failures in complex systems.
With Synesis:

Extract causal relations from technical manuals and troubleshooting guides
Document each incident with the causal chain identified
Build a knowledge base that speeds up future diagnoses

SOURCE @incident_report_2024_0892
    access_date: 2024-11-10
END SOURCE

ITEM @incident_report_2024_0892
    quote: "Intermittent disconnection during file downloads"
    memo: Pattern consistent with a MAC configuration error; reproducible under the same network conditions.
    chain: mac_configuration_error -> INHIBITS -> stable_connectivity
END ITEM



Scenario: a sales team wants to understand why some negotiations succeed and others do not.
With Synesis:

Record observations from each negotiation (meetings, objections, decisions)
Identify causal patterns between actions and results
Combine with engagement data to understand how internal factors affect external performance

SOURCE @negotiation_review_2024_156
    access_date: 2024-10-22
END SOURCE

ITEM @negotiation_review_2024_156
    quote: "The client mentioned trust in the technical team as the deciding factor"
    memo: Showing technical competence during the proposal shaped perceived trust, which in turn enabled the deal.
    chain: technical_competence -> FAVORS -> client_trust -> FAVORS -> deal_closing
END ITEM

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
SOURCE @engagement_survey_2024
    access_date: 2024-12-15
END SOURCE
All knowledge is traceable to its origin — a document, an interview, a report.



ITEM @engagement_survey_2024
    quote: "I don't know where the company is heading"
    memo: The employee expresses a lack of clarity about strategic direction
    chain: lack_of_strategic_clarity -> INHIBITS -> engagement
END ITEM
Each item connects textual evidence with your interpretation and the causal relation identified.



ONTOLOGY engagement
    description: The employee's level of commitment and emotional connection with the organization.
    group: organizational_outcomes
END ONTOLOGY

ONTOLOGY lack_of_strategic_clarity
    description: Absence of clear communication about the organization's direction, goals or vision.
    group: organizational_factors
END ONTOLOGY
Concepts are defined explicitly, keeping the project consistent over time.



The Synesis compiler:

Checks annotations against the defined model (the template)
Produces structured formats (JSON, CSV, spreadsheets)
Enables integration with analysis systems and graph databases

Field names and allowed relations are defined by the organization itself. To get started with an assistant, see the Synesis Skill for Claude Desktop; to code large volumes with AI and human review, synesis-coder.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
Every conclusion can be traced to the original evidence. When someone asks “why do you recommend this?”, the answer is documented.



Specialist knowledge, which usually exists only in people’s heads, is recorded and available to the organization.



Causal relations documented qualitatively can be combined with statistical analyses for cross-validation.



Organizations investing in Causal Knowledge Graphs need structured knowledge as input. Synesis provides that structure from documentary sources.



Instead of decisions based on guesswork or superficial correlations, the organization works with documented, verifiable causal relations.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
Imagine a company that wants to improve at the same time:

The success rate of sales negotiations
Employee engagement

Flow with Synesis:

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
Pick a pilot domain — HR, operations or sales are good starting points
Define the initial vocabulary — which concepts matter for your decisions?
Train the analysts — the syntax is readable; the main effort is defining concepts well
Integrate with existing processes — Synesis complements current tools, it does not replace them
Protect data — remove personal data before using AI services





Try a small project — a literature review, a set of interviews
Focus on causal relations — always ask “what causes what?”
Stay consistent — use the same terms for the same concepts
Document your interpretations — the annotation matters as much as the quotation

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
No. Synesis works with qualitative knowledge and integrates with quantitative tools. It is a complement, not a substitute.



The syntax is simple and readable. Research, analysis and management professionals can learn it quickly. No programming is required.



AI systems that reason about causes need structured knowledge. Synesis helps build it from textual sources, with a trail that lets people check what the AI or the analyst recorded.



Spreadsheets have no consistency validation, do not structure causal relations natively and do not guarantee traceability. Synesis was designed for capturing causal knowledge.

title: 1 Synesis: Structuring Knowledge for Data-Driven Decisions
text:
In a world where decisions need to rest increasingly on data, qualitative knowledge cannot be left out. Synesis offers a bridge between expert knowledge — scattered across documents, reports and observations — and the analysis systems that support decisions.
Combining structured causal knowledge with statistical analysis is the next step in organizational intelligence: decisions based not only on data, but on a causal understanding of phenomena.

Synesis: turning scattered knowledge into actionable intelligence.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
synesis-coder automates qualitative coding with a language model (Claude by default, or any server compatible with the OpenAI API). The tool reads your project template (.synt) and generates valid Synesis blocks (SOURCE, ITEM, ONTOLOGY) following the fields, relations, allowed values and instructions (GUIDELINES) of the template.
Use this guide if you:

want to code a passage selected in a .syn file
need to batch-process a corpus of abstracts (.bib) or records (.toml)
want to code a long document (interview, report)
need definitions for the concepts already used in the corpus
want to review what the AI annotated before accepting it







Nothing is hardcoded



synesis-coder knows no field name, relation or value. Everything comes from the template, read by the compiler. Change the template and the AI follows the new rules.








The AI proposes, the compiler checks, you decide



Compiling without errors shows that the form is right, not that the reading is. Review what was generated (Section 11). Data sent to the model leaves your computer, unless the model runs locally.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
2.1 Configuration
Create a .env file in the project folder (from where you run the commands):
# Anthropic (default)
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=sk-ant-...

# Optional: language of free-text fields
SYNESIS_CODER_LANGUAGE=en

# Optional: another model (default: claude-opus-4-6)
# SYNESIS_CODER_MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-6
For a server compatible with the OpenAI API (local Ollama, OpenRouter, RunPod…):
SYNESIS_CODER_BACKEND=openai
SYNESIS_CODER_API_URL=http://localhost:11434
SYNESIS_CODER_MODEL=model-name
# SYNESIS_CODER_API_KEY=...   # not needed for local Ollama
Precedence is: environment variable > project .env > defaults file named by SYNESIS_CODER_ENV_FILE. Never commit the .env.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
5.1 Output Layout
By default everything goes to a single annotations.syn. For large campaigns pick one of:







Option
Result




--per-reference
one .syn per reference (easier to review and redo)


--split-every 100
annotations_0001.syn, annotations_0002.syn… with 100 references each



If annotations.syn already exists, use --overwrite or --backup.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
5.2 Long Campaigns
synesis-coder abstract --project p.synp --input refs.bib --output-dir out/ \
  --per-reference --resume --batch-size 25 --cooldown auto

--resume skips what was already annotated successfully in the output folder; failed records are redone
--batch-size processes in batches; between them the project is reloaded and the concepts already generated enter the context
--cooldown sets the pause between batches (auto, seconds or 0)

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
8.1 How the File Is Updated

The .syno is edited block by block: an existing block receives only the generated fields; comments, other fields and order are left as they were
--update generates only what is missing: concepts without a block and absent required fields
Ontology CODE and CHAIN fields are structure and are not generated by this mode; labels (ROLE LABEL) are left to the synonyms phase
Use --backup to keep a copy, --prompt-only to see the prompt

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
section: 8.2 Rejected Blocks Do Not Contaminate the .syno
text:
8.2 Rejected Blocks Do Not Contaminate the .syno
A block that still fails validation after the correction attempts goes to a separate file (ontology.syno.rejected). The .syno stays compilable.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
8.3 Structured Generation (JSON Schema)
When the model supports structured output, synesis-coder asks only for the field values, with a JSON Schema derived from the template, and assembles the block in code. This removes syntax errors by construction. Without support the tool uses free text; compiler validation is the same.
The template needs at least one SCOPE ONTOLOGY field.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
11.1 critique: Propose
A model rereads each ITEM against the source text and the template.
synesis-coder critique annotations/interview_01.syn --project nave.synp \
  --sensitivity standard

critique mode options






Option
Description




--sensitivity
lenient, standard (default), strict or a number from 0 to 1


--output
path of the .synr


--model
critic model (SYNESIS_CODER_CRITIQUE_MODEL)


--concurrent, --debug
execution



High sensitivity produces more false positives, not more truth. The critique can use another connection (SYNESIS_CODER_CRITIQUE_BACKEND, _API_URL, _API_KEY), which reduces the bias of a generator judging itself.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
11.2 normalize: Canonicalize Codes
Looks at the whole corpus and unifies variants (Social_Acceptance, social_acceptance, SocialAcceptance).
synesis-coder normalize annotations/*.synr --project social_acceptance.synp \
  --confidence 0.65 --inventory code_inventory.txt

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
11.3 incorporate: Accept
Applies the .synr and writes the validated final .syn. No AI: deterministic and repeatable.
synesis-coder incorporate annotations/interview_01.synr \
  --output annotations/interview_01_final.syn
An ambiguous correction is refused, not guessed. Use --backup when the target already exists.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
11.4 refine: Re-extract (Optional)
Instead of applying point corrections, re-extracts the flagged ITEMs with the critique in context. It only accepts a version with a lower suspicion score.
synesis-coder refine annotations/interview_01.syn --project nave.synp --max-iter 2
Default output: <name>_refined.syn. The input file is never overwritten without --overwrite.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
11.5 Recommended Order
synesis-coder anchor      annotations/annotations.syn --project study.synp   # 1. free
synesis-coder critique    annotations/annotations.syn --project study.synp   # 2. propose
#                         (read the .synr)                                   # 3. decide
synesis-coder normalize   annotations/annotations.synr --project study.synp  # 4. canonicalize
synesis-coder incorporate annotations/annotations.synr \
              --output annotations/final.syn --backup                        # 5. accept
synesis compile study.synp                                                   # 6. compile
Step 3 is not decoration: the .synr is readable text, made for you to decide what enters your data.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
12.1 suggest: Suggest Codes
Returns project codes relevant to a passage, without generating a block. Codes that do not exist yet are marked [NEW].
synesis-coder suggest --project social_acceptance.synp \
  --text "Local ownership models significantly reduce opposition."

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
12.2 finetune: Prepare Training Data
Generates or enriches an Alpaca JSONL.
synesis-coder finetune --project social_acceptance.synp \
  --output enriched_dataset.jsonl --enrich vary --enrich didactic



--enrich
Effect




vary (default)
variations of wording


didactic
versions with explanation


counterfactual
counterexamples









Relation qualifiers



Pairs generated from the project do not carry the qualifier of a BUNDLE with a CHAIN (for instance a “hypothetical” status). For a faithful dataset, declare the composition in an EXPORT ALPACA block with MAP and pass that JSONL to --input.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
16.1 synesis-coder Not Found
The executable is not on PATH. Check with pip show synesis-coder, use python -m synesis_coder or set the path in the extension.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
text:
16.2 Missing API Key
Create the .env in the folder the command runs from, or export the variable. A .env next to the installation is not read.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
section: 16.3 Warning About a Field Without GUIDELINES
text:
16.3 Warning About a Field Without GUIDELINES
The model receives only the DESCRIPTION (or nothing) for that field. Write the instructions in the template.

title: synesis-coder: AI-Assisted Qualitative Coding
section: 16.4 The Model Cannot Produce a Valid Block
text:
16.4 The Model Cannot Produce a Valid Block
After the attempts the block is recorded as a failure (in ontology mode, in the .rejected file). Read the compiler message, revise the GUIDELINES of the field involved and run again (--resume in abstract mode).

title: 1 The Compilation Flow
text:
1 The Compilation Flow
Compilation in Synesis happens in phases, ensuring the formal and conceptual integrity of the body of knowledge.
In the syntactic phase, the compiler checks that blocks are properly opened and closed and that each file follows the grammar of the language.
Then comes the semantic and linking validation. The compiler checks that:

items are associated with declared sources, and sources with the bibliography;
the fields used exist in the template, in the right scope, with the declared type and requirement;
fields grouped in a BUNDLE appear paired;
codes used in items have a concept defined in the ontology;
chain relations are the declared ones and arity is respected;
the hierarchy and the labels of the organizing model are consistent (when there are ROLE lines).

All these criteria — field names, types, requirements and relation rules — come from the template file, which users adapt to their methodological parameters. The order of fields inside a block is free.
This layered process ensures that outputs are structurally sound and that the body of knowledge stays consistent and computationally reliable. It does not judge the reading: whether the source supports what was annotated is the researcher’s call.
